en: The *Keshi* (Excerpts from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), Scroll One (Part One of the Upper).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty by imperial decree;
the Sramana Fuxian of Western Shu established the topical outline (*ke*) for the Great Master.
Disciple: Zhìyī Xuědūn. Supplement to the Omissions. △ Seventh:
Separate Explanation of Textual Meaning Following the Ancients, divided into three parts. First: "Radiating Light to Set Out:

Questions and Answers on the Wisdom-Sphere, Instantly Revealing the Beginning and End" (i.e., the first, the Introduction Chapter). Second: "Relying on Recent Traces to Bestow Transformation, Opening up the Provisional and Revealing the Real," causing [beings] to...
1. The Section on Awakening to the Gate of the One Vehicle (from the "Expedient Means" chapter to the "Dharma Master" chapter constitutes the Main Body). 2.

The Section on Opening the Near to Reveal the Far, Erasing Traces to Enter Reality, and Causing Widespread Circulation (from the "Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" chapter to the end of the sutra, comprising eighteen chapters, constitutes the Dissemination Section).
The Preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter One.

The preface is divided into the sections on "Certified Faith" (*śraddhā*) and "Initiation" (*nidāna*), both of which serve to clarify the scope of the main teaching (*samyak-śāsana*). Regarding the term "chapter" (*pin*):
the Sanskrit word is *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter. It refers to a collection of items belonging to the same category gathered together in one place; hence it is called a "chapter."

Since this marks the beginning of all chapters, it is called "The First. The text has two parts: first, the testimony of faith; second, the introduction. Within the first part, there are again two sections:
first, the five phrases of testimony of faith; second, the listing of the assembly as testimony of faith. This is the first [section].
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

These five phrases at the beginning of the sūtra all serve as a certification of faith. This is because they possess the three meanings of severing doubt, quelling dispute, and distinguishing the heterodox.

As cited from ancient sources, the reason the Venerable Ānanda was able to compile the teachings was that he first attained the *dharmatā-bodhi-svatantra-rāja-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Awakening to the Nature of Reality),
and finally, after receiving his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he was able to fully penetrate the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable Buddhas of the past and present.
The initial statement "Thus" (*evam*) refers collectively to the dharmas of the secret prediction, which are free from doubt.

The opening word "Thus" (evam) serves to establish faith. It means that when the Venerable One was at the time of the Council, he held up what had been maintained by his own mind in the past and pointed it out, saying, "It is thus.
From the moment he first received this sublime Dharma, it has all shone clearly within the ocean of his mind;
nothing was omitted and nothing was forgotten. Therefore, it is called "thus. If one speaks of "faith" according to the core principle of the Sūtras:

Because words that accord with principle correspond to that principle, they are called "as-it-is" (*tathatā*). Thus, the single term "as-it-is" encompasses both the signifier and the signified, as well as both principle and phenomena.

"Principle" refers to the underlying logic; it is not limited solely to True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Is" (*iti*) means that the mind and its object are in perfect correspondence, free from doubt or error; it is a term for profound faith.
Regarding "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), there are two ways to understand it in terms of direct reception: 1. [The first is] by way of personal realization. By...
This is the "Certification of Faith" (*saddharmapratyaya*). It means that the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas is precious precisely because it can be transmitted; therefore, this is explained next.
"I" refers to Ānanda speaking of himself. "Hearing" points directly to his own faculty of the ear.

Thus, with the "True Self" (*bhūta-ātman*) that transcends both self and non-self, he employs the mouth to conform to worldly convention and the mind to create the wondrous "Self" of the true realm, utilizing the hearing-faculty and its object—which are neither identical nor different—to hear.

This is what is heard regarding the non-identity and non-difference between the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses. "At one time" (ekasmin samaye) is a threefold expression used to certify and inspire faith through a favorable occasion.
In Sanskrit, *kalpa* is translated as "time-period" (*shifen*). However, time has no separate substantial entity; it is provisionally established based upon phenomena.

If one were to depart from its basis, the substance of time could not be found. Now, following worldly convention, we say that "one time" exists. The term "one" serves to distinguish [it from others].
Regarding "at another time": the occasions when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma were immeasurable, so they cannot be cited individually; therefore, it is simply said to be "one.
This was the time when the Dharma King inaugurated his auspicious reign, which may also be called the time when the capacity of the disciples and the teaching met in resonance.

As for "Buddha," this refers to the fourth [element] concerning the teacher who inspires faith. The full term is *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*). Furthermore, its meaning includes...
Threefold: first, self-awakening (*svabodha*), which refers to awakening simultaneously to both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), like waking from a dream or the blooming of a lotus;

this distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Second, awakening others (*parabodha*), which distinguishes him from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Third, full awakening (*paripūrṇabodha*), which distinguishes him from bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, being free from mind is called self-awakening; being free from form is called awakening others; being free from both form and mind is called full awakening. These constitute [the basis for] the ten titles [of the Buddha].

This is the title "The Three Awakenings Perfectly Illuminated. However, although the Buddha-body was already clarified within the arising of the preceding teachings, since the Buddha is now the Teacher, it should be briefly restated.
This is because the scriptures contain two distinct aspects before and after [the teaching].
For the bodies perceived by the śrāvakas prior to their realization were inferior, being like those who have cast off fine robes and put on tattered rags.
Regarding transformation (*nirmāṇa*): after one has attained understanding and resolution, one ought to perceive something extraordinary and superior, distinct from what came before.
Yet, alas, there is no explicit teaching regarding a patriarch who, having entrusted his family estate to his heir, subsequently cast off his worn-out garments to don those of a sovereign.

Because the disease of cataracts is removed, the delusional flowers vanish of their own accord; thus, one attains further awakening to the realization that this Buddha is precisely the Buddha of one’s own mind (*cittamaya-buddha*), in its entirety.
Because the Great Essence (tǐdà) is that which manifests through its Great Function (yòng), this Essence is revealed by means of its Function; it is thus an inconceivable and wondrous transformation.
"Residing at Rājagṛha" and below refer to the places where the teaching was verified and authenticated. As for "Rājagṛha":

formerly, King Ṛṣabha ruled over a thousand kings who together established a city there and made their capital among the Five Mountains, thereby forming a great kingdom; thus, the place is named after the person.

Gṛdhrakūṭa is the territory to which it belongs; therefore, it is preceded by the name Rājagṛha. Gṛdhrakūṭa means "Vulture Peak" in this language, so called because the shape of the peak resembles a vulture.
It is called "sacred" (ling) because former Buddhas and the present Buddha have all dwelt together here.

After a Buddha passes away, Arhats reside there; when the Dharma perishes, Cakravartin kings reside there; and when even they depart, spirits and deities reside there. Therefore, it is popularly called...

Regarding "Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) and "dwelling": the Tathāgata internally dwells in the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*, wherein he encompasses the *Anantārthaviṣaya-samādhi*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, and others, all of which enter therein. He manifests in accordance with the capacities of beings.
Externally, he dwells on Gṛdhrakūṭa through his physical form and dignified deportment. Based on these five points, it is said: "Thus [have I heard]. This constitutes one section.

The *Saddharma* (Wondrous Dharma). All of these were personally heard by me from the Buddha. At the time when the relationship between teacher and disciple was in harmony, we were dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain.
II. Listing the Assembly to Certify the Faith, in two parts: first, listing the assembly; second, the general conclusion.

In the first part, there are four sections: first, the Śrāvakas; second, the Bodhisattvas; third, the three divisions [of the Vinaya]; fourth, the kings and their subjects. In the first of these, there are two sub-sections: first, praising their virtues.
Second, the listing of names. Now, for the first part:
"Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus... who had exhausted all fetters of existence and attained mastery of mind.
"Together" (yǔ) means accompanying. "Great" (dà) refers to one whose capacity and measure are revered, and who is attended by great beings such as celestial kings and human kings.
Reverence. Because there is the Great Way. In the Sanskrit language, *bhikṣu* is sometimes translated as "remover of poverty" (*chujin*).

This means that sentient beings, having meager merit, lack the means in their causal state to sustain themselves and thus obtain retribution; they suffer from much want and deprivation. As for those who have left the household life...

The practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). It is capable of eliminating the famine of cause and effect. Some say it has no direct equivalent [in Chinese], because the term contains three meanings:
first, the destruction of evil; second, the terrifying of Māras; and third, the mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Fearing that selecting only one would lose the others, the Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is used;

this is translated as "harmonious assembly" (*hehé zhòng*). This means that in terms of activity there is harmony and no separate groups, and in terms of Dharma there is harmony and no separate principles.
Furthermore, it is by receiving the bhikṣu precepts that one first attains the name "bhikṣu.

Because these disciplinary laws constitute the primary cause for the initial emergence from suffering, the person is designated first by the dharma; thus, there are twelve thousand [bhikṣus]. As for the arhats:

Some say there is a translation for this term, rendering it as "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), and also as "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). This is because within the realm of desire, the death and rebirth of the fragmented body has already been exhausted;
since reality is fully realized and delusions are eradicated, there is nothing further to learn. Others say there is no direct translation, for the name itself contains three meanings:
first, "slayer of thieves. These "thieves" refer to the two types of afflictions—conceptual and innate—that exist within the realm of desire and are capable of plundering sentient beings.

The wealth of merit and Dharma robs the life-force of wisdom. Because a bhikṣu, during the causal stage, is able to "slay" this [defilement] through concentration and wisdom, the fruit of Arhatship is called "Slaying the Foe.
Second, regarding the term "Non-arising": this is the title for the fruit of a bhikṣu’s terrifying of Māra.
When Māra sees that [the being] will not arise again, he is filled with great anxiety and fear, fearing that he might once more transform others; thus, the realm of Māra becomes empty and void.

Third, "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) is the fruit-title of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Because he possesses the merits of wisdom and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), he is worthy of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for humans and devas;
hence, he is called "Worthy of Offerings. Regarding "all outflows" (*āsrava*): "outflows" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*); though their names differ, their substance is one.
These consist of the twenty-six dharmas, such as the root and secondary afflictions. For now, we shall take the "outflows" to represent the seeds, and the "afflictions" to represent...
When the seeds of active manifestation are exhausted, there will no longer be any disturbance from their active functioning. This is also the meaning of "slaying the thief" and attaining the goal.
Since the causes and effects of the three realms are all termed "other," while wisdom, abandonment, and merit are all termed "self," one has now already attained one's own benefit;
this is also the meaning of being "worthy of offerings. Once the fetters of existence are exhausted, then...
When conditioned liberation is attained and conditioned wisdom is perfected, one realizes the unconditioned and thereby realizes unconditioned liberation.

Since there are no longer any fetters or bonds, the mind attains sovereignty; this is precisely the state of a *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) liberated from doubt, which is also the meaning of non-arising.
△ Second, the enumeration of names has two parts: first, the bhikṣus; second, the bhikṣuṇīs. Regarding the first, there are two [subsections].

First, those with many acquaintances; second, those with few acquaintances. Regarding the first, there are two parts: first, listing the names of the leaders; second, a general summary. Now, for the first:
their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya (up to) Subhūti, Ānanda, and Rāhula.
"Ājñāta" is his name; it means "one who has known. To have "known" does not mean to have no knowledge at all, but rather to know that there is nothing [to be grasped].
It is named for having known the True Reality (satya) by means of the wisdom of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna). "Kauṇḍinya" is his clan name; it means "fire-vessel."

His ancestors worshipped fire, and from this he was named for his clan. Because fire possesses two meanings—illumining darkness and not burning things when not ignited—they practiced false calculations, believing that by worshipping it they could transcend birth and death. He was also called Śākyamuni;
having heard the Dharma and attained the Way, he stands foremost among all humans, devas, and those of the Two Vehicles, and is the eldest son of the Buddha. Mahākāśyapa...
Master Ye said: "Mahākāśyapa is so called because the radiance of his body can absorb and eclipse the light of the sun and moon. The Āgama states:
"In Rājagṛha there was a wealthy householder named Kāviya; his wife was named Dhanā, and his son was named Pipphala."
The son’s wife was named Bhadrā. Her family was a thousand times more prosperous than King Bimbisāra’s, and there were no neighboring states equal to the sixteen great kingdoms.
Pippala is the name of a tree; because the Venerable One was born after praying to that tree, he was named accordingly.

*Mahā* is a Sanskrit term containing three meanings—great (*mahat*), many (*bahu*), and excellent (*praśasta*). Thus, among the five reasons for not translating (the *pañca-anuvāda*), this is an instance of "not translating due to multiple meanings" (*anekārtha-anuvāda*).
It is a translation. Because the lineage of Kāśyapa is the most numerous, the term *mahā* (great) is prefixed to distinguish it from other clans.
He was able to practice the dhūta ascetic practices and was renowned as the foremost in superior conduct. Uruvilvā means "Papaya Grove"; Gayā means "City."
The Nadi river and the Yūn (Hiraṇyavatī) river; the names of these three individuals were all established based on their respective places of residence. Śāriputra is fully called Śāriputra;
"Śāri" means śārikā, which refers to the hundred-tongued bird, also known as the spring wagtail.
Because the mother’s eyes were as clear and sharp as that bird, and "putra" means son, he was named after his mother and thus called Śāriputra, or the Son of the Śārikā.
Furthermore, it is said that Śāriputra is so called because this woman possessed an excellent physical form, and he was born from her body; thus he is called "Body-Son" (Śāriputra).
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, his wisdom is inexhaustible, and he is foremost in resolving all doubts. Mahāmaudgalyāyana says, "He is of the clan of those who gather beans."
In ancient times there was an immortal who dwelt in the mountains and ate beans; his mother was of that same lineage. *Jianyu* (揀餘) says he was called "Great" (*Da*).
*Zengyi Ahan Jing* (增一阿含經) says his supernatural powers allowed him to fly lightly, making him the foremost among those who could travel to the ten directions.

*Mahākātyāyana* (摩訶迦旃延) says he was "Ornamented by Letters" (*Wenshi*); he was skilled in debate and the most eminent among those who expounded the path of the teachings. *Aniruddha* (阿㝹樓陀) says he was "Free from Poverty" (*Wu Pin*). [He surpassed others...]
In the final dharma period of the Buddha Puṣya, he once offered a single meal of millet to a pratyekabuddha.

As a result, for ninety-one kalpas, throughout the heavens and among humans, his wealth and treasures were inexhaustible. Furthermore, because he had lost his sight due to his diligent practice, the Buddha instructed him to focus his mindfulness to seek the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Thereupon, the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the four great elements emerged from half his head; with this clarity, he could perceive both light and darkness across the great trichiliocosm.
He was like one looking at fruit in the palm of his hand; he was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Kapphiṇa means "the constellation Rohiṇī";
he was so named because he was born due to prayers offered to the constellation Rohiṇī, and he was also skilled in calculating the stars and foremost in clearly understanding diagrams and prophecies.

Gavāmpati means "the rumination ox"; because he had previously been a bull king, his residual habits constantly manifested as a habit of empty belching, hence the name. Furthermore, it was because he avoided people...
Mockery invites transgression. He constantly dwells in the heavens and receives the foremost of celestial offerings. Revata (Lípóduō) means "Far-Reaching";
he is foremost in skillfully entering meditative concentration with a mind that never falters or becomes confused.

Piṇḍola-bharadvāja (Bílíngjiāpócuō) refers to "Residual Habits," because having long been a Brahmin in the past, the habit of arrogance still manifests within the fruits of his present life. Bakula (Bó-jūluó).
Suyāma (Cloud-like Fine Appearance) was of upright and majestic countenance and lived for one hundred and sixty years.

Because he had once offered a single *harītakī* fruit in a previous life, he remained free from illness and untimely death in this present life; he always delighted in solitary dwelling as his foremost practice.
Mahākauṣṭhila (Great Thigh) was so named because the bones of his knees were large and thick. He was also called the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail), due to [his study of] the eighteen...
According to various sutras, he did not have the leisure to trim his nails. Nanda is said to mean "cowherd" and also "well-pleased";

he was given this name because he aspired to the Way, hence the prefix "well. Sundarananda—*Sundara* meaning "lovely" or "beloved," referring to his wife's name, and *Nanda* meaning "joy," referring to his own name—is so named by combining his wife’s name with his own to distinguish him from the cowherd Nanda.
Pūrṇa means "Full. Maitrāyanī is the name of his mother, meaning "Compassionate. *Nī* is a general term for a woman in India.
Because he received his name from both his father and mother, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. He was foremost in preaching the Dharma.
Subhūti means "Born of Emptiness," having received this name because at the time of his birth all the storehouses were empty; he was one who understood emptiness.

First, Ānanda is called "Joyful" because he was born on the day the Buddha attained the Way; as his fame spread throughout the entire kingdom, he became renowned for being foremost among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*).
Rāhula is called "Obstruction" (*āvṛti*): one reason is that in a former life he blocked a mouse hole, and another is that he failed to look after a brahmin for six days;
consequently, he received the retribution of remaining in the womb for six years, and thus he is named "The Secret One" (*Guhyaka*) due to this obstruction.

First, regarding the practice: Chenyu says that when Ānanda heard the Dharma, he was still a learner (*śaikṣa*), but at the time of the council, he first realized the state of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).
He is now listed among the Arhats. Rāhula’s rank was that of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), yet he had already realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
he is now listed among the great bhikṣus. This is because these two individuals were well-known to the assembly. Second, the general conclusion.
Regarding these great arhats known by all, they are called "known" (*jñāta*) because their names and virtues are praised upon hearing them;
they are called "recognized" (*vijñāta*) because one sees their forms and receives their instructions. Because those who know and recognize them are many, they are said to be "known by the multitude.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of those who know and recognize them: namely, the instructor (*śāstṛ*), the fellow practitioner (*sahāyaka*), and the external protector (*parigrahaka*). △
Second, those with limited knowledge.
Furthermore, there were two thousand individuals, both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), consisting of those in the three fruits and four stages of approach.
Those who possess true qualities yet must further investigate, and who possess afflictions yet must sever, are called learners. Fourth, the [stage of] Arhat...

The fruit of Arhatship: when truth is thoroughly realized and delusions are exhausted, one is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Ancient commentators claim that this [term] merely cites the title and numerical category of the stage without praising its virtues;
therefore, it is termed "one with little knowledge. In reality, there is no fundamental distinction between the noble and the ordinary regarding whether one possesses much or little knowledge.

It is only for those who aspire to the lofty and admire the distant that the term "much knowledge" is used to attract them, while for those who conceal their names and hide their virtues, the term "little knowledge" is applied.
I shall cite a small portion of it. One must certainly not lose sight of the fundamental principle because of the traces of quantity.
△ Second, the bhikṣuṇīs:
from "The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī" (until) "also together with her retinue."
Mahāprajāpatī is called "Great Path of Love" (Dà àidào) and also "Gautamī.

She is known as the Leader of the Nuns and was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Because she was able to transcend her delicate physical nature through profound insight, she was the first to ascend the shore of enlightenment.
She was named Mahāprajāpatī. Furthermore, because she followed the path her predecessors had sought and emulated their example, she was called the "Leader of the Assembly.
In the fourteenth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, she requested to leave the household life. The Buddha did not grant her permission. Ānanda made three requests on her behalf;

the Buddha then instructed Ānanda to convey the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), saying that if she could practice them, she might be allowed to go forth. She replied, "I can practice them."
Thus she was permitted [to ordain]. Yaśodharā—also called Yashas—is so named because, while living as a laywoman, she was the wife of a bodhisattva;
having renounced the world, she became the leader of the community of nuns and realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), thereby earning the title of "Renown" (Yaśas).

△ Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas has two parts: first, the designation of their names and the enumeration of their number; second, the praise of their virtues and the listing of their names. Now, the first:
eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
In full, one should say *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*. Now, we take this in brief:
*bodhi* means "path" (*mārga*), *sattva* means "mind" (*citta*), and *mahā* means "great. Thus, it is the "Great Path-Mind. Regarding the ancient interpretation:
*bodhi* is named the "Buddha-path," and *sattva* is named "accomplishing sentient beings"; this refers to accomplishing sentient beings by means of the Buddha-path. Furthermore, *bodhi*...
"Ti" (提) refers to practice for one's own benefit; "sattva" (薩埵) refers to practice for the benefit of others. Among those of a similar class to the Bodhisattvas, there were eighty thousand.

Part Two: Praising Their Virtues and Listing Their Names. This has two sections: first, praising their virtues; second, listing their names. The first section [praising virtues] further has two parts:
first, a general praise; second, a specific praise. Now, the first [the general praise]:
All have become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

*An* means "none" (*na*); *uttara* means "above" (*upari*); *samyak* means "correct" (*samyak*) or "universal" (*samanta*); *saṃ* means "equal" (*sama*) or "thorough" (*vyāpta*); *bodhi* means "awakening" (*bodha*).
Combined, it is called "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Awakening. This is the fruit toward which Bodhisattvas aspire through their practice.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression prior to completion, which refers to Bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*);

second, non-retrogression upon completion, which refers to those from the first to the seventh stages (*bhūmi*); and third, ultimate non-retrogression, which refers to those from the eighth stage upward.
As the subsequent text states: "When wisdom reaches the other shore, it is the pinnacle of all pinnacles; one thereby attains non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed enlightenment."
△ Second, the specific praise has two parts: first, making offerings to all Buddhas; second, extensively benefiting all sentient beings. Now, the first part:
they have all attained *dhāraṇī* and the eloquence of joyful speech (up to) being constantly praised by all Buddhas.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). It refers to the ability to maintain all wholesome dharmas so that they are neither forgotten nor lost.
Furthermore, it maintains the wholesome so they are not lost, and maintains [the restraint against] the unwholesome so they do not arise. There are three types:

first, *śrutadhāraṇī* (retention through hearing), which means that regarding all speech and dharmas, whatever is heard by the ear is never forgotten or lost; second, *vibhaṅga-dhāraṇī* (retention through discernment)...
All sentient beings and all phenomena are distinguished without error. Third is the entry into sounds:
regarding hearing insults or praise, one feels neither joy nor anger, for one has deeply penetrated the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all forms and sounds.
Furthermore, there are four kinds, namely the four *dhāraṇīs* of dharma, meaning, incantation, and patience. Eloquence in joyful exposition is the fourth.
The first of the unimpeded eloquences is also called the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s internal clarity of wisdom and external skillful eloquence regarding phenomena, their meanings, verbal expressions, and the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings, such that they accord with whatever [beings] wish to hear.
He then expounded it for them, causing each to rejoice. He turned the non-retrogressive wheel. "Wheel" carries the sense of turning as well as the sense of crushing and grinding.

As for "turning": having already crushed one's own hindrances, one further eliminates the afflictions of others, proceeding until all have reached the state of non-retrogression before finally ceasing.
Internally relying on *dhāraṇī* and externally employing eloquence (*pratibhāna*), one turns the wheel of non-retrogression;
this is precisely "first using the gift of Dharma to encompass the gift of material wealth," thereby making offerings to many Buddhas above.

Below these Buddhas, by not departing from the bodhicitta, one makes offerings above while transforming those below, thereby supporting the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, one plants the roots of all virtues; the root of virtue is none other than bodhi.
It is the mind. Because its fundamental virtue is perfected, it attains accord with the Buddha-mind and is praised by all Buddhas.
△ Second, extensively benefiting all sentient beings.
Cultivating the body through loving-kindness, one skillfully enters the Buddha’s wisdom (up to) being able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.

By means of the compassion of shared essence (*sārvakāyika-maitrī*), one perfumes and cultivates the three karmas, thereby accomplishing the three forms of non-protection (*trirakṣa*). It is precisely by means of these unimpeded three karmas that [one acts].
Discerning the dharmas corresponds to the faculties; it perfectly accords with great expedient means. Therefore, it is said that he "skillfully enters the Buddha’s wisdom.

When heavy obstructions are removed and great wisdom manifests, it is called "penetrating understanding. Raising the wind-sail of *prajñā*, he crosses the bitter sea of afflictions and reaches the enlightened shore of the three virtues.
As his sublime virtue flourishes, his excellent reputation also spreads far and wide; thus, his name is heard everywhere.

There is the "perfectly luminous intention," which is precisely that tenth [perfection], the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Regarding the "power of speech through patience":

because patience distinguishes between the arising of phenomena, it specifically highlights those instances of verbal abuse and physical assault, as these constitute the coarsest forms of conduct within the category of patience.

Thus, they are singled out. In the verses on meditation (*dhyāna*), the ancients said: "To abandon frivolous laughter is to eliminate the hindrance of restlessness and regret; to abandon deluded attachments..."
This belongs to the removal of the hindrance of ill-will; the removal of distraction dispels the hindrance of desire; and the gathering of mindfulness removes the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
Once these five hindrances are removed, that which is sought can be swiftly attained. Even if one passes through billions of years, it would not equal a single moment of the radiance of light.
This is because the spiritual power within that light gathers the nine periods of time and returns them to a single thought-moment. Suppose, by means of the radiance of light, [it were otherwise]...

Knowing this for a long time, he further develops the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) by means of light. The next five verses concern the fourfold offerings to the Triple Gem. Regarding the subsequent wisdom:
because the Dharma is fundamentally without words, it is called "quiescent" (*śānta*). Yet, being wordless does not obstruct speech; thus it can be described.
It is like an empty valley that has no sound, yet does not prevent echoes from pervading the world. This is due to its nature...

Because they are identical in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one can observe water becoming ice; because characteristics are identical to nature (*svabhāva*), there are no two distinct characteristics, and thus ice becomes water.
The preceding verse concerned the object of observation (*ālambana*), whereas this concerns the observing wisdom (*jñāna*).

As for the term "non-attachment": because nature is identical to characteristics, nature is detached; because characteristics are identical to nature, characteristics are detached. Since they have been dissolved by sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), [there is non-attachment].
"Without attachment. This verse may also be understood as applying doubly to the three preceding points.

Because one does not give rise to craving for dharmas regarding either the teachings expounded or the objects contemplated, it is called "non-attachment. Within the seven verses on *nirvāṇa*, there are two kinds of relics (*śarīra*).

The first is the physical body (*janmakāya*). That which is obtained through cremation after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa was originally accomplished by being perfumed with the five kinds of sublime incense;
therefore, it causes anyone who makes an offering to it to first obtain the reward of being reborn in the heavens a thousand times.
Ultimately, one attains the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. Second is the *dharmakāya* śarīra, which refers to the sūtras.
Although the physical body (*janmakāya*) truly arises from the *dharmakāya*, for the present, we shall speak of them collectively in terms of making offerings.
The following six verses clarify that this person has planted superior causes in past lives and now encounters the most supreme field of merit; therefore, they do not begrudge their home.
Precious offerings were extensively presented. Since the stūpas and temples he had constructed were already numerous, their height and breadth were now doubled;
both internally and externally they were adorned with various jewels, such that the eight classes of beings all rose to offer worship.
The realm was quite extraordinary compared to ordinary places, like the King of Trees, the *pārijāta*, in the celestial realms when its flowers bloom, manifesting the wonders of the heavenly world.
Excellent! Even more extraordinary. △ Third, praising the rarity of the light:
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light, I and the assembly [hear]... emitting a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands."
The first verse provides a general indication of what is seen within the light. The subsequent statement concerns the extraordinariness of that which illuminates;
it truly arises from the rarity of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, from a single pure light, immeasurable lands are illuminated, causing those in the Dharma assembly who are in places beyond sight or hearing to see and hear, and those in places beyond cognition or perception to [perceive].
"Perception. This indicates that although the preceding passage appears to inquire about the object illuminated, it actually inquires about the light that illuminates.
△ Fourth, resolving difficulties and initiating questions.
"We have seen this which we have never before encountered" (up to) "we gaze upon you, O Benevolent One; what do you intend to preach?
The first half-verse concludes the preceding section, while the latter half initiates the subsequent one, requesting a resolution for the four verses that follow.

According to the ancient commentaries, Mañjuśrī’s four types of "subdued challenges" (*vighāta*) refer to the difficulties he formulates within his own mind, of which there are three intentions: first, this auspicious omen...
How rare! One must not hastily pass judgment. Second, his ocean-like assembly of wisdom humbly defers to the exalted.

Third, because he was firm and hesitant, the assembly gave rise to deep longing; thus, he met their challenges with silence to resist them, while Maitreya clearly elucidated the resolution of those difficulties.
There are three reasons for this intention: first, the omen is great and the doubt is profound; if not resolved in advance, it may hinder the formal exposition.

Second, although the assembly of wise ones is vast, the capacity for understanding rests with you, O Benevolent One. Third, the entire assembly gazes upon you, and their earnest expectation is most weighty.

Therefore, to manifest the resolution of these difficulties and fulfill the request for a timely response, he first addresses the objection by addressing the host of the inquiry: "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī."
"I pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly. Mañjuśrī remained as he was and first posed this challenge: "You speak of the 'doubts of the assembly,' yet the assembly has never doubted.
If they were in doubt, they should have asked; since the assembly does not doubt, what is there for me to resolve? Maitreya then explained with the first verse:
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, Gazing upon you and me. They look to me because they wish to ask me; They gaze upon you [for the answer]."
Desiring to receive an answer from the Benevolent One, Mañjuśrī thereupon raised a second objection, saying: "Since the assembly has doubts, it will not be easy to provide an answer;
wait until the Buddha emerges from his meditative absorption, and then you may answer. Maitreya then explained with a second verse:

If there is doubt lingering in my breast and I am anxious that it will not be resolved, you should answer me at the proper time. The Tathāgata has entered meditative concentration; I know when that time is.

Therefore, I request an answer at the right moment so that my doubts may be severed and I may be made joyful. For this reason, Mañjuśrī raised his third challenge: "I and you, O Virtuous One, dwell together on the stage of training.
Desiring to fathom the Buddha’s intention, we have deliberated upon it together in subtle detail. Yet you alone command me to provide the answer."
This is logically untenable. Maitreya then explained with the third verse:

"I too have reflected within my subtle mind, hesitating between the two pillars as to whether to preach the wondrous Dharma or whether to bestow a prophecy. Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised the fourth objection:
"If it is as you say, then the doubt has already been resolved; why trouble me to answer? Maitreya then [proceeded] with the fourth...
The verse-commentary states: "How can one judge this great matter with a mind of hesitation? Therefore it says: "He manifested the various Buddha-lands; this was no small cause.
Once Mañjuśrī’s challenges had been exhausted, his modest demeanor also ceased.
Within this inquiry, Mañjuśrī’s challenges were implicit (*qian*), while Maitreya’s fourfold explanations were explicit (*xian*); thus, Mañjuśrī served as the guest (*bin*). Maitreya...
"Le" (勒) means "to take as a master. Furthermore, "zhanren" (瞻仁) refers to the mental seeking (*manas-paryeṣaṇā*); "weiyu shuo ciding" (為欲說此等) refers to the verbal seeking (*vāk-paryeṣaṇā*).

However, in terms of the Dharma-explanation (*dharmadeśanā*), it is called the "prediction of the fruit of seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā-phala-vyākaraṇa*); in terms of the metaphorical explanation (*upamā-deśanā*), it is called the "chariot of the fruit of seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā-phala-ratha*). This is the final verse.

This concludes the general request. Within the introductory section, it is clarified that while the light of the Tathāgata is of many kinds, the light emitted when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone is designated as the "rare light," because it is capable of initiating the causal conditions for the Great Matter.
II. Mañjuśrī traces back to antiquity in response, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has three sections.
First, a brief response based on initial reflection; second, a detailed demonstration of what is common; third, a comprehensive synthesis and concluding response.
Now, for the first: At that time, Mañjuśrī... [up to] "...manifested this auspicious sign because it is a dharma difficult to believe."

As for the Ancient Buddha Mañjuśrī, since he has manifested his traces as one of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi), his wisdom belongs to the stage of subsequent observation; hence it is said, "I contemplate" (*vici*). "Contemplate" (*vi*) means to deliberate;
it means that the past is like the present. "Deliberate" (*ci*) means to calculate and measure; it means that the present is like the past.
Although the times of past and present differ, the auspicious signs perceived in both past and present are identical; therefore, [the text] uses the first phrase.
The Master of Dharma signaled with his hand and said to Maitreya:
"Because I previously perceived an omen and subsequently heard the Great Dharma, I infer that the present Buddha will likewise expound the Great Dharma after manifesting an omen.

Mañjuśrī, for the time being, let us provisionally explain this single phrase of the 'Great Dharma' as a brief answer to your question, thereby resolving the doubts of both Maitreya and the great assembly."
Below, he further uses three parables to reiterate the explanation of the Great [Vehicle].

This is because it is said that although the World-Honored One, in the past, preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings, causing each to attain their respective fruits of realization, these were nonetheless not the Great Dharma; therefore, this [Great Vehicle] was intended to follow after them.
There should be a single-flavored, impartial rain of Dharma that universally moistens the flowers of humanity, causing them all equally to realize the ultimate fruit.

Therefore, it is explained through this metaphor: "About to rain down the great rain of Dharma, thereby providing universal moisture. Furthermore, although the World-Honored One in the past preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of the various bodhisattvas, there were distinctions among the five natures;
thus, even that was not yet the Great Dharma. It is for this reason that [the present teaching] is modeled after this.
Later, he naturally changed his title, transforming the provisional into the real and revealing the One Vehicle. Thus, the commentary by Yù says:

"He was about to blow the great Dharma conch, thereby changing his title. Furthermore, although the World-Honored One in the past relied upon the single nature to preach the One Vehicle, he had not yet clearly and manifestly set aside the former provisional teachings;
thus, with respect to the ultimate reality, it remained ultimately insufficient and was not [the final truth].
Therefore, following this, one directly abandons expedient means and speaks only of the Unsurpassed, pointing the way back to the Precious Abode.
Thus the commentary says: "It is as if striking the great Dharma drum to provide encouragement. Finally, it concludes:
"Specifically, the rain can universally moisten, the conch can change names, and the drum can provide encouragement; these are all meanings inherent within the Great Dharma."
Therefore, I intend that after the World-Honored One emerges from meditative absorption, he shall expound the true meaning within the Great Dharma.

In brief, because in the past, while amidst the light, I saw what had never been seen before and subsequently heard what had never been heard before, now that I have attained what was seen as before, it is likewise rare that I shall hear it as well.
This concludes the three metaphors above with a single summary, providing a general explanation.
In the heading, the intent of the single phrase "desiring to preach the Great Dharma" is explained, thereby resolving his doubts.

The subsequent extensive section demonstrating what is common [to all Buddhas] does nothing more than cite ancient precedents to corroborate the intention to preach the Great Dharma. Question: Previously, Maitreya raised doubts concerning two matters;
why is it that you now answer only regarding the preaching of the Dharma? Answer: Because the preaching of the Dharma and the bestowing of predictions [are inseparable].
All are subsumed within this one great matter. Since the Great Dharma has been preached, he must necessarily bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) after they have attained understanding;

therefore, this may be treated briefly. From the words "O sons of good family" onwards, [the Buddha] first uses what they have previously seen as a brief proof that his exposition of the Great [Vehicle] was intended for them, showing that these are not merely words from his own imagination.
As for the phrase "all hear it as difficult to believe," it is because the members of the assembly are all of a single class who have long been small-minded.
Regarding the capacity of great beings, it is said that there are fixed distinctions between the three vehicles and the five natures.

If one were to hear the teaching that throughout the lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle, it would truly be difficult to believe. Because he wished to speak what is difficult to believe, he manifested rare and wondrous omens.
II. Detailed Demonstration of What is Common [to All] (in three parts): 1. Establishing Teachings According to Capacity, and Comparison with the Present Buddha...

These are already identical. Second, entering meditative absorption and emitting light is the same as what the present Buddha now manifests. Third, preaching the Dharma and bestowing prophecies will be the same as what the present Buddha shall do. First:
"Good sons, just as in the past [up to] the Dharma that was preached was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end."

To discuss the divisions of time: setting aside the present single thought-moment as the "present," that which has already passed is called the "past," and that which is yet to come is called the "future.
*Asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable," and *kalpa* means "time-period.
Here, we refer to a time prior to immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and innumerable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. At that time, there was...
The Buddha descended as a spirit, with the specific title Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp). As Xuanzan’s *Huayan jing tanxuan ji* explains:

"The sun has two capacities: first, to lead toward illumination; second, to bring to maturity. The moon has two capacities: first, to remove heat; second, to provide coolness. The lamp has two capacities: first, to dispel darkness; second, to transmit light.
The reason this specific title is used to manifest his name is to signify that this Buddha is capable of leading [beings].
Leading those lost to awakening, he becomes a vessel for them as their faculties mature; he removes the fever of afflictions and attains the coolness of nirvana.

Having forever shattered ignorance, he transforms beings and transmits the Dharma. Even the illumination of the sun and moon is insufficient to metaphorically describe the luminous wisdom of that Buddha;
yet, by adding a lamp capable of illuminating even the most crooked recesses, one may borrow a mere fragment of these three lights to illustrate that which is inconceivable.
This is the wisdom [of the Buddha]. Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata Sun-Moon-Lamp. The following ten titles are the ten universal epithets.
Because the Way of each Buddha is the same and all possess these ten, the text of these ten titles is distributed throughout this sutra; here, they appear at the beginning of the scripture.
These should now be explained, both extensively and concisely. To be concise: one who is free from falsehood is named the Tathāgata;
one who is a field of merit is named the Arhat; one who knows the Dharma is named the Samyaksaṃbuddha; one who possesses the three types of knowledge is named the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna;
one who does not return again is named the Sugata; one who knows the realms of sentient beings is named the Lokavid; one who has no equal is named the Anuttara; one who tames others...
The mind is called the "Tamer of Men. He is the Eye of Sentient Beings and is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans. One who knows the three groups [of beings] is named a Buddha.
Possessing these ten virtues, he is called the Honored One of the World.

If one relies on the extensive explanation in the *Buddha-daśa-nāma-sūtra*, then "Knower of the World" (*Lokavid*) and "Unsurpassed Man" (*Anuttara-puruṣa*) are combined into a single title. Although there is this variation between expansion and contraction, their meaning remains the same.
Now, I shall preserve both [interpretations]. First, there are three meanings of "Tathāgata," namely: Dharma-body (dharmakāya), Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), and Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere. This refers to the Tathāgata as the Dharma-body. The *Cakra-pravartana-śāstra* states:

"The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called 'Thus' (tathā), and perfect enlightenment is called 'Come' (āgata). This refers to the Tathāgata as the Reward-body. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: [and so forth].
He has mounted the path of reality and come to achieve perfect enlightenment; this is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. Second, the Arhat:
this means that his myriad practices are fully perfected and his merit is complete, such that he is worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Third, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: this means that by means of all-encompassing wisdom, there is nothing among all phenomena that he does not know.

Furthermore, because he awakens all sentient beings by means of the equality of all phenomena and thereby achieves unsurpassed enlightenment, he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Fourth is "One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna): "Knowledge" refers to the three knowledges (*vidyā*); "Conduct" refers to body, speech, and mind.
Because he has perfectly cultivated and brought to fulfillment all practices through his own power of aspiration, they are truly pure. Fifth is the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata), which is...

The meaning of "wondrously proceeding" (*sugata*) is as follows: by means of immeasurable wisdom, one is able to sever all afflictions; wondrously transcending the world, one is able to proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
Sixth is "knower of the world" (*lokavid*). Regarding the "knower of the world" (*lokavid*): it refers to all that is mundane and supramundane.

There are no phenomena of cause and effect that he does not thoroughly understand. The "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara) refers to one whose karma and afflictions are completely purified, such that there is nothing further to be severed;
because he is the foremost, most supreme, and peerless among humans, devas, ordinary beings, and sages, he is titled the "Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One.
The "Seven Taming Lords of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi) refers to those who possess the power and function of a Great Man and thus teach.
Through various dharmas, he tames, guides, and restrains all sentient beings, causing them to leave behind defilement and attain nirvāṇa.
He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans; this means that he is not merely the teacher of the fourfold assembly, but of all those in the heavens and among humans.
The Māras, non-Buddhists, Śakra, Brahmā, devas, and nāgas all take refuge in him as their disciples.

Ninth is "Buddha," which means "Awakened," signifying that he is fully endowed with wisdom because his three types of awakening are perfected. Tenth is "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), meaning that through dharmas such as wisdom, he has destroyed greed, hatred, and delusion;
having extinguished the suffering of birth and death, he attained unsurpassed awakening and is thus honored by both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Because of its gravity, at that time, that Buddha, having manifested his body-wheel (*kāya-cakra*), further emitted sounds from his mouth-wheel (*vāk-cakra*) to proclaim the True Dharma.
He did so for the sake of those with gradual capacities, leading them from the small toward the great.

What he taught during the three periods—beginning, middle, and end—all accords with principle and accords with capacity; there was nothing that was not excellent. Thus, regarding these three excellences...
The term [“vehicle,” *yāna*] appears throughout all the sūtras, and its explanations also vary.

Now, wishing to illuminate the subsequent text thoroughly, one should take the dharma-gates of the three vehicles—the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva—as the three “wholesome” [vehicles]. One should provide both general and specific interpretations.
Regarding the general interpretation: the initial teaching of the Four Noble Truths enables those who hear it to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle.

"Good. Next, he explains the causes and conditions, which is good because it enables one to attain the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. Finally, he explains the six perfections, which is good because it enables one to attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This constitutes the division of that Buddha’s entire body of holy teaching into three "good" aspects according to its general meaning.
If explained specifically, however, each of the Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles should likewise possess these three "goods. First, regarding the Śrāvaka [Vehicle]...

Regarding the vehicle (*yāna*): knowing suffering and abandoning its origin is called the "goodness at the beginning"; cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path is called the "goodness in the middle"; and realizing cessation is called the "goodness at the end.

Regarding the teaching of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to contemplate the process of cyclic existence and its reversal: causing one to observe the flow of transmigration is called the "goodness at the beginning";

cultivating the seventy-seven insights (*jñāna*) is called the "goodness in the middle"; and realizing cessation is called the "goodness at the end. If it concerns a Bodhisattva, then not forsaking the bodhicitta is [the goodness at the beginning].
It is excellent in the beginning: not dwelling upon the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) is excellence in the middle. Dedication toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is called excellence in the end.

Regarding its meaning being "lowly" [in the sense of being accessible], this reveals the virtuous characteristics of the teaching; regarding its meaning being "profound," it refers to its ability to bring about benefit and happiness.
Regarding its words being "skillful," it refers to the excellence with which names and phrases are composed. It is not shared with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, it is pure and singular. Because its meaning is abundant and perfect, it is unadulterated. Because its self-nature is liberated in a single moment, it is pure.

Because it is also liberated through the continuity of many moments, it is bright white. As for the characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they refer to the eight branches of the noble path.
Extinction (*nirodha*) is termed "Brahma," and the path (*mārga*) is termed "conduct" (*carya*). These eight paths serve as the cause for extinction.

Therefore, it is called the characteristic of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). "In order to seek" [the following] correctly cites the original Buddha’s establishment of teachings according to the capacities of beings, manifesting that he is identical [to them].

Regarding the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*): "four" refers to the four of suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). "Truth" (*satya*) carries the meaning of being examined with precision and being authentically true.

This means that through the contemplation of analytical emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one precisely examines and verifies what the Buddha taught as the suffering and its accumulation in the mundane world, and [the cessation and the path] of the supramundane.
Cessation and the Path are both words that are truly sincere, authentic, and real; therefore, by practicing in reliance upon them, one immediately transcends birth and death and reaches nirvana.
A *pratyekabuddha* is called a "solitary enlightened one" (*yuanjue*) because the twelve links they realize are all termed "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This is because they function as causes by successively inducing results, and serve as conditions by mutually depending upon one another. For example, by means of the past...

The two links of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) act as the cause, giving rise to the five links of present consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) as the result.

Furthermore, from within these present results, the three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) arise as the causes for the present, giving rise to the two links of future birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as the result.
Thus, the continuity of the three periods of time proceeds in an endless cycle. For this reason:
These twelve are all termed "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*). Therefore, one who hears this Dharma-gate and awakens to these conditions is called a *pratyekabuddha*.
As for the six *pāramitās*, the "six" refers to the six consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"Paramita" is translated as "reaching the other shore. Taking the great ocean of afflictions as the metaphor: birth and death constitute this shore, while nirvana constitutes the other shore.

If one can take the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth—as one's boat and oars, or as one's life-preserving float, then one may avoid being swept away or sinking in the ocean of afflictions, cross to the other shore, attain bodhi, and achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is precisely the Buddha-knowledge; that is to say, one is able to know all paths through this single knowledge of all modes.

The preceding citation shows that the first Buddha established the teaching according to the capacities of beings and was already identical to the present Buddha. Next, further down, another twenty thousand Buddhas are cited, who were likewise identical to the present Buddha.
As for these twenty thousand Buddhas sharing the same name, it may be because they were identical [in their practice] during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
At that time, they were enlightened and likewise received the prediction of their future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
They were equal to the five hundred disciples of the present who have received the prediction of the name "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabha*). Pūrṇa was said to possess sharp faculties;

because that Buddha appeared in a time not subject to the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*), he left the household life from within a lineage of noble conduct and virtue, became a Dharma King endowed with the ten titles, and preached the first [turning of the wheel].
The Dharma that is good in the middle and at the end. △ Second, the emission of light and entry into meditative absorption, which is identical to the present Buddha’s manifestation;

this has four parts: first, the prince’s resolve to leave the household life; second, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the sutra and entry into meditative absorption; third, the Tathāgata’s emission of light as an auspicious omen.
The four great assemblies were filled with doubt and sought its resolution. First:
when that final Buddha was not yet a renunciant, he had already planted the roots of all manner of goodness in the presence of ten million buddhas.
The names of the princes are all derived from worldly conventions. That which the mind inclines toward is called "intention" (*manas*).
One who possesses intention is not one whose innate nature is neutral or weak, such that they have no inclination at all. "Wholesome intention" means that the intention is free from evil.
"Immeasurable intention" means that the intention is vast and far-reaching, and is not comparable to shallow or inferior consciousness. Treasure.

The "intention of self-respect" means knowing how to value one's own mind, not daring to pursue things with superficiality. The "increasing intention" means elevating one's mind, finding no pleasure in meanness.
The "intention of removing doubt" means that wherever the mind is directed, it is able to resolve all delusions.
The "resonant intention" means being as swift and responsive as an echo following a sound. The "dharma-intention" means that the mind dwells solely upon the Dharma.

He did not abide in what is contrary to the Dharma. Later, it is said that he gave rise to the aspiration for the Mahāyāna; all this arose from his worldly intention to give rise to the supramundane intention.
A single four-continent world-system is ruled by a single Golden Wheel-turning King. Possessing majestic power and sovereign freedom, each governs the four continents.
Below him was the Dharma Master Subhāṣita, who expounded the teachings for the people. Thus, eighty kalpas were fulfilled.
It is evident that in the land transformed by that Buddha, not only is the territory vast, but the lifespan of its people is also long.
I venture to suggest that since the eight sons renounced their royal positions to leave the household life, it is clear that this Buddha belongs to the Kṣatriya caste;
thus, he appears to be of a different lineage from the twenty thousand Buddhas. As for the father-king attaining Buddhahood...
Because they had left the household life, they followed their father in renouncing the world. They resolved upon the Mahāyāna path and immediately gave rise to the bodhicitta.

Cultivating the pure conduct (brahmacarya) was for their own benefit, while acting as Dharma-preachers was for the benefit of others. Thus, these eight sons were able, within the single body of their present existence, to achieve this.
Having seen through worldly conditions, as soon as he left home, he immediately possessed both benefits for self and others;

this was because he had already planted many roots of goodness under numerous Buddhas in the past, thereby attaining such a state. △ Second, the Tathāgata speaks the sutra and enters meditative concentration.

At that time, from the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa until [the assembly] rejoiced, joined their palms, and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion, the Buddha first preached the *Anantārthadharmaparyāya* (The Teaching of Infinite Meanings) in order to reveal the principle of the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This was intended to secretly demonstrate the meaning of the origin and the end. By causing them to realize that infinite meanings arise from the single true reality, he showed that [all phenomena] are, in fact, real.
Within these marks, the wondrous meanings are inexhaustible; yet of these inexhaustible meanings, there is none that proceeds without returning.
For this reason, that Buddha first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and then entered the *Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings*.
Because one can contemplate the principle of formlessness through this samādhi, it is called a "station" (*sthāna*). That is to say, the immeasurable dharmas are themselves—

The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark is itself the infinite meaning (*anantārtha*). Therefore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called the "locus" (*sthāna*). Furthermore, because it is elucidated by the teaching, the Sūtra is called "meaning.
Because it is elucidated by wisdom, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "meaning. The locus is that which is personally realized by wisdom.

From the phrase "At that time" onwards, it clarifies that the heavens and earth manifested auspicious omens and the great assembly rejoiced. Question: The World-Honored One preached the Sūtra and then entered meditative concentration.
Question: Why does the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) also manifest auspicious omens? Answer:

Because, since beginningless time, due to the conditions of the assembly of all dharmas, sentient beings have given rise to entanglements within the world of beings (*sattva-loka*). Consequently, they have been unable to transcend the vessel-world.

Now, by means of the Buddha who is none other than one's own mind, delivering sentient beings who are none other than one's own mind, [the Buddha] first uproots them with wisdom and subsequently moves them with meditative concentration, causing them to attain what they had not yet attained.

It will indeed be so; for since the primary retribution already contains the signs of emerging from ignorance, it causes the secondary environment to likewise be transformed into supreme awakening, and thus this sign manifests first.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The sense organs and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual.
△ Third, the Tathāgata emits light as an auspicious omen.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted light from between his eyebrows... [as far as] "the various Buddha-lands now seen.

This is the introduction for twenty thousand Buddhas, all appearing together in the same manner. This is the final Buddha’s introduction; he emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to preach the sutra, with the beginning and end mutually abbreviated by the skillful hand of the translator.
△ The four great assemblies give rise to doubts and desire to resolve them.
Maitreya, you should know that those in the assembly at that time— from those who wished to know the causes and conditions for which this light appeared,
to those who desired to hear the Dharma and were all addressed as "Bodhisattvas"— were intended to be the compilers of the teachings.
Since they were so addressed after [the Buddha] had already revealed and bestowed their predictions, the doubts they raised were entirely due to the extraordinary nature of the signs of light.

Because [the Buddha] has set it forth, he asks specifically about the light; other matters are not urgent. △ Third, the preaching of the Dharma and the bestowing of predictions, which shall be the same as those of the present Buddha.
This has four parts: first, the naming of the sutra being preached; second, clarifying the time when the sutra was preached.
The Three Clarities proclaim extinction and entrust [the teaching]; the Four Clarities propagate the sutra and become Buddhas. Now, for the first:
At that time there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light (up to) "teaching the bodhisattvas' dharma protected by the Buddhas."
The light of wisdom is subtle and wondrous; it can guide both those with provisional and those with ultimate capacities, and is therefore called "Subtle Light" (Miaoguang).

That which is taught by means of this Subtle Light is so named because Subtle Light is able to take its own mind as a lamp of wisdom to illuminate the profound nuances of the sutras, and is moreover skilled in transmitting and transforming others.
Thus, "Mahāyāna Sūtra" is a general designation for the various Dharma-gates through which the Buddhas teach and transform bodhisattvas.
The treatise enumerates seventeen names for the Mahāyāna; here, three are presented in full. The name *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* appears as the sixteenth.

Regarding the choice of the lotus flower as a metaphor: this "wonderful Dharma" (*saddharma*) is the unity of the provisional and the real, whereas the lotus flower represents the simultaneity of the blossom and the fruit;
thus, it can illustrate the meaning of the dual integration of the wonderful Dharma. This is the fourth [section on] names and teachings.
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva refers to this sublime principle, which can transform all roots of goodness and bring bodhisattvas to maturity;

by conforming to those who are vessels of the Dharma, it causes them to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. The fifth is named "Protected by the Buddhas," meaning that the sublime principle of the true mark exists equally within both sentient beings and Buddhas.
Although the Buddha has already awakened to it first, he constantly desires to reveal and teach it, yet because the faculties of sentient beings...
Because it is dull [to others], he did not dare to show it lightly; thus, he was protected and remembered by the Buddha. △ Second, clarifying the duration of the preaching of the sutra:
For sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat (until) there arose no weariness or fatigue in either body or mind.
That Buddha preached the sutra at one time and in one place, which differs from the present Buddha’s two locations and three assemblies.

As for the phrase "like the duration of a meal," it means that through the external empowerment of the Buddha and internal resonance with the Principle, his six sense faculties were all turned toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, allowing him to transcend time and eons instantaneously.
Thus, although vast ages have passed, they are experienced as if they were but the duration of a meal. △ Third, the proclamation of the name.
Regarding the entry into extinction:
the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* after sixty intermediate kalpas.
According to ancient accounts, on the very last day of those sixty intermediate kalpas, having finished preaching the sūtra at dawn, he then announced his passing into extinction.
This reveals that the sentient beings to be converted at that time were superior to those of the present;

they did not require the Buddha to gather them in through further effort, as he had already completely severed both the seeds and the fruits of the two obstructions—those within and without the realm. "At that time" and so forth:

[the Buddha] bestowed upon Guṇakara the prediction of his future attainment of the state of a *upapadya* (heir apparent). Among the ten titles [of a Buddha], he briefly cites three of them to cause [beings] to awaken.
There must be something upon which it relies. Question: The prediction (vyākaraṇa) received by Guṇakaraṇḍavyūha clearly indicates that he is a candidate for Buddhahood (upapatti-sthāna).

Since the text contains no mention at all of bestowing a prediction upon a śrāvaka, why is the section titled "Expounding the Dharma and Bestowing Predictions," suggesting he will be the same as the present Buddha?
Answer: The title follows the proposal made regarding Maitreya, and thus both are mentioned together; Mañjuśrī, however, follows the wording of the heading.

Commentary: Therefore, it may be treated briefly. △ Fourth, clarifying that through the propagation of the sutra one becomes a Buddha, in two parts: first, clarifying the propagation of the sutra by those of sharp faculties;
second, clarifying the propagation of the sutra by those of dull faculties. Now, the first part.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, from the time of the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Ghoṣadatta) until the last one to attain Buddhahood, named Dīpaṃkara, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light propagated this sūtra for eighty kalpas.
This sufficiently demonstrates that at that time, the human lifespan was exceedingly long and not subject to the five corruptions.
Although the previous statement mentioned sixty kalpas, the present figure of eighty kalpas both refer to the present to manifest the past, thereby revealing the duration of that time.
For a long time, one must know that the lifespan of humans at that time was such that even taking the present one eon as equivalent to a single day there, it remains uncertain.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* sequentially compares the durations of various lands, wherein there are instances where days and eons multiply by ten;
this may be consulted separately. Regarding the eight sons who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all took Miao Guang (Prabhāsa) as their teacher—it was because of Miao Guang...
This is an inconceivable person. Just as when he first emerged from meditative absorption, he spoke because of the presence of Wonderful Light (Prabhāsa);

since that Buddha had already taught the three vehicles for a specific class of gradual practitioners, and they have now reached maturity, he must now lead them to the ultimate convergence in the One Vehicle.
It was not possible for Wonderful Light alone to mutually encourage and proclaim this; therefore, he relied upon Wonderful Light to make this universal announcement.
All of them, now propagating [the teachings] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, could not have firmly established the Unsurpassed [Dharma] without Miaoguang (Prabhāpāla);

therefore, they all took him as their teacher. That the last one attained Buddhahood under the name Dīpaṃkara and that they all successively received the prediction of attaining the position of a successor (upapadyamāna)—to argue about this in terms of generations, such as grandfather and grandson, is trivial. 2. Explaining the propagation of the sutra by those of dull faculties.
Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one who—[from "until"]—made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised [the Buddha], yet his mind wandered outwardly.
He did not realize that all phenomena are like illusions; beginning with material gain, he developed deep attachment.
Although he possessed faith in the various sūtras and desired to read and recite them, because he lacked resolute understanding (*adhimukti*), he could not master them thoroughly.
Due to being marked by ignorance, they frequently forget and lose [the teachings], and consequently are held in low esteem by the world.

Furthermore, by seeking a name for themselves, they additionally cause the sound of the Dharma to pass through their ears, thereby developing the power of hearing; thus they gradually plant roots of goodness and encounter many Buddhas.
The preceding citation from the beginning and end of the text mutually clarifies this within the third identical passage;
it merely demonstrates that the Way of each Buddha is the same and that they must preach the Great Dharma to resolve the doubts of the assembly—this is the general outline.

If one were to immediately pair [the Buddhas] with specific conditions by saying, "This is like such-and-such a person today," or "This is like such-and-such a person today," then even the Dharma King would not possess mastery over the Dharma. Why?
This is because one contemplates that all phenomena belong to the realm of death and impermanence. △ Third, the reconciliation and conclusion of the answer:
"Maitreya, you should know that at that time, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light... [the Dharma] taught to Bodhisattvas and protected by the Buddhas."

By synthesizing these textual passages, we know that among the twenty thousand Buddhas mentioned previously, it was specifically the last Buddha who was cited to clarify the identity of the present and the future.
This is because Maitreya first gained entry into the Dharma assembly under that Buddha.

Furthermore, since the single instance of the former teaching being brief and the latter being extensive also occurred in the past—wherein he saw and heard them both together—why should he alone be made [to experience this]?
Answer: For this reason, he addresses him by name face-to-face. It is certain that after the present Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa, [the situation] will likewise necessarily be the same.

Part Two: The Verse Text has three sections. First, a verse on entering samādhi and emitting light; second, a verse on emerging from samādhi and preaching the Dharma; third, a concluding judgment and exhortation to wait. Now, the first section:
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall in past lives... (until) each asked one another about the causes and conditions of this matter."
This consists of eighteen and a half verses. Regarding the first line, "I recall": Mañjuśrī, through his great wisdom, reaches the very limit of the instant (*kṣaṇa*).
Even that which has not yet arrived he can bring back into the present; how much more so that which has already passed?
It naturally follows that it should appear vividly in the mind through recollection; hence, it says, "I recall. Thus, all former conditions are [recollected] from within this very recollection.

Each point is indicated in detail. The following verses are largely identical to those in Maitreya’s inquiry; however, they omit the passage regarding the sounding of the celestial drum found at the beginning.
As for the differences between the ancient and modern versions, there is only the discrepancy between the color of crystal and the present golden color.
Knowing that the Dharma is quiescent, it cannot be spoken; yet those who seek the Way through the Dharma must remain without words.

Because it is unimpeded in expression, and because phenomena—namely the dharmas of form, mind, and so forth—are in their very essence the true mark (dharmatā), when the mouth wishes to speak, words fail;
when the mind intends to engage with objects, deliberation is forgotten. All marks are perfectly extinguished, known only by wisdom.
△ Second, emerging from meditative absorption to preach the Dharma.
From "The Honored One revered by devas and humans" (up to) "the Dharma Master Wondrous Light," it is my own person [who speaks].
When that Buddha emerged from absorption, he praised [the teaching] with the eye of the world; that is, the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma, which both belong to Wondrous Light.
For sixty kalpas he did not rise from his seat; this period of preaching the Dharma is likewise like our current reckoning of seven years as the time our Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra.

That Buddha’s final instruction, wherein he uniquely exhorted [his followers] with the two words "diligence" (vīrya), was because he saw that not a single good quality arises from indolence and laziness. It is the unconditioned reality...
As for its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): because it possesses such modes of activity as being without arising or cessation, it is called the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Its essence is precisely *prakṛtiviśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity). Regarding "intrinsic purity": although wisdom is capable of realizing it, it cannot be purified, because there is no dharma that can be extinguished;
this is because its fundamental nature is pure. Furthermore, although afflictions and outflows may depend upon it, they cannot defile it, because there is no dharma that can arise.
Because its nature is fundamentally pure, we now take one aspect of its meaning—being free from faults—and name it the "uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) true mark" (*dharmatā*).

In the following phrase, we again take one aspect of its meaning—the wisdom capable of realizing it—and name it the "mind of thorough penetration. Question: According to the sequence, he will become a Buddha;
