The three illuminations are present. Regarding the first two: the first verse reveals and clarifies [the truth] for all Buddhas; the second uses skillful means to assist in that revelation.
Now, for the first:
"Throughout incalculable kalpas of the past" (extending to) "transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way."
△ Second, the assistance of skillful means in manifesting the two [truths]. First, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation. Now, the first:
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords (down to) further employ various other skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

"Different expedient means" (*anya-upāya*). For the time being, speaking in terms of the degrees of phenomena (*dharma-skandha*), the phrase "assisting in manifesting the characters" explains the meaning of "different.

It is called "different" because the time required for opening and revealing [the truth] is remote. Furthermore, it is a reflection that clarifies the preceding "opening the three to reveal the one," which constitutes the primary expedient means.
Question: Human and celestial causes may be termed "different. However, as for those preceding and following [this], they are the provisional means (*upāya*) actually bestowed by the Real. Since...
Both belong to the category of provisional teachings (*upāya*). How can you suppress the former and exalt the latter? Answer:

According to the intent of the ultimate teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), since every instance of spitting, sneezing, or picking up and showing [an object] is the functioning of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), it is precisely the locus where the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

What difference could there be? Now, because the roots of goodness have matured, one is close to the provisional means that reveal this manifestation; thus, these are subsumed within the correct skillful means (*samyag-upāya*).

[The section on] the Middle. Regarding the provisional practices that initially induce the arousal of the bodhicitta, these are termed "distinct" because the time until their full manifestation is very distant.
△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, manifestation assisted by the Three Vehicles; second, manifestation assisted by humans and devas. Now, the first part.

If there are any classes of sentient beings—[from "if there are any classes of sentient beings" up to] "all such sentient beings have already attained the path of Buddhahood"—among these, we take for consideration those who can hear even a single thought of goodness regarding the six perfections, as well as those who, upon seeing the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, give rise to a single thought of gentle and supple goodness.
This cannot be restricted to the profound discourse on practicing the six perfections; rather, the Tathāgata [bestows predictions] based on this very single thought.
This subtlety may arise from a single thought of sympathetic joy (anumodana).

Taking this as a foundation for instruction, one should protect it so that it does not become obscured, gradually expanding it from the subtle to the manifest; this is what is meant by "aiding manifestation.
Therefore, the provisional [teachings] within these distinct [vehicles] cannot be viewed on the same level as the provisional teachings opened at the very end; they already encompass [the ultimate].

Regarding the two teachings—the Common and the Distinct—at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who are able to give rise to even a single thought of wholesome, supple goodness and are not constrained by powerful, expansive, and difficult-to-tame afflictions will also be protected until they reach the stage of maturity;

they shall certainly be revealed [to the truth], and both shall together attain Buddhahood. Part Two: Revealing the Reality through the Assistance of Humans and Devas. This has two sections. First, revealing the reality by means of the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Second, revealing the reality by means of the *jñānahetu* (causal condition of realization). This consists of the first ten [sections]. First, regarding the construction of stupas with a resolute mind:
"After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa... down to... if one were to pile up earth in the midst of a wilderness to form a temple for a Buddha."
"Others" refers to those who are able to perform a single act of offering before a stūpa containing relics; they shall obtain the retribution of being reborn in the heavens a thousand times.
How much more so for one who actually constructs a stūpa, who will naturally receive such retribution. After the distant kalpas have passed, all remaining merit shall gradually be revealed.
△ Second, making stūpas out of sand.
"Even those who, as children at play, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—all such people have already attained the Way of the Buddha.

Although they were merely playing with sand to make stūpas amidst the midst of worldly afflictions, it was like striking fire from stone; once the flame is ignited, it becomes a fierce conflagration that consumes the vast plains.
How could it ever be apart from that single spark? Based on this, one knows that the six perfections mentioned in the preceding text are all...

Regarding the initial imitation of a single thought-moment, there is a further profound meaning. Therefore, in the sutra, it first speaks of a "resolute mind" (zhìxīn) and later speaks of a "playful mind" (xìxīn);
all subsequent instances follow this pattern. △ Third, creating images with a resolute mind.
If a person, for the sake of the Buddha—[down to] whether they create it themselves or cause others to do so—all have already attained the path of Buddhahood through the merit of creating images.
The Sūtra clarifies eleven kinds of merit: first, in every successive life, their eyes shall be clear and pure.
Second, one will be born in places free from evil. Third, one will always be born into noble families. Fourth, one’s body will be golden in color.

Fifth, one will abound in rare treasures and playthings. Sixth, one will be born into families of the wise and virtuous. Seventh, one will be born to become a king. Eighth, one will become a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).
Ninth, one will be born in the Brahma Heaven and dwell there for the duration of a kalpa. Tenth, one will not fall into the evil realms.
Eleventh, those born in future lives will again be able to revere and honor the Triple Gem. Furthermore, it is said:

"If a person, at the moment of death, resolves to create an image—even one as small as a grain of wheat—it can eliminate the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas across the three periods of time.

Based on this statement, although the karmic retribution does not exclusively occur in the heavens, the present text speaks of the heavens for the sake of brevity. △ Fourth: Playful Manifestations (Līlā).
One paints the Buddha with the mind.
Even if a child plays at drawing a Buddha image using grass, wood, a brush, or even a fingernail,
it forms five knots that manifest reality.
In this way, these various individuals (up to) merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
They also merely use the Dharma-gates revealed to them in the past to deliver many beings.
△ Sixth, making offerings by means of the various sense objects.
If a person, at a stupa or temple (up to) even with a single small sound, has already attained the path of Buddhahood.
△ Seventh, making offerings with a distracted mind:
If a person, with a distracted mind, makes an offering of even a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually see countless Buddhas.
△ 8. Clarifying physical acts of veneration:
There may be some who prostrate themselves, or again, those who merely join their palms, or even raise one hand, or again, those who slightly lower their heads.
△ 9. Summarizing the two sets of great benefits.
With these offerings to the image [and so forth], until entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted.
△ Ten: Clarifying Reverence through Verbal Recitation.
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stūpa or temple and recites "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
*Namo* (or *namo*), sometimes transcribed as *namo*, are both variations of the Sanskrit sound. This is translated as "taking refuge" (*guiming*) or "deliver me.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Buddha said, 'If there is a single person who utters the name "Namo Buddha," their merit shall not be exhausted until the end of suffering.
2. Revealing the Reality by Way of the Elucidating Cause (*lioyin*).
Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, whether they were in the world or had passed into extinction, if there were those who heard this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Within the teachings of the Buddhas of the past, merely hearing this Dharma once immediately constitutes the seed of the wisdom that serves as the cause for enlightenment;
it is the foundation for its manifestation. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "It is like a well or spring in the world, which has the ocean as its essence. If a person drinks from it..."
All of them obtain the flavor of the ocean; they are of one essence and no different. It is only according to the power of their karma that they perceive it as salty.
When those endowed with faith hear this, they immediately attain the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and great compassionate wisdom. However, those of icchantika nature have no capacity for it.
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata’s wisdom also acts as a generative cause (*janaka-hetu*), just as a mud clam is born from heaven, or as a stallion elephant reforms its wickedness.
...and so forth. △ Second, clarifying the future.
From "The World-Honored Ones of the future" to "the Guide, having known [this] at the site of enlightenment, speaks with skillful means.

First, it clarifies that the friend preaches the Dharma. From "All... onwards, it leads those of provisional capacity into the ultimate reality. From "The Buddhas... onwards, it clarifies their original vows.
"Regarding 'In the future' [it is] below": this correctly clarifies the teaching of the One. "Regarding 'All Buddhas' [it is] below": this explains the reason for teaching the One.
The *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*) states: "Because there is only a single nature, it is called the One Vehicle.

This single nature refers to the wisdom that realizes that all phenomena, such as form and mind, have been quiescent in their essential nature and characteristics from the very beginning; they are neither identical to nor distinct from self and other.

It is detached; it is serene and eternally abiding. When something comes, it is simply non-existent; it is not that one must push it away to make it non-existent. Therefore, it is called "the nature of eternal non-existence.

This nature of eternal non-existence is precisely the principle realized. This principle of non-nature is itself the seed for attaining Buddhahood via the Middle Way, and it is also the *dharmatā-buddhadhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the direct cause).
It is that which is illuminated by the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (the cause of realization), while conditions serve as the *pratyaya* (the contributing conditions).
Regarding "the Buddha-nature as that which is produced by the producing cause": its essence consists of the six perfections and the myriad practices.

Through this wisdom, it serves as the condition for the arising of that primary cause, enabling the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood. The above has been an explanation of the various aspects of the cause.

If one explains the lineage (*gotra*) in terms of the fruit, the *Guangzhong* [commentary] states: "The Buddha-retribution belongs only to the Buddha; its principle is unerring. This is precisely the meaning of "nature" (*xing*).

Furthermore, the manner in which he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is in every respect similar; this is the meaning of "this kind. As for the "nature of the fruit," it arises from ultimate truth, and thus it is said to "arise from conditions.
The intended meaning is that the Buddha arises by taking ultimate truth as his condition. Since truth is non-dual, he therefore speaks of the One Vehicle.
That is to say, one becomes a Buddha by realizing the truth, and in accordance with that truth, he speaks of the One. The phrase "This Dharma" and below provides a further explanation.
This refers to the preceding verse. It means that this Dharma is precisely the Dharma previously known.
The reason it is eternally without self-nature is that, by abiding in the true state (*tathatā-samyak-sthiti*), worldly phenomena are themselves suchness; therefore, they are all eternally abiding.

This means that when causes deviate from the principle of constancy, the three realms become impermanent. If one understands the reality of impermanence, then impermanence itself becomes permanence. Thus, it is eternal.
The two principles of impermanence and [eternity] are not partial. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* compares them to two birds.

Now, at this site of enlightenment, one realizes that the impermanence of all worlds is itself the principle of true eternity. It is like a mirror suspended in a lofty hall where ten thousand images are reflected therein.
Though they are two, they are non-dual, and cannot be fully expressed in words. Yet, through the power of skillful means, they are provisionally described by speech as "one."
This is still a provisional teaching; how could there be two or three? △ Third, clarifying the present:
"Worshipped by devas and humans" (up to) "metaphors are also words spoken according to the occasion through skillful means."
Suchness and the one mind are originally quiescent and extinguished. This is neither the extinction of the cycle of birth and death, nor is it an extinction achieved through antidotes;
therefore, it is called "supreme. Within the quiescence of the one mind, there is nothing that can be expressed, yet through the power of skillful means, various explanations are given.
△ Second, the explanation is established by means of oneself, which consists of four parts. First, two verses are presented as a heading. Second...
1. Observing their capacities, he gives rise to compassion. 2. He preaches the Dharma in response to those capacities. 3. He correctly employs the skillful means of relinquishment.
Now I am also like this (up to): using skillful means, I preach all dharmas so that all may attain joy.
The Tiantai school points to these two verses as the basis for the parables explained below.

In my private view, the metaphors below do nothing more than take the principles explained above and sketch them out in a diagram, merely providing a further comparative clarification. Why must one specifically point to [the phrase] "likewise" and so forth?
It is precisely because this serves to establish one's own interpretation that the Way of the revelation and manifestation by the Buddhas of the three periods of time is entirely...
It is the same. △ Second, observing capacities and activating compassion:
"Śāriputra, you should know" (up to) "...arising the mind of great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.

Within the Dharma-nature land, the Buddha-eye perfectly discerns the various capacities [of beings] and universally responds to all phenomena. This is for the sake of one class of those who progress gradually.

As for the capacity [of the audience], they should be gathered through the Dharma-gate of first employing skillful means and subsequently revealing the ultimate truth; thus, he manifested his body within the five turbidities.

One must know that from here below, the five turbidities are discussed horizontally (as a lateral exposition) to precisely clarify the signs of the heavy defilements of sentient beings during the period of the kalpa-turbidity’s chaos, manifesting the time when these five turbidities converge, which causes hindrances to be heavy and attachments to be deep, leading them to be... with the world.
Out of the World-Honored One’s compassionate vow, he further intervened; thus, [the Buddha] was startled and entered the burning house.

The six realms of existence are the domain for those lacking merit and wisdom—this is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Within these perilous paths, it is easy to repeatedly lose one's body and life.
The turbidity of the lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): externally one is shrouded by the dust of desire, and internally one falls, being self-obscured by craving and attachment.
This is precisely like the yak that is harmed because of its love for its tail; this is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Only a Buddha is able to break through these turbidities.
Since they do not seek the Buddha, they fall into the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Deeply entering into false views, they are already obscured by the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*);
even if there were ambrosia, they would be unwilling to drink it. Consequently, their sufferings are continuous, and they can no longer escape.

When evil people, evil teachings, an evil era, and an evil age converge together, and when the defilements of sentient beings are heavy and the turbulence of the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the impurity of the eon) causes upheaval—at such a time, how could one not give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to rescue and deliver them? △ Third, responding to capacities by preaching the Dharma, in four parts.
First, the thought of the Dharma attained by oneself; second, the thought of the various Buddhas employing skillful means; third, the clarification that the various Buddhas manifest praise;

fourth, the clarification of reverently following the Buddha’s teaching. Regarding the first four [points]: first, the clarification that what is attained is subtle and wondrous; second, the clarification that the faculties of those to be transformed are dull.
The third [section] explains how Śakra and Brahmā requested the Dharma; the fourth explains how he ceased his transformative activity due to a lack of receptive capacity. Now, for the first:
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment... the wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and most supreme."
The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is located to the southwest of the kingdom of Magadha, not far from the Nairañjanā River.

Because the Buddha first practiced here and attained the Way, it is called the site of enlightenment. This was initially explained in terms of time; however, if one considers the Buddha’s response to the capacities of sentient beings, [it is understood differently].
There is no time when there is no beginning. If the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) were not to encounter its stimulus, then there would be no beginning.

Furthermore, the noble ones who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) constantly perceive and preach the Sūtra of the Single Flavor; they see only a beginning, yet no end or limit. Speaking from the perspective of the Buddha, there is neither beginning nor non-beginning.
If considered in terms of expedient means (*upāya*), all are manifested as distinct characteristics from within the seal of the One Vehicle. [End of] Sitting.
As for the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): when emotions of past and present have perished and the mind is devoid of initial characteristics, it is called the "beginning.

To manifest a body where there is no body, and to abide where there is no abiding, is called "sitting. To illuminate through non-thought and perceive that the mind is eternally abiding is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment."

This is stated according to the ultimate, definitive meaning. In the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching), manifesting the eight phases [of enlightenment] is called "Transformation" (nirmāṇa-kāya), and the initial perfection of the four wisdoms is called "Retribution" (saṃbhoga-kāya) as he sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

In the Small and Middle [teachings], the severance of fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind and the initial perfection of the fivefold Dharma-body are designated as "sitting at the site of enlightenment" with the sixteen-foot body beneath the tree of wood. This is explained according to the Sudden Teaching.
Thus, there is neither completion nor non-completion. For example, while the world undergoes formation and destruction, space neither increases nor decreases.

If we consider the Perfect [Dharma-body], it manifests for the sake of sentient beings through the clouds of bodies of the ten Buddhas’ Dharma-realm, pervading the infinite time and places of Indra’s net, at every thought-moment and from the very beginning, encompassing the three worlds and presiding over them.
The perfection of attendants is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This currently refers to events prior to the full revelation [of the teaching].

Why rely on minor accounts? The remaining four [perfections] follow by way of convenience. Regarding "observing the tree": it is because he felt the grace of sitting beneath the tree and attaining the Buddha-way that he observed it.
Regarding "walking along the path": it is because he recollected the virtues of the earth; in both cases, the intention is to repay the favor. During the three periods of seven days...
Below, I have collated various scriptures. For instance, both the *Lalitavistara* (Puyao jing) and the *Guhyakapada-sutra* (Miji jing) state that the Three Vehicles were taught on the second day.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) states six or seven weeks; the *Xingxian jing* states seven or seven weeks; the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü) states eight or seven weeks;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhilun) states fifty times seven days; and the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra* (Shier you jing) states one year. Since the durations are inconsistent, the accounts of what was taught are likewise different.

All of these accord with the specific circumstances, which is why there are differences in what is seen and heard. As for the current mention of "three weeks," the *Nidāna Sūtra* (*Inguo jing*) states:
"At the beginning of his attainment of enlightenment, the Buddha reflected for the first seven days, thinking: 'My Dharma is subtle and profound; there is no one capable of receiving it.'"

During the second seven-day period, he contemplated the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings; during the third seven-day period, he contemplated who should first hear the Buddha-dharma.

This particular sutra accords somewhat with the present teaching. However, according to the contemplations of the present [text], it speaks exclusively of the Dharma being great while the capacity [of the listener] is small;
thus, they desire *nirvāṇa*. It should be understood that what is called "contemplation" in these cases is entirely in accordance with the capacities [of the beings].

[The Buddha] sees [them], because the Tathāgata has already transcended applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), because he perceives objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because these are what is seen within the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
△ Second, clarifying that the faculties of those to be converted are dull.
"Sentient beings have dull faculties; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance. How can such as these be saved? III. The Third Part:
The Request of the Brahmā Kings and Śakra for the Teaching.
At that time, the various Brahmā kings (up to) respectfully joined their palms, paid homage, and entreated me to turn the wheel of the Dharma.

Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, there is always a ritual protocol for the Brahma King to request the Dharma. △ Fourth, clarifying the cessation of transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity:
"I then reflected to myself... (until) 'Why should I not preach the Dharma and instead quickly enter Nirvana?'"

Although entering extinction offers no benefit, when compared to the cause, it is said that there is a reduction in loss and a superior excellence; therefore, it is said: "It would be better not to preach and enter extinction.
△ Second, the use of skillful means by recollecting the Buddhas.
Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past, [the Bodhisattva] thought: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles.
He further considered that since the Buddhas of the past had used skillful means to gradually entice [beings], he could not bear to abandon them all at once.

"Why, then, should I not adopt this method? Generally speaking, although all Buddhas employ the same principle of first using provisional means and later revealing the ultimate truth for those of gradual capacity, [he resolved to follow their example].

The gate encompasses those sentient beings who are its objects; yet there remain those who are difficult to transform and those who are easy to transform, because the times in which they appear differ.
For example, consider Krukusunda Tathāgata, the foremost of the thousand Buddhas of the present Bhadrakalpa.
He appeared when the human lifespan was fifty thousand years; Kanakamuni appeared when it was forty thousand years; and Kāśyapa appeared when it was twenty thousand years.

Although all of them employed provisional means first and the ultimate truth later, this was specifically because the times were favorable and the capacities of beings were superior, making them easy to transform.

Our Original Teacher should have appeared when the human lifespan was ten thousand years, but specifically because there were no beings with the capacity to be saved, he postponed his appearance until the human lifespan had declined further.
When the human lifespan had decreased to one hundred years, he descended as an incarnation.

Although there were those capable of being saved, alas, sentient beings were deficient in both physical form and mind, and were further oppressed simultaneously by the five turbidities. Therefore, these sentient beings were truly difficult to save;
even though all Buddhas possessed the Dharma, they still had to provide salvation through expedient means. △ Third, the Buddhas appear and offer praise.
While engaged in this reflection, although he spoke of the three vehicles, it was solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.
Because their essential nature is identical through skillful means (*upāya*) and because their resonance and response are mutually appropriate, he received the present praise as "the foremost.

This is because, manifesting his body amidst the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), he compassionately provided crooked salvation and transformed those who were difficult to transform; thus, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he is called Śākyamuni.
The term "Ní" (尼) is merely a difference between the "Chǔ" (楚) and "Xià" (夏) dialects of the character "Móu" (牟). △ Fourth, revering and following the Buddha’s teachings:
"Śāriputra, you should know... [omitted] ...the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted; I have always spoken thus."
When one hears praise and utters "Namo Buddha," it is a response intended to show reverence and compliance.

Regarding the passage beginning with "contemplating" (*sīwéi*), this clarifies how he established his teachings in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. *Vārāṇasī* is a region within Central India; it is the name of a river.
Not far from the river, he established a royal city. It is also translated as "the river encircling the city," and the country derived its name from this. Furthermore, in ancient times...
Because deer were fed here, it was also called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). Following the three weeks [of meditation] after [his enlightenment], he proceeded to this place to preach the Dharma.
He clearly omitted the events concerning the site of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) and manifested the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, which the śrāvakas had never before seen or heard.
Therefore, the devas and humans below also mention only two kinds of wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). In the subsequent text, the Tathāgata likewise mentions only the house.
The internal admission of the three [vehicles], the parable of leaving the house and giving one [robe], and the section on "All Dharmas" below, correctly clarify the establishment of the teaching.

Although all dharmas are vividly present before one's eyes and seem as if they could be fully expounded, because their very substance is the quiescent true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), how could they be proclaimed?
Though they cannot be spoken of, yet one does not cling to silence; therefore, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), [the Buddha] first [establishes] the five [precepts].
The Buddha went to Vārāṇasī and spent the first summer retreat there training his disciples. First, he taught the Four Noble Truths to Kauṇḍinya, who attained the Path.
Next, he taught Aśvajit and Bhadrika about the blessings and happiness of rebirth in heaven through the practice of giving; both attained the fruit of realization simultaneously.
Third, he taught the same as before to the two, Kāśyapa and Kolita, and they all attained the noble fruits. These constitute the three rounds of teaching.

He delivered the five bhikṣus; now, being pursued by their past affinities, they were the first to attain deliverance. This is called "Below": it clarifies the initial appearance of the names of the Triple Gem.
Regarding the wheel, there are two meanings: movement and the crushing of obstacles.

The Buddha now turns the Dharma within his own mind so that it enters the minds of others, crushing their afflictions and transforming the ordinary into the sagely; therefore, it is called "Turning the Wheel of the Dharma."
Furthermore, when disciples receive and practice [the teachings], the place where afflictions are severed is called "birth" (nirvāṇa).
Thus, the one who can teach is named the Buddha; that which is taught is named the Dharma; and those who attain the fruit by relying on the Dharma are named the Arhat Saṃgha.
In this way, the names of the Three Jewels of the Hīnayāna first appeared in the world. From the passage "From long ago... onwards, he explains away doubts, saying: "As for these people..."

Regarding the statement that one can attain the fruit immediately upon first hearing [the teaching]: because I have long observed their delight in the Lesser Vehicle, I have accordingly praised the Lesser.
Therefore, now that they hear it for the first time, they are able to attain realization in accordance with their original practice and can quickly realize the fruit.

However, the meaning of "long ago" also implicitly contains the parable of the *parinirmita-śrāvaka* (the "burnt-out city") and the Buddha’s lifespan. △ Four: Properly Abandoning Expedient Means. Part One: Clarifying the Appropriate Capacity to Strike [the Truth].
[Sage]. Second, the clarification of the skillful means of right relinquishment. Now, for the first [part]:
"Śāriputra, you should know... it is precisely now the time to preach the Buddha-wisdom for their sake."

This is like first seeing the ground at the intersection of the four roads.

"He did not come," [the father] said. "Because he was free from obstacles. Having investigated and exhausted [all paths], his pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) was established; thus, when the elder saw him, he was moved to joy.
One thereby knows that the path of the Three Vehicles is broad and the gates of skillful means (*upāya*) are wide; it is no wonder that the sons vied with one another to emerge.

Having already gathered on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, those of the three vehicles and the three faculties all spoke out, requesting a prophecy. The Tathāgata then spoke for them and granted their prophecies;

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) constitute the essence of the vehicle of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). The provisional wisdom of the eight-footed [Buddha-body] constitutes the essence of the ox-cart. Question:
When the three children exit the boundary, do they all reach their respective original fruits? Answer: The two vehicles reach their ultimate fruit, whereas the Bodhisattva has not yet reached it.

thus, when the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* arrives, his practice over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is as yet not yet complete. △ Second, the Bestowal of Equality by the Elder.
Śāriputra, at that time, the elder [arrives] accompanied by many servants who attend and protect him.
This is a metaphor for the present preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, which reveals the provisional to manifest the real and grants the prediction of Buddhahood equally to all.

The phrase regarding the "various jewels" reveals the general [meaning], while all others reveal the specific. The virtues accomplished through practice serve as ornaments. The "railing" signifies the meaning of *dhāraṇī*;

The layered, elegant mats signify the four dhyānas and eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). The vermilion pillow signifies the use of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to bring rest to all discursive attachments.

The ox is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which can lead the other five perfections to the same place—the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It also signifies the broad and pervasive benefit of the two-fold welfare (of self and others).

Being pure and clean signifies the purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Being beautiful and excellent signifies the subtle and wondrous nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Having strength signifies non-retrogression.
Equanimity is the meaning of non-contradiction between *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; it is also the meaning of the composure of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*). To summarize:
by means of the sublime teaching, which elucidates the sublime principle and cultivates the sublime practice, one causes every action to accord with reality as swiftly as a rushing wind.

This is like the severing of doubts and the arising of faith within the three vehicles, thereby leading to the bestowal of equal prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Third, the inquiry and explanation of the reason why.

thus, this was not their original expectation. It is as if they had originally sought provisional vehicles, yet obtained a single reality beyond their expectations. △ IV. Investigating and Answering Whether Granting Three and One is False or Not.

This section has four parts: first, the inquiry; second, the direct answer; third, the reverse explanation; fourth, the confirmation and permission. I. Inquiry. II. Direct Answer. III. Reverse Explanation. IV. Confirmation and Permission.
First: "Śāriputra, what do you think? (up to: Is there any falsehood in this great jeweled carriage?

Previously three were promised, yet now only one is given. Since the promise and the gift thus diverge, it seems close to being false or deceptive; therefore, he asks. △ Second: Conforming [to the answer].
Answer:
Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One,” [and so on, until] “he rescues them from that burning house.

First, this is explained in accordance with three meanings: first, by means of saving their entire bodies and escaping the calamity, he directly answers to clarify that [the teaching] is not in vain; second, by means of...

The entire body is attained; this clarifies that it is not in vain. The three analogies bring forth what was promised; since these were originally expedient means, they further demonstrate that it is not in vain.
△ Third, the inverse explanation.
"World-Honored One, if it is as you say—that the elder [desires to benefit his children by giving them great carts]"—this is explained through two aspects based on three meanings.
First, regarding the granting of small [vehicles] while not actually giving one: even the granting of small [vehicles] is not in vain; this is revealed by way of contrast.

Second, regarding the fact that there were originally no small [vehicles]: skillfully using the pretext of granting small [vehicles] as a causal condition, he leads the children out of the house; this is the explanation.
It is not false. Furthermore, the three parables demonstrate that [the Buddha] bestows the great vehicle equally upon all, so that they may perceive the reality. △ Fourth, the confirmation:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
Second, the "Excellent" and the "One Seal. To be able to know these three is expedient means; to be able to know that one seal and its corresponding one is the reality.
△ Second, the correspondence of the Dharma in two parts: first, the general correspondence of the analogy to the root; second, the specific correspondence of the analogy to the phenomena.
Now, first:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this... [up to] anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The first phrase generally combines the preceding metaphor, using the Tathāgata to correspond to the elder. Regarding the ten virtues of the elder mentioned previously:
However, from among the six qualities of the Elder, only one quality is explicitly mentioned, while the others are implied by its shadow.
Now, within the ten titles of the Tathāgata, only the first—*amṛṣāvādī* (the one who speaks no falsehood)—is named as the title "Tathāgata," while the rest are implied by its shadow.

The previous commentary, based on the three lands (*tri-bhūmi*), combined the nation, city, and villages; now, when we speak of "all worlds" (*sarva-loka*), it encompasses the fivefold bases of existence.
...the land. Regarding the five [lands]: first is the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land). This refers to the land upon which the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) relies;
it takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence. However, this body and this land are non-different in essence; they are immutable and unchanging.

Free from marks and quiescent, this is called the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kāya-bhūmi*). Second is the Land of Realized Reward (*pūrṇa-vipāka-bhūmi*), which refers to the land upon which the Tathāgata’s perfected reward-body (*pūrṇa-sambhoga-kāya*) relies.
It takes the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as its essence. This is accomplished through the cultivation of merits such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) in the past;
it is adorned with unimpededness, wherein object and wisdom merge and dissolve, and is summoned by the realization of true reward. Therefore...

The first is called the Land of Actual Retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). The second is the Land of Physical Characteristics (*lakṣaṇabhūmi*), which refers to the land upon which the Tathāgata’s body—the ocean of marks consisting of atoms—rests.
It takes the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of one's own practice as its essence; it is accomplished through myriad virtues and adorned with various jewels.

It is circular and boundless; this is called the Land of Form-Characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇabhūmi*). Fourth is the Land of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāyabhūmi*), which refers to the land upon which the Tathāgata’s body of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) relies.
It has the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that benefits others as its essence. This is accomplished through the cultivation of merit.
Next, in accordance with what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they manifest various pure lands and five kinds of transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*)—
that is, the lands upon which the Tathāgata’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) relies— through the power of compassion, appearing in both large and small, superior and inferior forms.
These have the wisdom that accomplishes the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpādaka-jñāna*) as their essence, and arise from having practiced deeds for the benefit of others in the past.
Therefore, they are able to manifest various pure and impure lands in accordance with the minds of sentient beings; this is called the land of transformation.
Furthermore, although these bodies and lands each have five layers, they all merge the one body into the five bodies and the one land into the five lands.
Their wondrous form and wondrous mind interpenetrate in successive layers, like the gods sharing a common vessel.
Regarding the receiving of food: when each morsel is placed in the hand, its color and flavor differ. Here, the general text [is the same] while the specific meaning differs;

this specifically refers to the transformation-land (nirmāṇa-kṣetra) upon which the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) relies. The section beginning with "In all... clarifies reliance on the practice of healing to manifest the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa).
The section beginning with "And all... clarifies reliance on the noble practice (ārya-caryā) to manifest the virtue of wisdom (jñāna-guṇa); that is, by means of reality...
"Wisdom" corresponds to the internal wealth. "Endowed with" below corresponds to the external fields and houses by means of skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
"Great compassion" below corresponds to the servants. "Constantly seeking" below corresponds to all those to be converted, numbering five hundred.

"And then born" below corresponds to the cause of being startled by the fire and subsequently entering the burning house. "In order to deliver" below corresponds to those with whom there is a karmic affinity (*sabhāga-sattva*).
"This child is still within the house. Birth, old age, and so forth, correspond to the fires breaking out on all four sides. "To teach and transform" corresponds to the single gate.
By means of a single nature (*ekaprakṛti*), he preaches the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to enable them to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.

II. The Specific Application of the Simile’s Content (in four parts): 1. The application of the children’s attachment to the house; 2. The application of the provisional assumption of the three carts; 3. The application of... [text fragment]

[The Buddha] bestowed great chariots equally upon them. Regarding the four points for cross-referencing and verifying whether [the text] is erroneous or not: the first three [sections] correspond to the elder seeing the fire;
the second corresponds to the elder intending to rescue [his children]; and the third corresponds to the explicit clarification of his attachment to the house. Now, the first [point].
He sees all sentient beings who, despite undergoing the great sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, do not regard them as calamities.

Previously, it was only mentioned that fire arises from the four directions; its characteristics were very brief. Therefore, within this section on the "conjunction," he elaborates upon what he perceives.

This restates the principle that one must swiftly rescue and emerge [from suffering]. The Sage uses fire as a metaphor for suffering because fire can scorch and oppress, and suffering likewise can scorch and oppress;
furthermore, suffering is the very "flavor" of fire. In brief, all sufferings are derived from the three types of suffering:

the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). Although the sutras emphasize the suffering of change, [all three are present].
Regarding "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): it is subsumed within the entirety of "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which pervades all forms of suffering.
Because it can displace all sufferings and lead them together toward impermanence before coming to an end, it is included [within the latter] and not mentioned separately.

Furthermore, the reason why most of the text explains matters primarily in terms of the two fires of cause and effect is that ignorance (*avidyā*) is capable of encompassing the three poisons in their entirety, as well as the fires of the afflictions of the "equal-share" category (*sama-bhāga*). Greed and attachment pursue...

"Seeking equality" means being able to encompass and exhaust the fire of karma consisting of the seven branches. Although afflictions and karma within the causal stage have not yet produced their results, they are already capable of scorching and oppressing the mind and body.
Birth, old age, sickness, and so forth encompass and exhaust the fire of the results consisting of the five aggregates.
This precisely belongs to the method of burning. It clarifies that sentient beings have already been scorched and boiled; yet they still take suffering to be pleasure.

This means they do not perceive the fire of karma within their bodies, nor do they realize the fire of delusion within their minds. They feel no alarm as body and mind are about to fall, and they feel no dread as the evil realms beckon.
They remain complacent with what is presently before them, saying they feel no revulsion, while remaining entangled and dormant regarding the future.

It is said: "Seeking no liberation, one wanders incessantly through saṃsāra. It is said: "Rushing to and fro in all directions, one’s entire being is transformed into the master of suffering, and the evil realms are transformed into one’s home.
Therefore it is said: "Though one encounters great suffering, one does not regard it as a calamity. Question:

Is the meaning of this section the same as that of "clinging to the house"? Answer: Only when one is enticed [by the realm] and does not emerge from it is it called "clinging to the house. 2. Combined with the Long [Text].
This refers to those who are to be rescued.
When Śāriputra saw this, [he realized that] sentient beings could not be liberated by these means.

"Those who should be pulled out" reveals the compassionate heart of the Father who shares the same essence, which internally bears the responsibility to extract them from suffering and bestow upon them happiness.
Question: Since the Buddha taught the Three Vehicles for the sake of his three sons who had a karmic connection with him, why do you speak of "sentient beings"? Answer:
From the perspective of the primary cause (*nidāna-hetu*), he regards all beings equally as if they were his only son, and intends to deliver them all impartially.

However, because those who are first able to resolve their minds toward liberation and whose roots of goodness have already matured are enabled to attain emancipation first, he always says [the teaching is] "for the sake of all..."

This is the general observation. From "Śāriputra" onwards, [the text] generally intends to apply both the distinct and the common teachings; yet [the beings] are unable to relinquish their expedient means.
△ Third, the explicit explanation of attachment to the house.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings (up to) by what means could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom?

Even if they were able to resolve their minds to seek liberation, because their current bodies specifically belong to the realm of *pariccheda* (segmented existence) and they are currently occupied with saving themselves from suffering, by what means could they enter the subtle and profound gate?
This corresponds to the aforementioned meaning of "the single gate being narrow and small.

II. The second section combines the hypothetical provision of the three carts into three parts: first, combining the preparatory application of skillful means; second, combining the actual application of skillful means.
Third, the skillful means of harmonious compliance.
First: "Śāriputra, just as that elder... [up to] "...the Buddha-vehicle for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The first part reiterates that his former body and hands could not be saved; the section beginning with "but" reiterates that he can be saved through skillful means; and the section beginning with "the Tathāgata" [reiterates this].
First, the general synthesis: by means of the power of spiritual wisdom, it is taught that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) cannot be saved [by those of inferior capacity]. Next, the specific synthesis:
intending to teach the Three Vehicles in order to accommodate the inclinations of their prior dispositions, the provisional Mahāyāna teachings are identical to the ultimate (real) teachings;
in terms of the cause, they are called the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and in terms of the fruit, they are also called the Buddha Vehicle. △ Second, the correct application of skillful means.
And he spoke these words: "You all must not [fear]... and so forth, until they attained immeasurable peace and happiness.

Although the following passage contains the sense of the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, one need not be overly literal regarding this. For within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there still exist the twelve links of dependent origination and the six perfections;
why, then, should it be explained solely in terms of the Four Noble Truths? Furthermore, the triple world is described as a burning house.

To speak of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as coarse and defiled is to point out their faults. This is because those sons [of the Buddha] have regressed from the Great Vehicle to the Small, and further encountered heterodox outsiders;

they are deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*) and mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Taking these five locations to be secure, they regard them as supreme, pure, and a refuge.
To counteract this, their faults are demonstrated, and by means of the wondrous fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which are free from outflows (*anāsrava*), [the truth is revealed].
This transforms that former mind seeking liberation. "I now" refers to exhorting them toward faith; "you all" refers to exhorting them toward practice.
Furthermore, "again" and so forth expresses praise for its rarity, causing them to give rise to a joyful aspiration. △ Third, the combined application of conforming skillful means.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings (up to) who, seeking the ox-cart, emerge from the burning house—those who possess the nature of wisdom within—because they previously regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and turned to the Small, they have cultivated and established the natures of wisdom of the three vehicles.

This phrase also extends through the following two sections. As for those who, upon hearing [the teaching] from the Buddha, are immediately able to believe it: this is because they have cast themselves toward what they originally delighted in.

Therefore, because they are able to emerge quickly, because they attain *nirvāṇa* early, and because they achieve awakening by hearing the teachings of others, they are called "Hearers" (*śrāvaka*) since people follow conditions.
Furthermore, because people are named after the Dharma, it is called the "Vehicle of Hearers" (*śrāvakayāna*). As for those who are like sheep:
although they dwell in reliance upon humans, they are unwilling to look back at the herd behind them; so too are the various Hearers, even though they [dwell]...

The assembly has no dissent. However, they lack the practice of benefiting others. In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* is called "Pratyekaka-ra," which means "Solitary Enlightened One" (*yuanjue*) or "Independently Enlightened One" (*dujue*).
Zhi Li said: "The Solitary Enlightened One also contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination;

however, there is a distinction between those who encounter a Buddha and those who do not, based on the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. This is because they too have previously heard this Dharma in the past."
Therefore, as for "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), by virtue of these causes and conditions, it has existed inherently from the beginning; it was not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans.
The wisdom capable of entering [this state] is likewise so. Hence, it is called spontaneous wisdom. Furthermore, the Pratyekabuddha is one who practices according to the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma from others, his practice was slight, yet his own investigation of its meaning was vast;

thus, he was able to contemplate it deeply, both in its forward and reverse orders, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes. Although he did not rely on others for his realization, he would occasionally manifest supernatural powers to deliver sentient beings, much like a deer that looks back with compassion.
One who seeks omniscience is one who is able to know internal phenomena and internal designations.
It can understand. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the phenomena expressed beyond the principles, as well as the names that express them, it can also know and understand them;
this is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), which is the wisdom of the *śrāvakas*. Now, for the sake of those seeking to become Bodhisattvas, one wishes to transcend the two vehicles.
Buddha-wisdom is precisely the "knowledge of the modes of the path" (*mārgajñatā*); it means being able to employ all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas to give rise to [enlightenment].

That which gives rise to all the seeds of goodness in sentient beings is called the Bodhisattva’s wisdom (*bodhisattvajñāna*). However, when considered in terms of its essential capacity for knowing, it is called spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*);
when considered in terms of not being obtained from another, it is called teacherless wisdom (*anācāryajñāna*).

Furthermore, although the name "spontaneous" is the same as that of the Pratyekabuddhas, their spheres of activity are not the same. These three aforementioned wisdoms all encompass both cause and fruit. Regarding...
The term "Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision" refers exclusively to the stage of fruition.
When a bodhisattva practices by taking this as their object, they penetrate from cause to fruition, like an ox moving from near to far.

One must understand that although the "ox-cart" is mentioned here, because it does not clarify the ox's virtuous characteristics or the cart's magnificent beauty, it belongs to the provisional (upāya). △ Third, the section on "Equalizing."
Two great chariots were bestowed. First, the presentation of the analogy; second, the application to the Dharma. Now, for the first:
"Śāriputra, just as that elder (up to) bestowed great chariots upon his sons."
A brief summary of the two meanings: escaping calamity and equal bestowal. △ Second, the application to the Dharma in two parts: first, the application to escaping calamity;
second, the application to equal bestowal. Now, the first:
"The Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "...attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa from the perilous path of fear."
Regarding the gateway of the teachings, as for the character "Buddha" (佛) being placed at the beginning:

when the Buddha was in the world, among the ninety-six kinds of heterodox outsiders, none did not claim for themselves that they had attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) and were able to transcend birth and death; yet these were merely empty words, entirely devoid of actual substance.

Only that which is spoken by the Buddha possesses both teaching (*śāsana*) and meaning (*artha*), and can lead toward *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the title "Buddha" is employed to distinguish [this teaching] from that of heterodox outsiders.
Teaching is precisely that which expresses the principle it intends to express; only then does it fulfill the function of being a teaching.
Just as a door has its function only when there is emptiness contained within it, so too does the gateway of conditioned phenomena have its utility.

Now, since the dharma and the metaphor are presented together, it is called the "Buddhist Gateway. Question: Previously, it was said that there is only one gateway, and again, that it is narrow and small.
Therefore, it was set aside and not employed. Why do you now say that immeasurable people have emerged through this gate? Answer:

Did I not say previously that this gate is a dual fusion of the provisional and the real, and is thus called "the sole"? Because it is the reality within the provisional, its principle is extremely profound and subtle.
Those with weak roots of goodness cannot sustain this; therefore, it was not employed because it was considered too narrow and small. Furthermore, because it is the reality within...

This is a provisional [expedient] means. Within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), he distinguishes and teaches three [vehicles]. Thus, hundreds of thousands of millions [of beings] emerge from it;

subsequently, they again receive the revelation and clarification. They attain *nirvāṇa*, yet this is spoken of according to the majority of cases, because bodhisattvas under the provisional teachings have not yet attained it.
This above summarizes the meaning of escaping the calamity. △ Second, the summary of the equal bestowal.
At that time, the Tathāgata had this thought: [omitted] "...it can produce the pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss.
This is the initial basis for the equal distribution. These [passages] below correspond to the mind of equal distribution.
The parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is precisely the Great Nirvāṇa without abiding. These [passages] below correctly correspond to the equal distribution, as established by all Buddhas.
Those who provide them with the means of entertainment [attain] the various three vehicles, which also yield a small portion of dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, and so forth.
Now, this is the wondrous principle of the true mark (*tathatā*) of the One Vehicle, the seed-wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*) of the One Vehicle Prajñā.
This is what the Sages have praised. Regarding the statement "able to give birth to equality" and so forth:

by means of this single characteristic and single essence, which is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*), one is able to give birth to the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*).

It is pure, wondrous, and supreme, for it is the Dharma-joy of the Distinct Teaching (*bie-jiao*). Therefore, this sutra is like the mouth of the ocean, capable of encompassing all streams and returning them together to the great sea.
The purport [of this teaching] can be seen here. △ Fourth, the combined inquiry and explanation regarding whether [the teaching] is delusory or not:
"Śāriputra, it is like that elder... (up to)... the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, yet they are simply unable to receive it all."
They were unable to receive it all. What should be done about this? △ Third, the conclusion of the answer:
Śāriputra, for these reasons... [up to] ...he distinguishes and teaches three within the Single Buddha Vehicle.
By means of my Buddha-eye, I see that all my sons within the burning house of the triple world are about to be harmed by the fire;
for the sake of the causal conditions to cause them to emerge quickly, I have differentiated the One Vehicle and taught it as three. △ Second, the verse-text has two parts:
first, the statement of intent; second, the citation of the verses. Now, the first [part]:
The Buddha, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses.
In the following text, he first briefly indicates the various fears and difficulties; next, he clearly explains the harms of poison and the calamities of fire.

He cites the three paths as metaphors for the six realms of existence—specifically humans, ghosts, and animals—as these are the ones that can exist within the house, and thus they are used here as illustrations. △ Second.

The verses are presented in two parts: first, an extensive restatement of the preceding parable; second, an exhortation to believe and propagate [the teaching]. The first part has two sections: first, the restatement of the parable;

second, the restatement of the Dharma. The first of these has two sections: first, an extensive restatement of the original parable; second, a brief restatement of the events of the parable. The first of these has two sections:
first, an extensive restatement of the dilapidated house; second, the formal restatement of the burning house. This is the first.
For example, it is as if an elder had a large house (up to) such immeasurable perils and terrors.
The verses and the long prose are seen in relation to one another through expansion and abbreviation. Where the long prose is extensive, the verse is abbreviated;

where the verse is brief, it is because the matter has already been expanded upon in the long prose. Generally, the long prose treats the darkness of ignorance and [the cycle of] birth and old age in detail.
The "fire of illness" is discussed in terms of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).

Now, as for the verse’s reference to the three realms, it is because the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists solely of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), and thus the manner in which it is burned is very evident; therefore, by means of the secondary retribution, the primary retribution is revealed.

If one were to further apply the metaphors of "sharp" and "dull" afflictions to represent ghosts and animals, it would likely be too far-fetched. The two characters "Elder" (*sthavira*) encompass the ten [stages].
Regarding "Virtue" (*guṇa*), it is equivalent in meaning to the Buddha’s pervasiveness (*vyāpti*). There is one [section] below;

among the three types of suffering, first concerning material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they are collectively subject to the *saṃskāra-skandha* and are said to be impermanent. This is very similar to the characteristic of a great house being worn out and never ceasing.
The two phrases "pervasive" (*pari*) and "obstructing" (*vṛti*) resemble the foulness within material phenomena. There are five hundred [lines] below, clarifying "abiding" (*sthiti*).

These consist of three categories: namely humans, ghosts, and animals. However, by using "five hundred" as a metaphor for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), the three types of beings are thereby included within it.
The following verses collectively manifest the state of being filled with the three poisons (*tri-doṣa*).

From "owls and hawks" onwards, they reveal the various strange and monstrous appearances of the animal species within the house. From "in every place" onwards, they further clarify that [these creatures] pervade the interior of the house.

It was filled with malevolent spirits, each manifesting its own hideous form. Seeing that all things inanimate were dilapidated and decayed, as well as foul and putrid, they were certainly unfit for habitation;
as for those that were sentient, they were treacherous and wicked, appearing entirely like vengeful enemies.
Furthermore, it is not possible to dwell there for even a moment. △ Second, the formal verse on the burning house:
"This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person... [omitted] ...poisonous harms, fires, and calamities are manifold."
"The house belongs to one person" means that, as it says below, "I alone am able to provide protection. Regarding "having recently gone out":

because the Buddha had previously instructed them to carefully guard against the fires of ignorance and so forth, and because not long after the World-Honored One had departed for other regions due to various conditions, his sons became negligent and unrestrained;
this was precisely the cause for the fire to break out. As for the passage following "afterwards":
The fire blazes forth. The three lines beginning with "Suddenly" manifest the extreme ferocity of the burning power.
The lines beginning with "Beams and rafters" manifest the state of both sentient and insentient beings being consumed by the flames—terrifying and pitiable—all due to their meager merit.
Consequently, it was difficult for the multitude to assemble. △ Second, a brief verse on the parable and its meaning, in three parts: first, the verse on attachment;
second, the verse on the hypothetical assumption; third, the verse on exceeding expectations. Now, the first.
At that time, the owner of the house stood outside the gate (until) he still took pleasure in his play and would not cease.
As for "standing outside the gate," the Buddha observed that sentient beings are constantly afflicted by burning heat and distress, and thus do not rest upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas;
therefore, he stands like a man. Sentient beings and the Buddha share the same compassion and longing. Now that they have been set ablaze, he is their savior.

This is because their compassion is interconnected. It is like hearing the words of others, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the *nāga*, it is also because the Dharma is identical to the person.

As for the passage beginning "You sons," although the sons had originally not yet left the house, the statement that they "entered" is because they possessed the causal conditions for hearing the Dharma from the Victorious One (the Buddha) in the past;
thus, by relying on the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), they gave rise to the manifesting cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
The "great mind" is like having already emerged, because the fruit does not depart from its cause.

Next, because ignorance and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are powerful and dominant while the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are weak, [the mind] is forgotten as soon as it arises; therefore, it is like re-entering. Regarding the passage "the elder went down," the previous section concerned entering out of fear of seeing fire burning due to the cause of visual perception;
the present section concerns entering out of fear upon hearing someone speak of it due to the cause of auditory perception. Thus, the person and the phenomenon are mutually illustrated.

This is the meaning. "Appropriately" (方宜) refers to what follows below; although it praises the instructions, it already contains the sense of "providing what is suitable" (擬宜). "The various sons" and so forth refer to their attachment to the house.
△ Second, the verse on the provisional assumption.
At that time, the elder had this thought... (up to) "...therefore, all you people, I am now happy.
(First three lines). The verse uses the three vehicles as a metaphor; "announces to the subordinates" refers to the actual use of the three vehicles.
"The sons... and below refers to the verse on conforming to skillful means. "The elder sees his sons... and below clarifies that the elder rejoices in having preserved their innate natures. However—

Regarding the statement that "nurturing and giving birth is extremely difficult": it is because one must teach and transform [beings] over many kalpas, employing various skillful means to gather them in and cause them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment;

this alone is already difficult. How much more so after they have resolved their minds, when one must repeatedly guide and protect them, causing them to grow gradually and ensuring they do not regress, until they finally reach maturity.
Therefore, it is said that nurturing and giving birth is extremely difficult. This is still...

This refers to those who have resolved upon the Great Mind and do not regress. As for the practitioners of the three vehicles today, they initially resolve upon the Great Mind, but midway they regress and practice the Small [Vehicle].
