Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "If one possesses the internal cause but lacks the external condition, one will not attain the fruit of Buddhahood. If one possesses the external condition but lacks the internal cause, one will likewise not attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Only when both internal and external causes and conditions are complete will one attain the fruit
As his years grew older and he became increasingly impoverished, he gradually wandered until he encountered his own native land.

This section of the parable illustrates that although one may regress from the Great Vehicle and practice the Small Vehicle, by swiftly seeking liberation, one establishes the primary cause for the Buddha to manifest his body.
"As his years grew older" means that although one has regressed from the Great Vehicle, through the power of internal permeation by True Suchness (tathatā), it causes...
The roots of goodness previously planted gradually increase; yet, though they have grown large, they still lack a place to rest.
How much more so for those who are destitute of the wealth of the Dharma and externally afflicted by suffering and distress?

Therefore, they race within the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena—sometimes seeking the light of fire, craving the purity of water, delighting in the circulation of wind, or contemplating the formation of dust.
Thus, I hope to obtain the Dharma-robe to cover my body and the flavor of the Dharma to nourish my mouth.
Although such pursuits are heterodox and can only increase birth and death, this very mind that seeks them out nonetheless accords with its original nature.

Therefore it is said: "Gradually traveling on, one encounters and heads toward one's native land. One's "native land" (honkoku) is none other than one's original nature (honshō), or alternatively, it is the fundamental vow (hongan) embraced by the World-Honored One.
Because this accords with one's original nature and fundamental vow, it brings about the manifestation of the Buddha’s body, which serves as the direct cause for escaping suffering.
2. The second section, "The place where one dwells does not conflict," uses this to illustrate that external conditions do not [conflict].
There are two parts. First, it clarifies the city where the elder resides; second, it clarifies the thoughts the elder conceives.
Now, for the first:
his father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him (up to the point where) merchants and traders were also very numerous.
The following passage speaks of the body and the land; it should be understood, for now, in terms of what is seen by those of middling faculties during their entry, abiding, and realization.
Regarding the phrase "from the beginning": this does not mean a chronological beginning, but rather conveys the sense of concealment and manifestation.

It means that in the past, when these four sons had already resolved upon the Great Mind from the perspective of the responsive transformation (nirmāṇa), the fire of the response ceased along with the exhaustion of the fuel that could provoke it.

He remained hidden; yet, because the World-Honored One did not abandon his great compassion, he manifested through the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that is identical with the Dharma itself, never departing for other lands but always remaining in this realm.
Thus it is said he "came first. Because he sought those with the capacity [to receive the teaching] and found none, he temporarily halted in *nirvāṇa*.
He is like the capital city that can repel the enemies of the five abodes and prevent the errors of the two deaths.

Regarding "cessation": because it advances toward the nature of the non-dharmic and its own enjoyment, it retreats from the impure lands of transformation and is instead the pure land inhabited by the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Below that, "his household" reveals the elder’s wealthy family; this may be metaphorically aligned with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Just as people, laborers, and wealth all depend upon a house to dwell, so too do the dharmas of form, mind, and so forth, likewise depend [upon it].
One abides in the true state of suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the passage "gold and silver, etc.," this is a separate enumeration;

it need not be paired with every detail, for its general meaning does nothing more than manifest his wealth. Some point to this as the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet even in the *Avataṃsaka*, within a single land...
It is able to harmonize all lands, yet it cannot be pointed out directly; thus, the *Sūtra on the Exposition of the Heavens* states:

"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the Wheel of the Four Truths; now, once again, you turn the most wondrous [Dharma]. Furthermore, in the Tathāgata’s response to Śikhin and others, although it says, "I have seen my body for the first time," it seems that the *Avataṃsaka* has already been revealed.
This is according to the statement: "Except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna. Based on this...
These two passages indicate that those of the Two Vehicles are directly within the category of those who neither see nor hear [the Buddha].
This section and the subsequent section on "what is kept in mind" together serve as a metaphor for the four children not losing the external condition of the World-Honored One’s care;
therefore, he stops midway to await their arrival. △ Second, clarifying what is kept in mind.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages (until he reached a state of) tranquility and happiness, no longer harboring any anxieties or worries.
This passage consists of three sections: first, it clarifies the wandering of the impoverished son, beginning from the four quarters; second, his encounter with his native land;

and third, his journey through districts and towns until he finally arrives at his father’s city. These stages all proceed from the distant to the near, serving as a metaphor for the gradual growth of internal causes.

Each time the father descended, he manifested the sorrow of losing his son to illustrate the absence of an opportunity [for awakening]. Again, he descended to manifest the joy of regaining his son to illustrate the presence of an opportunity.
Furthermore, in the preceding section, it was explained in terms of the World-Honored One’s bodily karma providing secret empowerment, as expressed by the phrase "the place where he dwells."
This refers to the secret empowerment of mental karma; by means of what is contemplated through speech, it becomes a superior, augmenting factor for opening understanding.

△ Second, although father and son see each other at the poor shop, they do not seek [one another]. This has two parts: first, the meeting of father and son; second, not seeking at the poor shop. The first part has two sections:
first, using the son’s seeing of the father as a metaphor for the mind that fears the Great [Vehicle]; second, using the father’s seeing...
The following is the first illustration of how he consoled and comforted him with a parable.
At that time, World-Honored One, the impoverished son, having been hired out for wages... (until) having formed this thought, he fled away in haste.

Regarding "those who work for hire": after the four sons had retreated from the Mahāyāna, they midway adopted the practice of the Hīnayāna as their strength and sought swift liberation as their reward;
thus, they were like hired laborers. Alternatively, some relied on heterodox paths and abandoned right view, while others relied on right view and abandoned heterodoxy;
this is called "turning back and forth. Both types were driven by the power of their vows to seek liberation.

Holding [this], they are secretly aided by the Right Path, thereby eventually perfecting the roots of goodness for seeing the Buddha; thus it is like unexpectedly encountering one’s father’s house. These are all the causes for seeing the Buddha.
“Standing at the door” clarifies the realm that the impoverished son fears. Standing at the side of the gate means he is not standing directly in front;
seeing from afar means he does not face him directly. This is like the roots of goodness of those who aspire to the Lesser Vehicle, which, though matured, have not yet—

Upholding the orthodox teaching is identical to dwelling at the side of the gate. Furthermore, although there may be those with the capacity to strike upon the teaching, they have not yet personally been warmed by its fire;
thus it is said, "seen from afar. If one were to apply the Dharma to the person, these four sons would still be outside the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
How could the commentators dare to treat them merely as words of partial truth or mere emptiness? Seated beneath the lion throne, he is adorned with all manner of ornaments.

These are all that which should belong to the noble and eminent; they are like the land of the Victorious One (Sambhogakāya), naturally endowed with the adornments of the ten thousand virtues (*daśasahasra-guṇa*).
However, because these ten thousand virtues are brought about by ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*), those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle are made to give rise to fear.

From the passage "The impoverished son" onwards, it correctly clarifies the arising of this fearful mind: seeing that the elder possesses great power and influence, he subsequently regrets having come, and because of... [text truncated]
Regarding the place where he is seen: it does not coincide with the mind that seeks him out. Thus one reflects:
"This might be the King, or perhaps someone like the King. To obtain that object, one must be able to enter and exit his gate.
If I were to entrust myself to this [situation] while still a mere commoner, and if he were to force me into service, what means would I have to resist him? It would be better to depart quickly.
To depart would be the wondrous course. Moreover, in this poor neighborhood, food and clothing are easily obtained; thus, one may quickly relieve oneself from hunger and cold.
This is like the four sons who withdrew from the Great Vehicle because they possessed only a mind that delighted in the Small Vehicle.

Had they heard of the majestic adornment of the practice of the ocean [of the Mahāyāna], they would not only have refused it, but would have felt fear. They merely exerted the power of their petty wisdom within the poverty of "mere emptiness" (prajñapti-śūnyatā).
He sought the robe of the eightfold patience and the flavor of the four noble truths merely to sustain his body and mouth;
for this reason, he was terrified by the great [fire] and fled in haste. △ Second, using the analogy of a father seeing his son to describe the manner of comforting and reconciling him.
At that time, the wealthy elder [from the passage] on the lion throne... became even more terrified and fainted, falling prostrate upon the ground.
Yet the World-Honored One, in his supreme field of response, did not abandon his compassionate vows from the lion throne, but awaited all those with whom he had a karmic affinity.
Because those who had previously resolved their minds naturally cast themselves toward him, a single knock was answered; it was like the moon appearing in clear water.

"Upon seeing his son, he recognized him and his heart was filled with great joy. This is because, in the past, there was no capacity within him to evoke such a response, so he constantly felt compassion;
now that he is finally able to evoke it, his heart is filled with great joy. The following passage explains the reason for this arising of joy: "Because his wishes have been fulfilled. Question:
There are those who interpret the lion throne as the state of fearlessness within the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Furthermore...
If some take the city of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) to refer to the "remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*), is this not a contradiction between what precedes and what follows? Answer:

Neither of these two explanations is correct, for they do not accord with the meaning of "intermediate" as used in the sūtras. Although the scope of the term "intermediate" is broad, [it does not apply here].
Furthermore, this advancement is not the self-natured self-enjoyment [body]. Why, then, is it designated as the "emptiness of the ultimate meaning" (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?

If it were restricted solely to the remaining lands (sāmbhogika-kṣetra) and did not encompass the fruit of retribution (vipāka), then those who enter and abide therein might perceive the Buddha at this location.
However, for those of the highest capacity, once the truth is revealed, they are able to transcend and ascend directly to the stage of sainthood; in such a case, where else would one seek the Buddha?

Therefore, it stops here. It should be understood as referring to both the *sāmbhogika* (enjoyment) and *nairmāṇika* (emanation) lands of the *mahā-śrāvaka* (great disciple), yet it speaks of them by way of "seeing.

Advancing, it is not the *svasaṃbhogika* (self-enjoyment); retreating, it is not the inferior *nairmāṇika*. If one does not interpret it thus, how could the superior function of this sutra merely cause one to enter the kalpa and then stop?

It then sends [the practitioner] downward; the metaphor indicates that the Buddha intends to employ the Great [Vehicle]. Thus, with... The translation reflects the technical terminology of Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda scholasticism.)
The wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) acts as the agent of elimination, while names, phrases, and syllables are the objects to be eliminated.
Regarding the "secondary" [teaching]: since these four types of disciples are of gradual capacity, it would seem appropriate to apply the Hīnayāna as the primary teaching for them;

however, because the Tathāgata caused them to resolve upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) in the past, he still employs the Mahāyāna as the intended application. Thus, the Great Teaching conversely becomes the secondary application. Regarding the "urgent pursuit": one desires to proceed directly...
This explains the Mahāyāna. As for those who are about to return [to the source], their past roots of goodness can be awakened; they are taught to revere the life of wisdom like a messenger.
The meaning it elucidates is most consistent with principle and exhilarating to the nature, like a swift run that achieves its result with great speed.

He said, "Go and seize him. The impoverished son was startled and jumped down; this clearly manifests the state of being terrified by the Great [Vehicle], thereby illustrating his lack of spiritual capacity (*anāśraya*).
He was startled because he had suddenly heard the Great Teaching. When the objective realm and the mind are at odds, it is called "startled" (*e*).

If I were to seek *nirvāṇa* within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), or seek *bodhi* within afflictions (*kleśa*), how would that differ from being attacked by a murderous bandit? For this reason, he voiced his resentment.
Again, he cried out loudly. The next two lines mean: "If I originally lacked compassionate vows, why would I employ this ultimate teaching?

The passage from "The messenger descends" onwards clarifies that since [the recipient] will not accept the profound and wondrous Dharma, why not immediately inform them of the sudden teaching on the truth that suffering and affliction are like illusions?
Therefore it is said: "The more one clings to them, the more urgent they become"; even if they lack the capacity [to understand], they will surely be compelled [to listen].
Because he was compelled to accept it, it is said that he was "forcibly led back. This serves as a general analogy for those who do not accept [the teaching].
In the passage beginning with "At that time," the text further clarifies the state of those who lack the capacity for the profound fear [of saṃsāra].

Those who are seized despite being innocent are like the great bodhisattvas (*mahāsattva*), who, taking compassionate vows as their motivating karma, should return to the realm of existence to manifest birth and death that are like illusions; yet they remain among those of the two vehicles.
He looked at them and saw that they were all undergoing the punishment of imprisonment for their karmic offenses. "Since I have no such karma, why am I being seized? he thought.
"If there is no means of escape, how can I avoid falling directly into saṃsāra? Thus he said, "I shall surely die. As he reflected further, his fear grew;

he lost his original mind and fell into a state of stupor, which is called *mūrcchā*. His seven limbs were bound by shackles and fetters as he lay prostrate, submerged in ignorance; this is called *patita* (falling).

The "ground" (bhūmi) is the sign of being terrified of greatness. Regarding what follows, whether in terms of principle or metaphor, these do not exceed a forced accommodation to the sentiment of fearing greatness and desiring smallness;
one need not be overly pedantic regarding them. △ Second, the poor at the marketplace who do not seek.
The father saw them from afar and spoke to his messenger, saying: "Go to the poor quarter to seek food and clothing.
As for "seeing from afar," one was standing to the side outside the gate, while the other was sitting upright inside the gate;

because they were both separated by a great distance, both the father and son are said to have seen them from afar. Furthermore, the elder son seeing his father is like the way those of the Three Vehicles can evoke a response.
The internal cause: now that the father sees his son, it is like the external condition provided by the Tathāgata’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because this stimulus and the teaching strike one another, he is able to move the Buddha to manifest his body and deliver him. Regarding the passage below, there is no need for forced interpretation;

it all expresses the intent to cease [the Buddha’s] transformative activity. The phrase "with coldness" (or "below") means: since they have already formed a karmic connection, one must not cast them aside as being beyond concern.
Furthermore, as for this person who has fallen to the ground and not yet regained consciousness, one cannot immediately give them the nectar of immortality;
rather, one first pours half a cup of cool water to relieve their distress, so that their minor roots from past lives may first ripen.

Thus, one employs a minor method to instruct them and cause them to awaken; therefore, the sprinkling of water to rouse them serves as a metaphor for not engaging them in conversation [until they are ready].
Just as one does not say, "This son should have a share of the treasure store. Below this, the intention for not speaking is explained:

because he has carefully examined the conditions and the seeds [of the son's capacity], he employs skillful means to protect him, suppressing his original aspiration so that those of lesser faculties do not likewise succumb to despondency.
Thus, he intentionally allows him to proceed wherever he wishes. Regarding the passage "The impoverished son," it refers to the joy born from seeing himself released. Furthermore—

Hearing that [the people] follow their own inclinations, he rises from the ground and goes directly to the quarters of the poor to seek the dharma-robe and the joy of dhyāna, so as to enable them to save themselves.

Having thus spoken this internal parable, he harbors within himself two kinds of roots of goodness—the great and the small—to serve as pillars for those who fear the Great Vehicle and delight in the Small.
First, because the capacity of the Great Vehicle has not yet matured, he manifests the appearance of fearing the Great.

First, because those of small capacity ripened first, their inclination toward the Lesser Vehicle over many kalpas was clarified. Since the small [vehicle] ripened first, they heard the Lesser Dharma first;
since the great [vehicle] ripened later, they subsequently heard the Great Dharma. Second, the account of this present life, such as being a hired laborer, who does not seek [the Lesser].
This has three parts: first, indicating the employment of skillful means; second, the actual employment of skillful means; third, the conclusion and demonstration.
He does not seek it. This is the first [section].
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, established a skillful means.
The preceding section spoke in terms of successive kalpas; from here below, he recounts the events following the Deer Park. △ Second, the main [section].
There are four types of skillful means (*upāya*). First, the skillful means of secret dispatching; second, the skillful means of wearing tattered clothing;
third, the skillful means of increasing the price; fourth, the skillful means of using a name. Now, the first.
He secretly dispatched two men whose physical appearance was haggard... (until) his father saw his sons, felt pity for them, and marveled at them.
"Secret" (*mi*) means to conceal within while manifesting without; "dispatched" (*qian*) means to send out by command.

Just as the World-Honored One commanded the great bodhisattvas to manifest the dual forms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is thus called "secretly dispatched. Since they had concealed their sublime marks, their physical appearance [was thus].

Emaciated. Because one has restrained the fragrance of the body, one’s majestic virtue (*tejas*) is diminished; it is not for this state of distress that one can find companionship. How could one draw near?
To investigate the truth and sever delusions is precisely the place of practice. "Direct" refers to the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.

As for the phrase "twofold giving," it likely means that the precepts and wholesome deeds within the realms can only suppress delusions and yield the fruits of human and celestial rebirths. If one were to let loose directly...

He exerts himself in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Not only does he subdue [the afflictions], but he can also sever them; not only does he obtain the fruits of humans and devas, but he can also attain the sublime, untainted (*anāsrava*) fruits beyond the realms.

Therefore, it is said that he is "doubly rewarded. Whether through subduing or severing, this is like the lowly labor of clearing away filth, which is further invigorated by working together with others.
In the passage beginning with "At that time," those who first take their wages are like those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Because his longing for the sublime and his aversion to the mundane were particularly intense, he first aspired to the cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), and subsequently eliminated suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

Thus, the Elder felt pity that he had abandoned the Great [Vehicle] and marveled at his grasping for the Small. If one relies on the fact that he has already attained this and fully recounts the aforementioned matters, then through the harmony of causes and conditions, the way of resonance and response is accomplished.
Nevertheless, it was simply because he had previously matured small-scale wholesome roots that he was able to encounter the Tathāgata.

He came to manifest his transformation and was born in the same place, yet he had not yet personally received the teacher’s guidance. Second, employing the expedient means of wearing tattered clothes:
on another day, through a window (until) by means of this expedient, he was able to draw near to his son.

The minor wholesome karmas capable of producing [the results] for the four sons above had first matured. The World-Honored One, intending to conceal his excellence and manifest inferiority, therefore first recounted the circumstances thereof.
The ancient commentary points to the "other" of another day as the Dharma-body.

Now, according to the various sons' subsequent regression from the Great Vehicle, the World-Honored One sought him at the place where he had originally resolved his mind but could not find him; having thus ceased his supreme response, [he manifested in an inferior form].
If one waits [for him], then the manifested body should likewise be designated as the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Therefore, it is said below that "devas and humans are constantly filled," so why must it necessarily be designated as the eternally quiescent [nirvāṇa]?

Although seeing from afar through a window is not comparable to looking closely within a bright hall, it is nonetheless different from the previous time when one could not see him while searching in the four directions.

Now, when the elder saw him from afar, he again longed to meet with him; yet, considering that the other possessed such a lowly and inferior body and dwelt upon a defiled ground, how could he bear to set foot there?
Nevertheless, because their natures were bound by kinship, he could not help but humble his own dignity to approach one of lower station.

Thereupon, he removed his fine robes and put on tattered rags; he covered his body in dust and took a refuse basket in hand, coming to work alongside them so as to remain near them without causing alarm.
This was the Tathāgata’s seventh of the ten great acts of grace toward sentient beings:
the grace of concealing superiority and manifesting inferiority. The *Dàcǎo* states: "The number of lotus-petal treasuries and atoms..."
The marks—the inconceivable and inexhaustible virtues as numerous as drops in the ocean—were all hidden and not manifest;

it was merely said that he had cultivated the thirty-two marks over a hundred kalpas and, through thirty-four moments of mind, severed the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

At the moment the Dharma-body of five factors was first perfected under the Bodhi tree, he appeared like an old bhikṣu, identical to the five arhats. Thus, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, he cast off his precious and noble robes and donned tattered garments.
Wearing soiled garments and holding a refuse-removal vessel, he went to where his son was. The commentary explains: the "dust-like" marks refer to the precious robes;
the thirty-two marks are the tattered, soiled garments; and the thirty-four minds are the refuse-removal vessel. The afflictions of seeing and cultivation are the very filth to be removed.
The right hand’s utility is like the provisional wisdom of the six-foot-tall [manifestation], appearing as if possessed of fear to demonstrate [the truth].
The practice of sharing the same illness: first, he speaks to his attendants; next, he draws near to his son's body, exhausting every means of compassionate salvation.

His speaking to the attendants is like the Dharma-gate for revealing the conditions of the Truths (*satya*). This section is due to the fulfillment of causes and conditions accumulated over many kalpas.
Now, he first manifests an inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) to accommodate them. △ Third, employing the skillful means of adding value, he later further declares:
"Ho! Man! (omitted) ... I also have old, worn-out servants; if you need them, I shall give them to you."
That he first addresses him as "man" after having rebuked him is intended to first rouse him from his stupor and then encourage him.
"Do not depart" is like using meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to subdue a distracted mind. "Increase the price" is like, based on concentration, further causing wisdom (*prajñā*) to arise;

it is not merely to subdue, but to cause one to progress toward severance. The *Śāstra* states that because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the impoverished son were burning intensely, [the Buddha] increased [his resolve].
Tainted by pride, they are ignorant of the supramundane Dharma-gates and seek only the superior and wondrous realms of humans and devas.
Now, in accordance with them, I shall first employ the remaining power of my precepts and meditative concentration as the price for the fruits of retribution for humans and devas.

Thus, the excrement that has been removed is like the delusions that have been subdued. Furthermore, because they have recently attained the opportunity to gather together, they employ sublime wisdom to sever the causes of rebirth;
yet even as they experience the fruits of rebirth beyond this realm, they still encounter old age and decay, which occurs due to their cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom.

Furthermore, one may employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). As for those who attempt to minutely correlate these numerical categories with the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), I fear they are being overly pedantic.
△ Fourth, the application of the term "usage" as a skillful means.
"Be at ease; I am like a father to you. (Until: "I shall further bestow upon you a name and call you my son.
Having received this exceptional encouragement, he again offered consolation, saying: "In my house, be at ease; I am like a father to you.
Do not harbor any further anxieties. He spoke of him as being like a father because he had come as a hired laborer for nearly twenty years.

Although you have now drawn near, there remains a distinction between the noble and the humble; one does not leap over the stages. Therefore, I first used the character "ru" (如) to grant you permission.
Had I rashly used the words "ji zhen" (即真)—meaning "immediately realizing the truth"—I fear you would have been startled and filled with doubt. This is why [I proceeded as I did].
The Buddha granted his permission, saying, "It is as your father intends. I am already old and incapable of further action; you are still young and should exert yourself.
Moreover, during your regular work, you have never shown the faults of others, such as deceit or indolence. From now on, you should act like a son born of me.
Although your advancement may not equal my own biological son, your retreat shall at least not be like that of other laborers. Thus he spoke.
At that time, [the Buddha] was about to change his name and bestow a title upon him.

This is like the case of the various sons who, from their initial resolve at the Deer Park to practice the Lesser Vehicle until now, have already attained for the first time a semblance of understanding of the "World-First Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Although they have not yet truly entered the stream of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), they do not fall back into the state of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). In a short while, they may be called "those born from the mouth of the Buddha through expedient wisdom."
True Son. This is like the impoverished son who first discards the title of a hired laborer and is already admitted into the stream of the sages.
△ Third, the conclusion showing that he does not seek to be a hired laborer.
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still remained in his original dwelling.

Because he had severed the arising of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), he was granted the name "son. Thus it is said: "Although he rejoiced at this encounter," yet because innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) was not yet exhausted and he remained in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), it is said:
"He still considered himself a hired laborer. These three successive instances refer to the twenty [years].

If these are combined, they amount to only forty years. This is because the twenty years of clearing away filth are used as a metaphor for the period from the Buddha’s first teaching of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park until his final teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. These represent the *Āgamas*;
during these twenty years, one merely clears away the defiled ignorance within the realm [of the senses], and thus it is likened to "filth. As for the practice...
The twenty household duties (*gṛhakārya*). If one explains the *Prajñāpāramitā* as commanded, it precisely corresponds to forty [years].

If one includes the current preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it then corresponds to the traditional accounts of his preaching for over forty years, including the supplementary characters and meanings.
If one does not permit the assignment of "removing filth" to the *Āgamas*, one likewise should not believe in the assignment of the twenty household duties to the *Vaipulya*.
This is the teaching. Regarding the phrase "those below this level trust each other in their hearts and minds":

it means that not only does the elder know that my body and mind are free from falsehood, but I too am able to know the elder. First he offers me a fair price, and subsequently he increases the value;
since both are not false, thereafter my mind and speech naturally correspond, being entirely devoid of falsehood or exaggeration. It is just as if the Tathāgata alone knew [my sincerity].

Question: Previously, based on two instances of twenty years, it was refuted that there was a separate period for the Vaipulya [sūtras] or a distinct Vaipulya section. However, if one examines the present text, it appears to fall after the Āgamas and before the Prajñā[pāramitā]. Although no specific time can be pointed out, it seems as though there is indeed a separate category. Answer: This is precisely the Vaipulya. Nevertheless, within the entirety of the Tathāgata’s holy teachings throughout his life, there are various stages. Specifically, regarding the Vaipulya, there are three types: first, the Vaipulya of the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, the Vaipulya of the Bodhisattva vehicle; and third, the Great Vaipulya. Regarding these three types of Vaipulya, the first is the Vaipulya of the Śrāvaka vehicle, which refers to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, and so forth. These were all taught during the period when the Tathāgata was still manifesting the Śrāvaka vehicle. The second is the Vaipulya of the Bodhisattva vehicle, which refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Pratyutpanna-buddhasaṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra*, and so forth. These were all taught during the period when the Tathāgata was manifesting the Bodhisattva vehicle. The third is the Great Vaipulya, which refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. These were both taught during the period when the Tathāgata was manifesting the Great Vehicle. Thus, although the Vaipulya is not distinct from the other vehicles, it is not the case that it does not exist separately. It is simply that the Tathāgata, within the body of his holy teachings throughout his single lifetime, taught them at different times. Therefore, the Vaipulya cannot be said to have existed only after the Āgamas and before the Prajñā[pāramitā]. Furthermore, the Vaipulya of the Śrāvaka vehicle is not necessarily limited to those sūtras mentioned above; rather, all sūtras taught during the period when the Tathāgata was manifesting the Śrāvaka vehicle are included therein. The same applies to the Vaipulya of the Bodhisattva vehicle and the Great Vaipulya. you may truly be called a *śrāvaka*. In the past, your capacity to receive offerings was limited to humans and devas; now, you may respond to the needs of the world.

This is an offering to those who have transcended the world. Within the text, there are seven instances of the character "jin" (now), all of which contrast the present with the past to express a heart of joy.

1. The grace of bestowing the Dharma; 2. The grace of manifesting the body for the sake of beings; 3. The grace of being solely devoted to others; 4. The grace of descending in form into the six realms;

In the fifth chapter, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," the Treatise states:

Thirdly, there are those who seek the Mahāyāna and possess a one-sided, fixed, and arrogant mind, giving rise to the thought that there are no separate vehicles for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas.
Because they grasp this erroneously, the Cloud [Parable] is taught as an antidote to this.
The parable of the rain should be understood as follows. Furthermore, it says: "As for the third person, they are made to understand the various vehicles;
the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach the Dharma with equality, so that according to the seeds of the roots of goodness of sentient beings, sprouts are produced.

Regarding the medicinal herbs, the ancients said: "That which possesses divine power to remove disease is called 'medicine' (yao). That which takes the form of being moistened and nourished is called 'herb' (cao). This is used as a metaphor for the medicine of practice."

Regarding "grass" as that which is cultivated through the practice of the teachings: the five aggregates that one grasps are the "grass," while the meditative concentration and wisdom based upon those aggregates are called the "medicine.

Although this section explains these matters specifically for those who are the intended audience, in reality, the earth serves as the basis for the growth of plants and trees, and the rain serves to moisten them so they may flourish; thus, whether plant or tree, all are the primary objects of its purpose.

Each has its own reception, flourishing individually like clouds. Now, in accordance with those who are the intended audience—like the medium-sized medicinal herbs—the parable of the medicinal herbs is taught by taking the general from the particular.
The text has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse. The first [part] has four sections: first, praising and assenting to what is to be said;
second, extensively explaining what was not previously reached; third, formally providing a corroborative exposition; fourth, the concluding praise.
[He] can know. First, at that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] "...the true merit is exactly as you have said.

Regarding the repeated praise "Excellent! Excellent!", there are two points: first, it describes how he skillfully grasped the provisional and the real regarding the preceding dharma and parable; second, it is because he was able to rely upon...
The analogy exhaustively depicts the states of both great fear and compassionate salvation. That which is herein explained is entirely the Tathāgata’s true and actual merit;
therefore, it is certified as being truly so by the Seal of Truth. △ Second, the extent to which others cannot reach.
The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable and boundless [teachings], such that even if one were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they could not be exhausted.
The four disciples have recounted only what they could recall, managing to capture the meaning of a single door of his transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa-vinaya*).

Beyond this, there are further immeasurable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for gathering and sustaining sentient beings; how could these be fathomed by the four disciples? Based on this, throughout the Tathāgata’s single lifetime...
Regarding the ritual of transformation (*huà yí*), one must rely upon the ten gates of our own school to ensure that nothing is omitted.

If one were to judge it solely by the principle of a single gate—proceeding from the small to the great—the inclusion of its meanings would likely be incomplete; even if one were to add the five periods of the general and specific teachings, it would still be difficult to encompass them all.
△ Third, the formal presentation and exposition, which has two parts: first, a brief citation of wisdom and teaching; second, an extensive citation of analogies.
The Dharma has three initial points. First, it establishes that the teaching set forth is not in vain. Second, wisdom and the teaching mutually clarify one another.
Third, it explains the non-falsity by way of wisdom. Now, for the first point:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never in vain."
The Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas. Regarding all dharma-gates, he possesses mastery whether teaching vertically or horizontally.
Fearing that others might not believe him, he speaks words that cannot be fully exhausted; thus, he cites the title of "Dharma King" to address them directly and manifest the ultimate truth.
The intent is this: if even the words of a human king are non-dual, how much more so those of the Dharma King? △ Second.
Through the mutual illumination of wisdom and teaching,
one reaches the ground of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā-bhūmi) regarding all phenomena through the skillful means of wisdom.
All phenomena— namely, the dharma-gates of sudden and gradual, partial and complete, provisional and real, and so forth— all flow forth from wondrous wisdom.
This [section] reveals the teaching by means of wisdom. What follows, "That which is taught," reveals wisdom by means of the teaching.

This means that although the Dharma-gates thus expounded have various distinctions of small and great, when investigated to their ultimate conclusion, they are nothing other than worldly conventional language that necessarily penetrates its own source;
nor does it allow them to stagnate in provisional shallowness. Therefore, it is said that "they all reach the ground of wisdom, the ground of omniscience."

This is precisely the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Because it is able to initiate all seeds of goodness in sentient beings through all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas, it is metaphorically compared to the earth.
△ Third, the explanation of non-futility based on wisdom, in two parts: first, the analytical explanation of knowing the Dharma and knowing the capacity;
second, the synthetic explanation of being able to comprehend and demonstrate. Now, the first part.
The Tathāgata contemplates and knows all dharmas (up to) the practices of the profound mind, penetrating them without obstruction.
First, this clarifies the gateways of knowing all dharmas and their respective powers and functions.

Although there are various proximate points of convergence, if one considers the ultimate point of convergence from a distance, they all equally reach the ground of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*). This is the knowledge of dharmas. Furthermore, it is known that... [the following].
This is the knowledge of the opportune moment (*jñāna-kauśalya*). The profound mind is the habitual cause of what is practiced; "what is practiced" refers to the karmic actions manifested before one.

Although their number exceeds that of the sands of the Ganges, he thoroughly penetrates them all. Because he can simultaneously discern them without obstruction, everything he speaks is entirely non-erroneous.
△ Second, the combined explanation of "being able to understand" and "being able to know."
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, he exhaustively investigates and clearly understands them, demonstrating to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom.
All phenomena consist of the five aggregates and the ten realms; these are the objects that define meaning, each possessing its own origin and culmination.

The World-Honored One, through his provisional wisdom that accords with reality, exhaustively investigates and realizes them as being the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom of equality, he reveals them.
All sentient beings, though they currently abide in various causes of habituation and fruits of habituation, ultimately and finally return to the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
In the preceding section, it was explained that what was taught is not false by means of the correspondence between medicine and disease;
in this section, it is further explained why this is so—namely, because wondrous wisdom can penetrate to the very depths of the Dharma—which also implicitly contains the teaching of equality.

[This is] the intention. Therefore, the following explains the metaphor of clouds and rain being without partiality. △ Second, the extensive presentation of the metaphors and the Dharma has two parts: first, the explanation of the two dharmas through the metaphor; second, the application [of the metaphor] to the Dharma.
The first part has two sections: first, non-differentiation within differentiation; second, the conclusion through concession and refutation. The first section has two parts:

first, discussing non-differentiation within differentiation regarding the producer and the produced; second, discussing non-differentiation within differentiation regarding that which moistens and that which is moistened. The first [of these two]: regarding the producer and the produced, it discusses non-differentiation within differentiation. The second [of these two]: regarding that which moistens and that which is moistened, it discusses non-differentiation within differentiation.
[Answer: It is so. Now, first:
Kāśyapa, it is like the trichiliocosm (the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system). [From here until] "various kinds with different names and forms":

the great trichiliocosm is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which is formed by the combination of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands.
Now, we shall restrict ourselves here to taking the meaning of "equal capacity for production.

Just as the Buddha-nature as the primary cause (*hetu-buddhadhātu*) is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which then combines with the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). That which is produced likewise takes the meaning of equal capacity for production.
Next, it clarifies that the grasses and trees produced therein equally possess the power to cure diseases; yet, within the clusters of these plants, there is a distinct variety.
Those that possess great power and are able to cure diseases are given the name "medicinal herbs. Nevertheless, each has its own seeds and species, as well as its own names and characteristics.
Here, within the context of what is produced, we simply take up the general meaning of the distinction between this and that.

Just as based upon the impartial primary cause (*hetu*), there arise the distinctions of the three vehicles and five natures, as well as the differences between the causal conditions of practice (*śikṣā-hetu*) and the fruits of practice (*śikṣā-phala*).
These two sections together reveal the meaning of non-differentiation within differentiation. "Mountain" (*shan*) means "to proclaim.

It refers to that which can proclaim and circulate the qi of yin and yang, thereby bringing forth the myriad things. "River" (*chuan*) means "to pierce. Any place where water flows through is called a river. Mountain...

Piercing through the void, those places where water is present are called "streams" (*khi*); those that do not retain water are called "valleys" (*ku*). "Herbs and grasses" (*hui cao*) is a collective term for vegetation;
"trees" (*mu*) is a general designation for all arboreal plants. △ Second, discussing the lack of difference and the presence of difference based on the moisture-provider and the moisture-received.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the three thousandfold world system (until they reach the point where) flowers and fruits grow, and blossoms and seeds flourish.
This first clarifies that the moisture is provided without distinction. The clouds are like the Buddha’s body, filling the Dharma-realm;

the dew is like the teaching, which, based on the single voice of equality, is proclaimed throughout the great chiliocosm. The herbs and trees are like the capacities of those to be transformed. By means of these clouds and rain—

Universally moistening, it causes the small, medium, and great seeds to each attain growth in their roots, stems, branches, and leaves, just as on the ground of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
Moistened by this, all small, medium, and great seeds of habitual causes (*vāsanā-hetu*) attain growth in small, medium, and great faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Beneath the various trees, it is clarified that there are differences in what is moistened; that is to say, the superior [moisture] is able to...
Although the clouds and rain that moisten them are equal, within the experience of receiving them, there are trees of small and large size, and grasses of superior, middling, and inferior quality;
thus, each receives a different amount. Upon investigation, the cloud that covers them is one and the same, and the rain that moistens them is likewise one and the same;
yet, each grows according to its own specific nature (gotra). This is not so for others.
The same applies here. For example, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
Since their understandings differ, the practices that arise based on those understandings and the fruits obtained through those practices are likewise entirely distinct.
These two sections together reveal the capacity to moisten and that which is moistened; they are non-different yet different. II. Conclusion by way of concession and refutation.
Although they grow from the same ground and are moistened by the same rain, the various plants and trees each have their own distinctions.

Likewise, although all sentient beings equally possess the ground capable of generating wisdom and are equally moistened by the rain of the Dharma, they receive this moisture according to their respective capacities;
therefore, there are distinctions such as those of three or two types. Furthermore, if they do not receive the two causes—the condition and the direct cause—[they cannot attain enlightenment].

The arising of this [teaching] is such that even its differentiated characteristics cannot be apprehended. △ Second, the application of the Dharma has two parts: first, teaching that there appears to be difference because the capacities of the disciples vary;

second, teaching that in reality there is no difference because the wisdom [of the Buddha] is one. The first part has two sections: first, briefly applying the previous point that there is no difference despite the appearance of difference;

second, concluding by showing that the differences spoken of are precisely non-different. The first of these two has [two further points]: first... (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the structure and content of the extant portion.)
There is no difference at all. Second, there appears to be a difference. Now, for the first [point]:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "...all should come here in order to hear the Dharma."
He manifests his body like a great cloud that universally covers all. With a great voice, he summons all beings, causing them to know that a Buddha has descended as a spirit.
The ten titles are all names given to the body based on the fruits of virtue accomplished through the cultivation of causes.

The phrase "those not yet delivered" and below clarifies the reason for descending as a spirit: those who have not yet been delivered from suffering, he vows to cause to attain deliverance. Those who have not yet...

Regarding those bound by the fetters of karma, I vow to liberate them from their bonds. Regarding those not yet established in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), I vow to establish them therein.

Regarding those who have not yet realized *nirvāṇa*, I vow to cause them to realize it. Concerning matters of the present and future, I possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*) and am able to know them as they truly are.
Furthermore, I possess the five eyes and the four wisdoms; I am one who knows and sees with a mind that is luminously clear.
"Jian" (the mirror) means that for those who know the Way, the six sense organs are not obstructed; this is the one who opens the Way.
"Eight sounds" being without stagnation means he is the one who speaks the Way. "You all, below" clarifies the reason for the summons.

This above section generally reveals that the Tathāgata, through his three karmas of equality, universally covers all beings without any distinction whatsoever. △ Second, it appears as if there were distinctions.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings (up to) were fully moistened and each attained growth.

As for the assembly that was summoned and gathered, who all arise together from the ground of the wisdom of the true cause, yet exhibit the distinctions of the nine realms, this is the manifestation produced from seeds formed by habitual tendencies. Regarding this, the Tathāgata...

"At that time" means first observing the capacities [of the beings]. Just as the aforementioned plants and trees have distinctions of large and small roots, stems, branches, and leaves, so too do sentient beings now possess differences in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.

According to those capacities, [the Buddha] employs the principle of a single voice of equality to preach various teachings that correspond to various capacities, just as a single rain universally moistens all things. "These [beings]"... [and so forth].

Regarding those who clarify the hearing of the Dharma and gradually enter the Path, they first each attain the distinctions of the five fruits: attaining peace and security in the present life is the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit);
being reborn in a favorable realm in future lives is the *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit); experiencing happiness through the Path is the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort);
also obtaining the hearing of the Dharma is the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit); and being free from all obstacles is the *visamyoga-phala* (fruit of dissociation).

Regarding the section "In all the lower [stages]," this concludes by demonstrating that one acts according to the capacity of one's own power, thereby revealing the distinctions between them. Regarding the section "As in that [previous] lower [case]," this restates the analogy to clarify the application.
△ Second, concluding by showing that what has been explained is without difference.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has a single characteristic and a single flavor, culminating ultimately in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The "single characteristic" refers to the Dharma; the "single flavor" is a metaphor for the Dharma explained above.

While it appears as though there are differences according to the varying capacities of sentient beings, in reality, they all equally drink the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), with no difference in flavor whatsoever. This is what is meant by "inferior," in terms of the abandonment [of afflictions].

The three obstacles are eliminated, the three virtues are realized, and the principle of the single characteristic is revealed, enabling those who hear it to equally perfect the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).
Being liberated from the bonds of karma constitutes the characteristic of liberation; being free from the suffering of the two deaths constitutes the characteristic of the Dharma-body virtue;
and extinguishing the delusions of affliction constitutes the characteristic of the Prajñā virtue. If one can reach this ultimate realization, one returns to the three virtues.
The secret treasury of perfect interfusion, the omniscience of all modes, is precisely the Prajñā of the perfect interfusion of the three mysteries.

Although the teachings expounded therein are manifold, because they all flow forth from the wondrous wisdom of Prajñā, they nonetheless constitute a single characteristic and a single flavor—an equal Dharma-gate.
△ Second, the teaching that while wisdom is one, in reality it is non-existent.

There are three parts. First, it clarifies that sentient beings do not know; second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to know; third, it correctly clarifies that the teaching follows wisdom as one.
Now, for the first:
"If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata... (up to)... they do not themselves realize or know the merit they have obtained."

The faculties and convictions of sentient beings differ; their understanding upon hearing the Dharma likewise varies. Yet they do not realize that what they have attained is entirely the cause for Buddhahood.
△ Second, explaining that the Tathāgata is able to know this.
Why is this so? It is because only the Tathāgata [knows all], yet [sentient beings] do not know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures.

First, regarding the ten realms as the objective sphere, it is clarified that the Buddha is able to know them because, through the influence of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), they manifest as the categories of the nine realms.
How could one who is not endowed with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) possibly know these many varieties as being of one kind, one characteristic, one essence, and one nature?

Regarding the phrase "contemplating what is below," this refers, for the time being, to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), which encompass five categories of persons to demonstrate that the objects of knowledge are not erroneous.

The term "three things" (*trivastu*) refers to the objective spheres and essential natures (*ālambana-svabhāva*) of the three types of wisdom. [These are] recollection (*smṛti*), reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The three characters refer to the essential nature of that which acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka*).
That all of these are permeated by the two characters "how" (*katham*) indicates the examination of the object and the arising of its function. For example, one asks, "What kind of object is this?

only then does the thought of "what kind" arise. The phrase beginning with "by what" (*kena*) combines the aforementioned subject and object; it means that, based upon the perceived object, [the subject arises].
The three types of wisdom arise. The "three dharma-words" refer to the aforementioned three things;

they do not necessarily depend on hearing the Dharma, because hearing the Dharma occurs prior to the arising of the three types of wisdom. From the words "By what... onwards, it clarifies the results induced by their respective causes:
by taking what dharma as the causal means of attainment, one obtains what kind of result. Sentient beings currently abide in various [states].
In the ground of habitual defilement, only the Tathāgata perceives these various distinctions as they truly are;
they all ultimately converge in the ground of the wisdom of equality, understood with clarity and without obstruction, just as the preceding metaphor and its application clarify.
△ Third, the correct elucidation that the teaching follows wisdom (1).
The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to: yet he does not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes). *Hui-xuan* says:
"A single characteristic" means there is no different characteristic, because it is the characteristic of formlessness (*animitta*). Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"All are of one and the same characteristic, namely, the characteristic of formlessness. The *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa* says: "A single characteristic is formlessness; a single flavor is..."

First is the flavor of the untainted (*anāsrava-rasa*). Because it is a superior nourishment and lacks a separate substantial entity, what is the essence of this "one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and "characterless" (*alakṣaṇa*)?
This refers to the essence that follows below. The text consists of five phrases: the first four are the four virtues, and the last one is the single nature.

The characteristic of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*) is my virtue, because by being freed from the bonds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), one attains mastery. It is the bliss of detachment from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vivikta-sukha*).
The virtue of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*) is because it is free from the suffering of change. The virtue of purity (*śubha-guṇa*) is because its nature is utterly severed from deluded defilement.

The virtue of permanence (*nitya-guṇa*) is because the characteristic of eternal quiescence does not migrate through the four marks of existence. As for "ultimately returning to emptiness": these four virtues are the treasury of non-emptiness, yet they all return to the treasury of emptiness as their essence;
this is the single characteristic and the single nature. Furthermore, ultimate *nirvāṇa* is the [true] direction.

It is pure, because it is attained through cultivation based on causes and skillful means. It is the mark of eternal quiescence, which is *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity), for its fundamental nature is pure.
Ultimately it returns to emptiness, manifesting the single mark of marklessness. Regarding the passage "The Buddha knows" and below, he explains away a doubt, saying:
Although the Buddha previously knew that the beginning and the end are both one, the reason he did not preach this "one" at the very outset was due to his prior observation.
Regarding the minds of sentient beings, when their faculties are not yet mature, one protects them out of fear that they might give rise to slander;
thus, one does not immediately explain the One, thereby manifesting that difference is itself non-difference. △ Fourth, the concluding praise for those capable of knowing.
"You disciples, Kāśyapa, are truly rare and extraordinary... [the teaching] of preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
For the sake of those with gradual capacities, the World-Honored One has for over forty years taught only the Three Vehicles; it is only until this day [that he reveals the ultimate truth]."
He then preached the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) as the beginning of the destruction of the three [vehicles] and the initial step toward returning to the One.

The four sons were thus able to awaken to the past teachings of provisional expediency and explore the secret essentials from this point forward; hence, the World-Honored One offered his praise and description.

Although the four sons of the preceding chapter had already caught a glimpse, within the ten modes of transformational teaching, of the principle of the "returning of the branches to the root" through the single gate, they remained nonetheless—
It is difficult to encounter. Furthermore, the World-Honored One feared that they might think [the teaching] was already fully perfected;

therefore, in the subsequent section on "Establishing through Narration," he took what they themselves knew and extensively expanded upon what they had not yet reached. First, by means of the metaphor of clouds and rain, he illustrated the transformative Dharma that can encompass all beings.
It should be understood that this is not intended to mean, as you suggest, that one begins with the small and later proceeds to the great, gradually leading them forward. One must know this.

Fundamentally, this is a single mark and a single flavor, a Dharma-gate of equality. Next, regarding that which is covered by the clouds and rain, it is not as you think—that only a single blade of grass grows;
beyond this, there are further three types of grass and two types of trees, each attaining growth according to its capacity, and such meanings are all unknown to you.
If one were to reconcile the *Daichao* (Great Commentary) with the present sutra:
Treatise: Within this single ritual, one should collectively encompass seven types of capacities, namely: the three kinds of grasses and two kinds of trees;

as well as those who previously received the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), who, although they now hear the Great Dharma, have not yet turned their minds [toward it]—for whom one may establish the causal conditions for their future liberation—and those who now directly hear the Great Dharma, who, although they did not previously receive the Lesser Vehicle, already understand [it].
Previously, the "lesser Dharma" was taught, as in the case of the dragon girl and others. △ Second, the verse-text has two parts: first, indicating that wisdom and the teaching are not in vain;
second, describing and establishing this through extensive demonstration. Now, the first part.

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [up to] ...the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.
The preceding section clarified the remote causes for establishing the connection; from here below, the proximate causes are clarified.

Because the great assembly harbored doubts regarding the Buddha’s acceptance of the invitation to preach the Dharma, the prince was first able to provide a detailed exposition to establish the connection. As for the "three turnings," it means:
The demonstration, the exhortation, and the realization constitute three parts, as the Dharma of the Four Truths is taught in three successive cycles.

Just as a worldly wheel has the function of crushing and grinding, the Dharma taught by the Buddha can crush all the afflictions and karmic actions of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
First, the turning that indicates: namely, "This is suffering," up to "This is the path. Second, the turning that exhorts: namely, "Suffering should be known; the origin should be abandoned;
cessation should be realized; the path should be cultivated. Third, the turning that certifies: namely, "Suffering has been known by me;
it need not be known again," up to "The path has been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again. These are the three. (10)

Regarding the two types of practice: first, a general clarification; second, a specific determination. In the first part, there are two sections: first, concerning the teaching of the Four Truths; second, concerning the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).

As for the "twelvefold teaching," this refers to the three turnings of demonstration, exhortation, and realization. As for the "twelvefold practice," all three turnings give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
Furthermore, the twelvefold teaching acts as the agent of turning (*pravartaka*), while the twelvefold practice serves as the object of turning (*prāvartya*).

Therefore, the practice follows the teaching, and both together comprise twelve. Second, regarding the sixteen practices: this means that the teaching and the practice mutually follow one another and are both capable of destroying delusions;

thus, both are termed "wheels" (*cakra*). However, the "eye," "knowledge," and so forth have no separate substantial entities; they merely refer back to the "patience" (*kṣānti*) and other stages, which are designated as "teaching" and "practice.
Thus, when these four mental states are expanded, they constitute sixteen. That is to say: the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

The Dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*); subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) constitutes clarity (*vidyā*); and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitutes awakening (*buddhi*).

The same applies to the remaining three truths (*satya*). Thus, sixteen moments of mind are established. For each of the three types of individuals (*pudgala*), these sixteen moments of mind constitute forty-eight applications (*ākāra*).

Next, regarding the proponent of the momentary theory (*kṣaṇika-vādī*), they maintain that the one who turns the wheel of the teaching possesses only a single skillful means-wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), while that which is turned [by it] is...
There are twelve teachings in total. If one turns the Wheel of Dharma, there are twelve teachings by which it is turned;
the practices that are turned likewise number twelve. These may apply to three types of persons or be restricted to a single person.

Now, regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dharma through the three revolutions for the three faculties—superior, middling, and inferior—when combined at the initial moment of seeing the Truths, they are said to constitute twelve. If [it concerns] a śrāmaṇera...
"Below. As for the śramaṇas, if they have not heard the Buddha’s teaching, they cannot even understand it, let alone turn the wheel of Dharma.

Others may hear the names, yet they will certainly not comprehend the underlying principle; therefore, none of them can turn it. This is what is meant by "below. First, regarding the Four Noble Truths, this provides a general demonstration of the two types of cause and effect:
mundane and supramundane. The first two phrases first demonstrate mundane cause and effect. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is that which oppresses...

The meaning is "affliction. This means that the practitioner does not know that the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth, are phenomena that oppress and afflict, causing the conditioned body and mind to quickly return to extinction; therefore, it is pointed out: "This is suffering.

Furthermore, because one does not know that the accumulation of past afflictions and karma is the cause that summons suffering, it is shown: "This is the origin of suffering" (*duḥkhasamudaya*). Next...
Two phrases indicate the causes and effects of the supramundane. "Cessation" (nirodha) has the meaning of the unconditioned cessation (*asamskṛta-nirodha*).

This means that if afflictions and karma are extinguished, then sufferings such as birth and death no longer exist; therefore, it is called the essence of the cessation of suffering, which consists of the two types of *nirvāṇa*:

with remainder and without remainder. "Path" (*mārga*) has the meaning of being able to lead through; by means of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one subdues and extinguishes afflictions and karma, leading [to liberation].
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, it is therefore shown as the "path to the cessation of suffering. However, there are two aspects to this path that leads [to liberation]:

namely, the extinction of hindrances through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the realization of the principle manifested by the extinction of hindrances through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Furthermore, below, the four truths are expanded into the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): from "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions aging and death," and so forth; thus it is demonstrated.

The "characteristic of arising" extensively explains the Truths of Suffering and its Origin. From "the cessation of ignorance" up to "the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair," it demonstrates the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment, extensively explaining the Truths of Cessation and the Path.
The preceding section briefly presented the coarse characteristics for those of inferior faculties; now, one contemplates the Four Truths in detail.

This is for those of middling faculties. Regarding the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): they function as causes by producing effects through a successive series, and they function as conditions by mutually depending upon one another.
First, as for ignorance (*avidyā*), its essence is delusion; its nature is that of confusion and darkness, such that nothing is clearly understood.
Therefore, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*); this encompasses all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the past life.

"Formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the karma produced by the sevenfold actions of body and speech in the past life. Since karma arises from delusion, it is said that "formations are conditioned by ignorance."
These two constitute the two causal links of the past existence. "Consciousness" (vijñāna) refers specifically to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Through the fulfillment of the aforementioned karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), it draws forth birth within the three realms and enters the mother’s womb; hence it is said that "formations are the condition for consciousness. Once within the womb, there are then vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness.
Every seven days, these undergo a transformation, resulting in "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). "Name" refers to the four aggregates beginning with mind (*citta*).
Form (*rūpa*) consists of the four great elements; therefore, it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). As for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*):
after one has entered the womb, by the fifth seven-day period, the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) unfold, and they then possess the function of entering into sensory objects.

Therefore, it is said that name-and-form conditions the six sense bases. Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the period from after birth until the age of three or four, when the six faculties encounter the six sense objects.
Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*): although there is contact, it cannot yet give rise to the perception of suffering or pleasure; therefore, it is said that "the six sense bases condition contact.

Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*): this refers to the mental faculty of experiencing. From the age of five or six until twelve or thirteen, because the sense faculties and their objects come into contact, one is able to experience objects such as suffering and pleasure, yet the mind of craving has not yet arisen; therefore, it is said that "contact conditions feeling. These are the five [aggregates].
This refers to the present fruit. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) occurs from the ages of fifteen or sixteen up to eighteen or nineteen.
At this stage, one craves various excellent and wonderful requisites, as well as objects such as forms and sensual desires; yet, one is still not yet able to pursue them extensively and universally.

Because one experiences these objects, craving immediately arises; hence it is said that "feeling is the condition for craving. "Grasping" (*upādāna*) occurs after the age of twenty, when covetous desire increases further.
Because one intensively and seeks in all four directions within the objects of the five sensory realms, it is said that "craving conditions grasping.

Furthermore, this craving and grasping serve as the causal substance for future birth and death; thus, they are equivalent to the afflictions, while [the previous link] ignorance pertains to the past. As for "existence" (bhava):

Once one has become attached to the preceding objects, one immediately gives rise to karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—which accumulates and exerts a drawing power that leads to rebirth within the three realms;

therefore, it is said that "clinging conditions becoming. This also serves as the essential substance of the cause for future birth and death, being identical in nature to the "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) of the past.
When combined with the preceding "craving" and "clinging," these constitute the causes of the three present links. As for "birth," it refers to [rebirth] within the six destinies.

It is "birth" (*jāti*). Because karma has matured, one again experiences birth in a future life; therefore, it is said that there is "conditioned by existence" (*bhava-pratyayā jātiḥ*). Regarding "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*):

the maturation of the aggregates (*skandha*) resulting from birth is called "old age," and the disintegration of the aggregates is called "death"; therefore, it is said that there is "conditioned by birth" (*jāti-pratyayaṃ jarāmaraṇam*).
These two links—birth and old age and death—are the results of the future. Furthermore, they are augmented by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and so forth.

Afflictions all arise conditioned by old age and death. From "ignorance" (*avidyā*) downward, the two truths of cessation and the path are explained extensively in terms of the process of reversal (*pratiloma*).
Whether observed in direct or reverse order, both proceed with ignorance as their root;

therefore, when ignorance ceases, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, and so on until birth, old age, and the rest are all extinguished. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* clarifies forty-four types of knowledge, namely [the knowledge of] old age and death...

The knowledge of the origination of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the path leading to the cessation of aging and death; this applies likewise down to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, it is said there are seventy-seven knowledges: namely, the knowledge of aging and death conditioned by birth; the knowledge that aging and death are not conditioned by anything other than birth; the knowledge of aging and death conditioned by past birth;
the knowledge that aging and death were not conditioned by anything other than past birth; and [the knowledge of] future birth conditioned by...
The knowledge of old age and death; not merely the knowledge of old age and death as conditioned by future birth, but also the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).

These two—the knowledge that [phenomena] are impermanent, conditioned, mind-dependent, subject to arising, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to detachment, and subject to cessation—are both forms of clear wisdom regarding the gate of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*). △ Second, the attainment of benefit.
Among the great assembly of devas and humans, [the Buddha] is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
For one who does not grasp at any phenomena, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises like a great mass of fire;

[He] attains it. His mind attains liberation. This reveals a small portion [of his realization], for he has destroyed the cognitive obstacles that hinder meditative concentration.

This clearly indicates what was previously taught, all of which pertains to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Why then insist on forcibly inserting [the Prajñāpāramitā] here?
This is what is being said. Furthermore, although it is said that when Buddhas appear in the world, their paths are identical, this merely expresses the general outline.

How much more so when there has not yet been the manifestation of such auspicious omens? Why must they necessarily correspond? △ Fifth, the uncertainty of belief and disbelief.

They shall all remain on the same stage without falling back. Among them, there are four types of persons.

This was the proximate cause for establishing the connection [with sentient beings]. Because the Buddha remained in concentration, those who had not yet gained faith or harbored doubts had no one to request a resolution;

II. The actual explanation of the formation of the karmic bond has four parts: first, knowing the Buddha had entered concentration; second, preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* again; third, emerging from concentration and expressing praise and approval; fourth, being born into the world and meeting one another. Now, the first part: [The Prince] knew that the Buddha had entered concentration. [He thought: "The World-Honored One has entered the *samādhi* of the 'Lion's Play' (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*). At that time, the Prince, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and leaped for joy. He thought: "I have now obtained a great benefit; I have already attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Having made this vow, he took leave of the Buddha and departed. Later, he was born into the world and met the Buddha. This is the first part.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration.
