they then first give rise to the Great Mind. Furthermore, there are two types: the first are those for whom both precepts and vehicle are urgent;

such individuals have already been able to ascend early to the stage of non-retrogression among the ranks of the "foremost influences" and similar classes, and it is certain that these people are not few. The second are those who, from the moment they first resolved their minds...
Although they have not yet retreated or become discouraged, they still remain submerged in saṃsāra.

Those whose aspiration is urgent but whose precepts are lax nevertheless experience the growth of the internal perfuming of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) and the secret empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata accumulated over kalpas.

Thus, even while within the three miserable realms, by virtue of the power of the maturation of causes and conditions, they are able to transcend to the ranks of the sages all at once upon hearing the wondrous Dharma, and swiftly reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It is not necessarily only the dragon girl who has reached this state.

In short, regarding these aforementioned cases of successive masters and disciples meeting throughout many kalpas from beginning to end, they are all spiritual capacities transformed by the single Buddha Śākyamuni; thus, one may discuss whether their realization is complete or incomplete.

The intention behind the "establishing of a connection" (*kṣaṇa*) in the Sūtra refers to those who previously resolved upon the Great Mind but later regressed; it speaks of those who merely encountered [the teaching] on a small scale.

The commentary states: As explained above, this is intended so that those who attain realization throughout the three assemblies may all achieve a seamless transition.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [sat] at one place with a single mind for eighty-four thousand kalpas."

The commentary on the meaning has been explained at length in the refutations by Fang and others within their annotations. △ Second, the formal conclusion of the conditions for connection, in three parts:
first, explaining the concealed teaching; second, explaining the meeting; third, reconciling the ancient and the modern. Now, the first part.
These śrāmaṇeras, numbering as many as six million billion Ganges-sands, [constituted the assembly].
△ Second, explaining their meeting:
after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these who heard the Dharma were always born together with their teacher in various Buddha-lands wherever they may be.
△ Third, correlating the past with the present:
"These sixteen śrāmaṇeras... therefore, by means of skillful means, I lead you toward the Buddha-wisdom.
△ Third, preaching the Lotus Sūtra.

For these fundamental reasons, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra to lead you into the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm. △ Fourth, the explanation through dharma and parable has two parts:
first, the explanation by way of parable; second, the application of the dharma. The first [section] has three parts; first, the verse on what is being brought forth.
Regarding the first of the three verses on the cessation of emanations:
it is like a perilous and evil road... [the mind] clearly resolves to rescue all beings from their hardships while remaining within that very danger.

The ancients held that the clarity and stillness of the water represent meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the differentiation of the grasses represents wisdom (*prajñā*); these are precisely the provisions for awakening (*bodhisambhāra*).
△ Second, the verse on regression:
"All the people become weary... (until) they all conceive the thought of peace and security, deeming themselves already delivered."

The house is the place where one dwells; it is the dwelling place of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), wherein all afflictions (*kleśa*) are stilled. The groves and gardens are places for wandering and contemplation;

they are the wandering and contemplation that accords with principle through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). The channels and streams are gradually opened and cleared, so that there is no obstruction internally or externally, like the liberation through the absence of doubt (*aniyata-vimokṣa*);
this is the realization of the names of the internal and external. The bathing pool is the concentration of the mind without distraction, used for washing and purification.
His body is like the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), not overflowing outward, serving as a realm for the repose of the spirit.

Through the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), he further enters the signless (animitta) and the wishless (apraṇihita). The multi-storied pavilions are like the samādhi of transcendence (vyutkrāntaka-samādhi); all are within the city of nirvāṇa.
This is the virtue he possesses. △ Third, the verse on the cessation of transformation:
"The Guide, knowing they have rested... (until) 'You should now apply yourself with diligence; together we shall reach the place of treasure.'"

△ Second, the threefold application of the Dharma. First, the application regarding the establishment of karmic conditions; second, the application regarding the disclosure of provisional means; third, the application regarding the proclamation of the ultimate truth. Now, for the first:

△ Second, the conferring of predictions.
Chapter Eight: The Conferral of Predictions upon the Five Hundred Disciples.

Hereafter, predictions are bestowed upon those of inferior capacity; however, the fact that many "reveal their origin and manifest their fundamental nature" is precisely a reflection of what was previously discussed regarding those of superior capacity.

Among those with the two faculties of the intermediate stage, there are those who have already attained realization through the bond of affinity (*karmayoga*) but manifest their arrival through skillful means (*upāya*).
As the *Acintyaviṣaya-sūtra* states: "At that time, there were further ten billion bodhisattvas who manifested in the form of śrāvakas and also came to the assembly.
Their names were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and so forth, down to Ānanda and Devadatta."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Nanda, Upananda, and others were their leaders.

Having long cultivated the six pāramitās and being close to the Buddha’s bodhi, they manifested in the forms of śrāvakas and so forth within the defiled lands in order to transform sentient beings. Question:

If they are all merely provisional manifestations, then the benefit of the World-Honored One manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma would be entirely in vain. Answer: There are indeed those who are real.
One employs provisional manifestations precisely because there is no reality; if there were no reality, for what purpose would provisional manifestations exist?
Furthermore, the Treatise states: "There are four types of śrāvakas who receive predictions: first, those who are fixed as śrāvakas; second, those with overweening pride;

third, those who have regressed from the bodhicitta; and fourth, those who are śrāvakas through transformation. Two of these types are given predictions by the Tathāgata, namely, those who had regressed from the Mahāyāna and returned [to it]."
Regarding those who have resolved their minds (*cittotpāda*), as well as those who are transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*):

because those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) have not yet matured their faculties, the Bodhisattva employs the skillful means of bestowing a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to cause them to resolve their minds. Question: Since the transformation-body has already reached a state of certainty regarding the mind, what is the use of a prediction?
Answer: If they receive such a prediction, they will immediately attain the increase of the path and the reduction of births. Question: Since the chapter title lists five [categories],...
[Question]: Why was Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra prophesied first? [Answer]: Because he is the leader among these five hundred [monks]. Therefore, he should be prophesied first;

it is through the five hundred that the primary recipients of the prophecy are established, and thus the chapter is named after him. The text has three parts: first, the prophecy for Pūrṇa; second, the prophecy for the twelve hundred;
third, the prophecy for those in training and those beyond training. The first two [parts] consist of: first, the prose section; second, the verse section.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra— having heard the provisional and ultimate truths through the two cycles of Dharma and parables,
having heard the prediction of enlightenment for the śrāvakas, and having again vividly recalled his past causes and conditions—
further heard of the sovereign power of spiritual transformations that skillfully transcends existence and non-existence, and is adeptly employed.

Regarding the provisional and the ultimate, you are truly like a guide on a perilous path; therefore, wondrous understanding has suddenly burst forth. △ Second, the description of the joy of realization:
"I have attained what I never had before," and my mind is pure and leaping with exultation.
To hear what has never been heard before is called "understanding. To realize that one is fully perfected as a Buddha is called "attainment.

To know as a Buddha and see as a Buddha, without being obstructed by the attachment to dharmas arising from discrimination, is called "purity. △ Third, the description of the ritual for receiving this understanding.
He immediately rose from his seat and went before the Buddha (until) gazing up at the Honored Countenance without casting his eyes away for even a moment.
△ Second, the narration of mindfulness and the request, in two parts: first, the narration of mindfulness; second, the narration of the request. Now, the first.
And he formed this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary... (up to) regarding the Buddha’s merits, they cannot be fully proclaimed.
Generally, there are three types of ritual for requesting the Dharma: first, the verbal request, which is speaking the words with one's mouth;
second, the mental request, which means not speaking with the mouth but forming the thought in the mind; third, the verbal-mental request, as in the case of Maitreya...
In the preface, [the author] first forms a thought and subsequently utters words; here, however, he silently petitions.

As for the previous two cycles where all spoke to receive the teaching and attain understanding, this was specifically because those of inferior faculties had not yet awakened, and thus it was necessary to stimulate them from the side with words.
Since they have now attained awakening, he therefore petitions in silence. Regarding "pulling out from every place" and so forth, it is as previously stated: "At that time..."

Regarding those to be converted: after sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges had initially formed a karmic connection with him and subsequently regressed from the Mahāyāna, they were born together with the Bodhisattva in every successive life.
The instances of his rescue and deliverance are too numerous to list exhaustively, yet they may be pointed out.

Previously, by means of four parables, he refuted four types of people with overweening pride; as for the statement that "it cannot be fully proclaimed," it is like the parable spoken by the four sons. It is not so.
I have barely caught a glimpse of a single facet; how much less so for those of middling or inferior capacity?
Furthermore, he first employed the metaphor of clouds and rain to extensively illustrate that which others cannot reach, thereby manifesting the greatness of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Subsequently, he further stated that even this very analogy of clouds and rain is but a single drop in the ocean, thus making the greatness of the Buddha’s wisdom even more evident. Therefore, it is said: "It cannot be proclaimed in words."
△ Second, the request.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our deep-seated original vows.

For the sake of transforming those below, he maintains a profound inner intention that is concealed while manifesting outwardly; thus, we request him to reveal his origins. This is for the sake of seeking what is above.

Therefore, there is a fundamental vow to adorn the Buddha-lands; here, we shall clarify that original intent. Alternatively, one may simply seek a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) in order to increase the Path and diminish birth-and-death.

△ Second, the narration of the fulfillment and the bestowing of the prediction, which has two parts: first, the narration of the fulfillment; second, the bestowing of the prediction. The first part has two sub-sections.
First, the initial manifestation of the proximate traces; second, the revelation of the remote origin. Now, for the first:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... [up to] ...none could exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
The single character "No" (否) is used to raise up the person to show the assembly. It means: although you know that Pūrṇa’s manifest trace is that of a Śrāvaka, do you also know his original nature?
Now, because I wish to reveal this trace, I first alert the great assembly not to be obscured by the manifest trace.
When I previously descended [to this world], I first elucidated those who assist the present Buddha’s manifest trace—whether they turn the Dharma wheel themselves or assist in doing so.
"Transforming" refers to the profound resolve manifested externally. Being foremost in preaching the Dharma is the primary practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); it is also a constant phrase.
"Aiding practice" refers to diligent effort and so forth, which clarifies the supportive transformations. From "Having abandoned... onwards, this generally reveals unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Since it is said that outside of the Buddha, there is no one capable of exhausting his eloquence, it is not only in the seven directions... [that he is unsurpassed].
It would be impossible for a person to exhaustively recount them. △ Second, revealing the distant origin:
"You all must not say that Pūrṇa... [omitted] ...is always diligently and vigorously teaching and transforming sentient beings."
You all have a single phrase. Because [the previous section] revealed his origins based on what preceded, this section now brushes away those traces.
One should know that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra did not stop at my school; he was able to roar the lion’s roar even below. Furthermore, it is precisely here that his original nature is revealed.

However, regarding Pūrṇa’s distant origin, it was from the beginning a matter of establishing karmic conditions. As for his being able to achieve realization first, it was because he took pity on those of a similar kind; therefore, he again used those of a similar kind [to lead them].
This refers to the transformation through affairs; it serves as an introductory lead. Among the ninety billion Buddhas, he was also foremost in realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, in the passage below, he deeply penetrated the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). When one can examine with precision, then analogical contemplation will not err.

When there is no doubt, one severs attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). All these are termed Śrāvakas; this is because the trace covers the fundamental [nature]. This is done through skillful means (*upāya*).
"Those who benefit" refers to manifesting in the body of a śrāvaka. "Furthermore, those whom he transforms and establishes" refers to manifesting in the body of a bodhisattva.
"In order to purify... and below concludes by revealing his original vow. "All you bhikṣus... and below clarifies his remote origin.

From here on, the text further employs the three periods of time to reveal both the provisional traces and the fundamental reality, ultimately returning to the original vow of purifying the Buddha-land. △ Second, bestowing predictions (vyākaraṇa), in seven parts.

First, the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits are clarified; second, the purity of the environment (the *āśraya-vipāka*) is clarified; third, the excellence of the primary retribution (*sambhoga-kāya*) is clarified;
fourth, the support and sustenance are clarified; fifth, the merits of the holy assembly are clarified; sixth, the conclusion reveals their immeasurability;
seventh, the duration and proximity of the kalpas and lands are clarified. Now, the first [section].
Gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva, [he becomes] a Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
The first phrase clarifies the perfection of the cause; "surpassing those below" clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit.
That he attains *bodhi* in this very land is because the conditions for transforming defilement into purity here are the most profound; thus, regarding all phenomena, he is fully capable of—
Because he possesses perfect and clear understanding, he is titled "Dharma-Illumination" (Famíng). △ Second, the purity of the external environment:
That Buddha [is surrounded by] as many [attendants] as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River... [until] humans and devas interact, both being able to see one another.
Since the teaching that can transform others is so vast, the realm of those to be transformed is likewise great. Regarding the phrase "the ground is as level as the palm of a hand":
among the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, the seventeenth mark states that "seven places are flat and full.

This refers to the two feet, the two hands, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck; these seven places are all entirely flat and full, upright and symmetrical, without any depressions or irregularities.
Therefore, he used the Buddha’s own palm present before him to demonstrate this; it is unlikely that he was referring to the "palm-stone" found at a distance.
△ Third, the excellence of the primary retribution:
there are no evil realms nor are there women (up to) being adorned by the thirty-two marks.
The female body is the root of greed and the source of falling into suffering; thus, it is driven along with the three evil realms.

Furthermore, although there are women in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, they lack the characteristics of womanhood. Because they do not consume "earth-fat," they attain mastery in flying through the air.
△ Fourth, clarifying the dwelling based on what is consumed.
The sentient beings of that land constantly subsist on two kinds of food: first, the food of Dharma-joy; second, the food of dhyāna-delight.
When they go out, they hear the Dharma and give rise to joy; when they enter, they settle in dhyāna and experience sublime bliss.

Both of these are able to nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), fostering the embryo of the Path and thereby fulfilling the function of food. Consequently, they have no need for solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). △ Five: Explaining [the Land].
The virtues of the noble assembly are immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas, [extending] up to the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the eight liberations.

As for the assembly of bodhisattvas, they consist only of those on the stages (bhūmi), with none prior to the stages; as for the assembly of śrāvakas, they consist only of those who have attained the fruit, with none who have not yet attained it.
Those without wisdom. △ Sixth, the conclusion that reveals the immeasurable:
The Buddha-land possesses such immeasurable meritorious adornments as these, fully accomplished.

Although the text of the successive predictions [of Buddhahood] extensively reveals these merits, they are specifically set forth in detail in this chapter because the practice of preaching the Dharma is sublime.
Because it stands at the very pinnacle of all practices. △ Seventh, clarifying the duration and proximity of the kalpa and the land:
the kalpa is named Precious Radiance (*Ratnaprabhāsa*) and the land is named Good Purity (*Sudarśana*). (Extending to: seven-jeweled stupas arise and fill the entire land.

△ Second, the verses consist of two parts: first, a general presentation of the original and manifested traces of all the sons; second, a specific presentation of the original and manifested traces of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Now, the first:
At that time, the world, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Monks, listen attentively... (until) when sentient beings hear this, their minds will harbor doubt and confusion.

'Desiring little' means delighting in the small. 'Laxity' means retreating from the Great [Vehicle]. 'Having few desires' means not coveting the sensory objects within the realms and seeking swift deliverance.
'Being weary of birth and death' means that although one does not yet realize that birth and death and nirvana are fundamentally equal, [the teaching] reveals it."
To possess the three poisons is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). To manifest the possession of false views is to be a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).

Regarding those sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way (up to) Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi:

from the initial stage of abiding up to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), all are collectively termed *bodhi*. Although there is a distinction between cause and fruit, they all share the same source as the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Nevertheless, those who seek the Buddha-way must begin from the point of entering and abiding [in the stages]. As for the practitioner who has not yet entered...

Prior to abiding [in the stages], if one is able to see this sutra, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, then there is no need to traverse kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges or ten thousand kalpas;
through the sublime practices of one’s own vehicle, one will draw near to Bodhi. Therefore, know that this sutra is the direct shortcut to attaining Buddhahood.
△ Second, the explanation by means of metaphors to establish the point, which has two parts: first, the explanation by metaphor; second, the explanation by dharma. Now...
First:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is as if there were a person suffering from thirst who required water... [up to] "...his mind became resolute, knowing that water must be near.
There are two meanings for "suffering from thirst": first, being parched by the heat and affliction of ignorance; second, seeking the Buddha.
Faith and aspiration are like thirst; water is like the Dharma. A level place where there is no water is like a high plateau.
The soil of the high plateau is like the teaching; the water beneath the soil is like the fruit.

To dig and excavate is like practicing contemplative cultivation according to the principles explained by the teaching. However, if one practices according to the provisional teachings, there are merely words and phrases, and no reality at all.

The meaning is as follows: seeing dry soil represents practicing according to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras; although these explain the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they lack the wondrous intent of full revelation.

Seeing moist soil represents relying on the present sūtra, which directly abandons expedient means and reveals only the truth, wherein essence and characteristics are mutually fused and principle and phenomena penetrate one another, like seeing the appearance of mud when water and soil are blended—this is the nature of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The thirst for the Dharma remains; thus, although one has not yet entered the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the mind is already resolved and cannot be shaken.
△ Second, the explanation by means of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva is also like this... (up to) he manifests the attainment of a Bodhisattva for the sake of instruction.
First, based on what has been heard and what has not yet been heard, it clarifies the slowness or swiftness of the path traversed. Below, the meaning of "attaining proximity" is explained:
there are two types of Bodhisattvas, namely the sudden (*tun*) and the gradual (*jian*). As for those who proceed by the sudden path, they already know all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). That is to say—
The self-nature of the mind does not require further elucidation.
What is now referred to as "all" refers to the two vehicles that enter from the Small [Vehicle] into the Great, as well as the three types who have integrated the provisional into the ultimate.

If one encompasses the teachings by means of the persons, then the two characters "Bodhisattva" should include the causes and resultant dharmas of the provisional, Small Vehicle teachings, principles, and practices. By means of these four dharmas, all...
This must be definitively resolved; therefore, it belongs to this sutra, for it possesses the merit of fully revealing [the truth].

Now, regarding the single character "kai" (opening/revealing), if contrasted with the teachings of the past, it should be explained through two meanings: namely, "abandonment" (*hai*) and "convergence" (*e*). As for "abandonment":
It is like the promise made within a householder’s home that consists of nothing but empty words; thus, after leaving the house, no carriage is to be found.
Because this is a skillful means used to entice the child, it may be discarded—just as the doctrines, principles, and fruits of the past may all be set aside.
Therefore, it was said previously: "In reality, he has not yet attained complete liberation"; this is the opening of the gate of skillful means.
The provisional fruits are abolished. Once the fruits are abolished, then the teachings, principles, and so forth may all be abolished as well.
Previously it was also said: "To transform all sentient beings is no different from [transforming] ourselves. This precisely demonstrates the true aspect.

Regarding the second point, the interpretation of the opening through the convergence of meanings: because the sons rushed out of the house in competition, they were also those who boarded the vehicle; thus, nothing is abolished.

Therefore, as it was previously stated, "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path," this present passage now reconciles provisional practices so that they may all proceed toward the ultimate fruit;
this is precisely what reveals the true aspect [of reality].
Consequently, is it not fitting that all the causes and fruits of the gradual bodhisattvas should be subsumed within this sutra and revealed therein? For this reason, this sutra...
It is most profound and vast; it cannot be glimpsed by those with limited vision. It is most firm and solid;
it cannot be entered by those who do not possess a diamond-like mind. It is most subtle and hidden; even those who have attained non-retrogression cannot know it. It is most remote;
even if one were to travel three hundred *yojanas*, one would still not reach it. Now, the Buddha, in order to transform those of provisional and inferior capacities, [has spoken thus].

These good sons and good daughters, up to the fourfold assembly, extensively expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Robe, seat, and chamber" are called the three requisites (*trayāṇi niśrayāṇi*). In the final age, those who propagate the sutra must rely on these three to obtain the two benefits.
That the Tathāgata names the chamber "Compassion" is because the sublime practice of a Bodhisattva must first take sentient beings as [the object].
Because it takes that as its object of focus, the gathering of sentient beings is the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.

If one can cause them to leave suffering and attain happiness, that is precisely the time when benefit and merit return to oneself. Therefore, the chamber of great compassion does not cover only itself, but likewise covers others.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata uses the name "garment" for gentle forbearance, it is because he internally employs gentleness to cover [himself].
To eliminate the two obstacles: externally, one uses patience to block all violent and evil influences so that they cannot enter;
thus, while the inner mind becomes tranquil, external objects also dissolve. Furthermore, for the Tathāgata to take the emptiness of phenomena as his seat, he must extinguish all marks.
Otherwise, one will be bound by attachments to a self, persons, and so forth, and will be unable to deeply accord with the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva dwells within this state, forgetting both subject and object, they are then fit to propagate the teaching. However, one must employ a mind free from indolence to universally exhort all wholesome dharmas;
only then can this sutra be widely propagated. △ Second, dispatching people to listen and protect it.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I dispatch emanated beings—down to the level of asuras—to listen to their preaching of the Dharma.
A preacher of the Dharma must possess six kinds of accomplishment; therefore, I dispatch emanated beings to extol his virtues and gather the assembly that listens to the Dharma.
Furthermore, those who come to listen, if they see these various emanations, will follow them without opposition and will likewise give rise to emulation.

The main body (*samyak-āgama*) of all sutras relies upon the present causes and conditions to elucidate the principles and phenomena of that specific assembly;
having done so, it concludes with the dissemination section (*parīndanā*), which merely extols the subtle meaning of the current sutra and reveals its superior benefits.

within its primary doctrine (*samyak-artha*), it merely reveals and clarifies the wondrous meaning by unfolding it in three stages.

It intends to eliminate all the provisional teachings established within the holy teachings of a single lifetime for those of a certain class who first follow the Small Vehicle and later the Great Vehicle, thereby enabling them to see [the ultimate truth].

It is true. Having sublated the former three vehicles, it relies upon the originally inherent single nature to harmoniously integrate the three vehicles and establishes the real teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the present day as its orthodox core.
Although the text consists of nine grades, its meaning comprehensively subsumes all teachings.

Regarding the transition from the "Correct Teaching" (*shōjū*) back to the "Extensive Teaching" (*kōkyō*), one must understand that this text is capable of serving as a means of universal penetration.
It functions to reveal and circulate not only the provisional teachings of the past and all the secondary wheels of the Dharma (*shimatsu hōrin*), but how could it be limited to a single sutra alone?

Furthermore, although within the Correct Teaching he has already eloquently expressed his fundamental intention (*honkai*) accumulated over forty years, regarding the dispensation of a single lifetime...
The various traces of expedient manifestations have not yet had the leisure to be fully revealed.

Therefore, within this section on the Propagation of the Teaching, I shall now sweep away those former traces, causing [the reader] to look back and realize that what was previously seen mostly belonged to expedient manifestations.

Thus, it is not only the traces of the Original Teacher—such as his departure from the palace of King Śuddhodana—that are swept away to reveal one aspect of his long-established attainment; nor is it merely that... [the previous traces are swept away].
The traces prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* refer to the period when the three assemblies were being correctly taught;
at that time, because there was no opportunity to sweep away [delusions], the provisional means he employed have now all been swept away.

For instance, when the four sons heard the causes and conditions of the teaching, although they realized the long-term guidance [of the Buddha], how could they have known that the Great Universal Penetration (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*) was not itself the ultimate? Therefore, the emergence of the stupa served as [a sign].

Regarding the beginning of its circulation: henceforth, whenever one encounters this trace, one shall immediately brush away [delusions] to awaken them to the profound gate, expand their vast and great knowledge and vision, and cause them to give rise to great vows for its circulation.
One must ensure that this sutra has a designated recipient before ceasing [the effort].
Thus, it is known that although the texts for circulation are many, they are by no means wearisome. Herein, I shall now record all that pertains to the circulation.

The essential purport of this revelation is briefly summarized in several points to demonstrate the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics (*dharmatā* and *lakṣaṇa*) and the mutual penetration of principle and phenomena (*li* and *shi*).
This ensures that one does not become stuck in provisional traces. For example, when the Many-Jeweled Stūpa emerges from the earth, it and the earth do not obstruct one another;
thus, the trace of the earth being "greatly obstructive" is brushed aside, revealing the harmonious integration of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). [This applies to] the Pure Land...
The three transformations sweep away the traces of impure lands as having real existence, thereby manifesting the fundamental purity of the Buddha-land;
they shift the focus from other directions and sweep away the traces of those of good nature who pride themselves on being contemporaries of the Buddha.

By summoning the Dragon Girl to emerge from the sea, it is shown that anyone possessing sublime faith possesses the path to transcendence. Thus, even those of slight capacity who might otherwise be held in contempt are swept into the fold.
The traces of his manifestations are gathered in light; he sweeps away the traces of a single transformation within this Sahā world, revealing that his wondrous responses pervade everywhere.
The Many-Treasures Buddha shares his seat, sweeping away the traces of birth-and-death and the separation of ages, thereby merging past and present into a single consistency.

He records the proclamation regarding Devadatta, sweeping away the traces of actual transgression or compliance, while simultaneously manifesting the Original Teacher. This is also due to the merit of the sutra, which brings swift realization.

To verify this through reality: Mañjuśrī emerges from the ocean, sweeping away the traces of transformation within a single state of concentration, so that one may know the Sage’s response is capable of possessing the virtue of manifesting both concealment and appearance simultaneously.

Furthermore, since the land has already been transformed into purity, his re-emergence from the ocean sweeps away the boundaries between the pure and the defiled, as well as between water and land, revealing that the essence of the Buddha-land is infinitely layered and unimpeded. Moreover, he emerges from the earth to transmit and uphold [the Dharma].

It reveals the vertical pervasiveness of wondrous transformation to sweep away the vast disparities between above and below. By passing into extinction in the intermediate state, it sweeps away the traces of receiving a prediction upon lighting a lamp;
by revealing the long duration of attaining the Way, it further sweeps away the traces of entering a stupa and proclaiming extinction to manifest the permanence of the Dharma-body.
It distinguishes merits to reveal how hearing the Dharma for a single thought-moment allows for immediate transcendence.
By this, the hierarchical distinctions of the provisional vehicles are swept away. The six sense organs function interchangeably without departing from the physical body;

thus, this root-body is revealed to fundamentally transcend the categories of "one" or "six," yet possesses the virtue of being capable of both "one-ness" and "six-fold-ness. Beyond this, following the text, there are further subtle meanings for the wise to examine in detail.

From this chapter onward, all sections belong to the section on the Propagation of the Teaching (*parīndanā*).

Following the preceding exposition of the Dharma and its parables, the text further cites past causes and conditions so that those of all three faculties may receive their predictions of enlightenment. Thus, at the beginning of the sutra, the emission of light serves as the prologue.
A single episode of causes and conditions has thus reached its conclusion. However, for this Dharma to circulate, it cannot be entrusted to anyone who is not the right person;
nor can it be relied upon unless one is a manifested emanation of the Buddhas of antiquity gathered together.

Therefore, from the time he proclaimed his own extinction and sought a successor, until his final manifestation to entrust the teaching, he did not cease his efforts. This includes the King’s quest for the Dharma and the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood.

This serves as proof of the rarity of the Dharma. When calculated through successive multiplication up to the fiftieth stage, the merit of even a single atom derived from relying on this sutra is already inconceivable;
how much more so for the six kinds of Dharma-preachers! Furthermore, regarding those who were not disparaging:
before they heard this sutra, they practiced the path poorly, but after hearing it, they were finally able to practice well.

Only when the Bodhisattva path has moved the void to open its mouth—so as not to allow those who disparage it lightly to fall into suffering—and only then manifests its divine power to entrust [the teaching], ensuring that the Dharma endures.

All phenomena are integrated within a single nature and ultimately return to the eternally abiding and unobstructed.
Therefore, he first demonstrates this through the unobstructed realm in which one who has attained direct realization dwells, thereby inspiring great vows for its widespread circulation.

Regarding "unobstructed," it is commonly thought that the stupa and the earth element both belong to the category of material obstruction; however, here, due to illusory form, they do not obstruct themselves.
It collapses of its own accord; its very substance is the true emptiness. Therefore, when it surges forth, the two do not obstruct one another, abiding with brilliant clarity within the void.
Furthermore, this wondrous stupa has never been separate from my original teacher;
now, as the conditions for its circulation have matured, it manifests though it was previously unmanifested. This is nothing other than the operation of his divine power. △
