II. First, the general indication; second, the specific indication. Now, the first:
"O sons of good family, within this interval... [omitted] ...able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy."
Although the previous resolution of this near doubt is complete, I fear another doubt may arise:
"The *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras state that in a past life, Śākyamuni was once the Rishi Supuṣpacandra; at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he received the prediction of his future Buddhahood.
Only after passing through two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* did he reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), whereupon he entered parinirvāṇa. How can this be explained? Now, to clear this away: all of these...
This is the skillful means manifested after the fruit [of enlightenment] to bestow transformation. The passage beginning with "If there are, O sons of good family, those who...

demonstrates the skillful means of response and resonance (*saṃgati*). First, it clarifies that which evokes the response; the World-Honored One employs direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in his activities, yet he speaks of "observing the faculties" (*indriya*).
This is also speech that accords with reality. Furthermore, while the faculty of discernment is the Dharma-eye, it now possesses the full function of all five eyes by means of the Buddha-eye;
therefore, the term "Buddha" encompasses them all. That they have come to my presence is the response to the silent invocation of the nine realms.
According to those to be saved, he manifests bodies within the nine realms by means of his true self, which universally responds without partiality, thereby delivering them.
Furthermore, there are various names for his essential body and constant lifespans.
There are those who are great and those who are small; all of these are cases where non-arising is manifested as arising.

Furthermore, below this, it clarifies that those who attain liberation through the manifestation of non-extinction are likewise taught. Moreover, below this, it clarifies that within the two limits of arising and extinction mentioned above, various dharmas are preached through various skillful means, all of which involve the inconceivable interplay of the provisional and the real, the hidden and the manifest. In essence:
These various skillful means do nothing more than seek to cause sentient beings to first attain joy, so that they may gradually be led into the Buddha-wisdom through the *siddhāntas*.
△ Second, the specific demonstration.
"O sons of good family, the Tathāgata, seeing all sentient beings... [omitted] ...causes them to enter the Buddha-way, and thus speaks these words.

The preceding section generally clarifies the universal response throughout the nine realms. From here below, it specifically addresses those of dull faculties by demonstrating the near accomplishment through the eight phases of manifestation.
However, with the words "But I... and so forth, he directly brushes away the traces of this present near accomplishment and establishes the reality of the remote past.

To resolve the doubts of the multitude is what is meant by "revealing and manifesting. Based on this, those of sharp faculties—whose understanding extends beyond the literal text—constantly behold the Buddha, just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* there is no need for further revelation.
II. Clarifying that the Buddha’s deeds are not in vain (in three parts):
1. Directly demonstrating that they are not in vain; 2. Questioning and demonstrating clear vision; 3. Demonstrating that what is performed is not in vain. Now:
First:
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata (down to) all that he has spoken are true and not false.
This clarifies that the sūtras spoken after manifesting his body and attaining enlightenment above are all capable of being beneficial.
That is to say, either by means of causes and conditions, he speaks of the traces of his own and others' past lives;
or by means of physical characteristics, he manifests the bodies of himself and others; or by means of deeds, he points out that these are the works performed by himself and others.
All that he speaks is true and not false. △ Second, the inquiry and demonstration of clear vision.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata perceives reality as it truly is (up to: the Tathāgata sees clearly without error).
Since the Tathāgata is endowed with perfect, ultimate wisdom (*tathatājñāna*), his actions are never in vain.

Indeed, True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions (*pratyaya*) to manifest the appearance of the wild flowers of the triple world, causing the cataracts of the nine realms to see various things according to their own perceptions. Only...
The Tathāgata has perfectly realized its essence; thus, by means of the pure eye, he perceives the true realm.
Therefore, the appearances of the triple world are themselves the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since there is neither birth-and-death, who then could enter nirvāṇa?

Furthermore, since there is no one who regresses from the bodhicitta, there is likewise no one who generates the mind to seek liberation. Because there is no retreating from cultivation, within the fruition—
How could there be a Buddha who dwells in the world, or one who has entered parinirvāṇa?

Furthermore, if one seeks these various marks of emergence and cessation within the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*), nothing at all is found; therefore, they are not real. If one seeks the marks that follow conditions apart from this essence, they likewise cannot be found;
therefore, they are not non-existent. Because they possess the meaning of following conditions, they are not the same [as the essence].

The "suchness" (tathatā) perceived by those of the Two Vehicles possesses the meaning of immutability; thus, it is not the same as the "separateness and difference" perceived by those in the five destinies.

Only because it differs from the "two extremes" perceived within the triple world can one, through the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way, fully perceive the phenomena of the triple world as they manifest according to conditions. Regarding such matters as these, I have thoroughly penetrated their very depths.
The aggregates are without error. What constitutes error? It is the inability to know the single reality of *tathatā* (suchness) as it truly is;
consequently, one perceives signs of delusion such as emerging and retreating. △ Third, the efficacy of what is performed is not in vain.
Because sentient beings possess various natures (up to) the Buddha-works they perform are never for a moment abandoned.
First, the conditions that evoke [these works] are clarified:

because sentient beings, due to various natures formed by habitual tendencies in previous lives, manifest various inclinations before them, causing their sevenfold limbs of body and speech to perform various [deeds].
Regarding these karmic actions, one further establishes various conceptualizations and discriminations upon the specific objects of the preceding realm;

this constitutes the capacity to evoke a response. To clarify that the response follows the evocation so as to cause the production of roots of goodness, [the Buddha] has, since his own attainment of Buddhahood, been fervent and courageous in this teaching that responds to what is evoked and in the deeds he performs, never for a moment ceasing.
Question: According to the karma produced by the seven branches [of physical and vocal action], there should be a distinction between good and evil.

While that which is good can be said to produce its result (*vipāka*), how can that which is evil be said to do so? Answer: Suppose one sees a sentient being about to commit a grave offense for which they would inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell, and there is no other skillful means (*upāya*) to rescue them.
One must sever their life; though one falls into hell oneself, this causes the other to be liberated from suffering.
Is this not a response? △ Third, concluding that it is imperishable:
"Thus, since I attained Buddhahood (up to) even now it has not yet been exhausted; it is again double the aforementioned number."

Thus, below, there is first a general summary of the lifespan of the three bodies. This means that since the *tathatā* (suchness) realized is without beginning and without end, the wisdom that realizes it likewise attains a profound resonance with it and is not distinct from it;
how, then, could it have a beginning or an end? This is the non-extinction of this Dharma.
If it manifests through the realization of suchness, it may appear to have an initial arising, but in reality, it has no final exhaustion. This is the [lifespan of] retribution.

It does not perish. If one speaks of its "greatness of essence," then the transformations manifested according to conditions through its function appear to have arising and ceasing within the eyes of those with cataracts;

yet, because appearance is identical to nature, it is also eternally abiding and imperishable. From the phrase "all virtues" below, he again addresses the specific conclusion regarding the eternity of the retribution-body as it manifests, resolving further doubts:
namely, from the time I first entered and dwelt [in this state], that which I...
The lifespan attained is already double the aforementioned number; how much more so for that which follows the Way, the attainment of the True—how could it have any limit?
The reason for making this conclusion is that the various śrāvakas once identified with the body that achieved enlightenment beneath the tree.

This constitutes the retributive body (*vipākakāya*). Subsequently, it is refined through the *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies and other teachings, leading one to further realize that while the tree under which he sat was a transformation (*nirmāṇa*), the retributive body still resides in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Upon hearing this present sutra, one finally awakens to the principle that the three bodies are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*) and that their essence and function are all-pervasive.
Thus, one understands that what manifests before one is precisely the Dharma-body and Retribution-body within the transformation-body. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* [speaks of] permanence.

He provides the analogy of two birds flying together to illustrate [the relationship between] permanence and impermanence. △ Second, clarifying that the skillful means are not extinction while manifesting extinction. Now, first:
yet this is not a true extinction (parinirvāṇa); rather, it is by means of this skillful expedient (*upāya*) that he teaches and transforms sentient beings.

Now, through this revelation, he causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom and to know that the Buddha-body is eternally abiding. One must understand that previously, regarding their entry [into nirvana]...
The proclamation of his passing at the time of the construction of the stūpa was a skillful means (*upāya*). Indeed, this skillful means was precisely intended to awaken sentient beings.
Thus, among the ten benefits, the Tathāgata possesses the ninth: the benefit of generating wholesome roots by manifesting extinction.

This means that if the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for a long time, those of meager merit would not conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter; therefore, he manifested [his passing].

[The Buddha] enters extinction so as to cause sentient beings to feel longing and attachment, whereby they plant roots of goodness. This is precisely for the sake of those who form karmic conditions with the Buddha during his lifetime, as well as for future sentient beings;
it is by means of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) manifesting extinction that he causes them to give rise to wholesome states.

Regarding the ancient commentary which claims that all three bodies possess the meaning of manifesting extinction, I do not know what benefit there is in this. △ Second, the investigation and explanation of the reason [for this], in two parts. First, regarding...
The first part provides an inverse explanation of "dwelling for a long time. The second part provides a direct explanation regarding the difficulty of encountering [the Buddha]. Herein is the first:
Why is this so? If the Buddha were to dwell in the world for a long time, [it would lead to] the thought that he is difficult to encounter and a heart of reverence.
Those of meager virtue, though they encounter the era of a Buddha, do not plant roots of goodness; consequently, in future lives, they fall into poverty and lowliness.
Upon encountering the objects of the five desires, they give rise to deep attachment and enter the net of the three inversions. If they see what is inferior, they think:
"If one does not proclaim extinction, it is not only useless, but even harmful. At worst, this conversely gives rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, such that [virtue] is not produced.
Reverence. Regarding the three inversions: first is the inversion of mindfulness (*smṛti-viparyāsa*). This arises from the mutual confrontation of the sense faculties and their objects;
it is the source of manifold delusions, for it establishes various forms of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Second is the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).

This refers to the failure to understand the faults and afflictions of the six sense objects, which can destroy one's roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); it involves falsely establishing boundaries and distinctions within objective conditions. Third is the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). [This] gives rise to...
Because of various inversions, false views are themselves inverted views. This means that the eye is the root of all views;

because one does not understand that the objects of perception are like illusions, one clings to annihilationism or eternalism, thereby giving rise to perverse inversions. △ Second, the explanation in accordance with the difficulty of encountering [the Buddha].
Therefore, the Tathāgata, through skillful means, speaks [of nirvana]—though there is no actual extinction—he says "extinction.
For the Dharma-body is all-pervasive and its function is eternally constant; thus, its wondrous transformations are inconceivable and its emergence from the earth is unfathomable.
Therefore, those whose Dharma-eye is clear and pure see that his birth at the Lumbinī Garden and his passing between the twin trees were both wondrous responses of his essential nature.
They realize that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni was originally subject to no extinction;

yet, for the sake of those whose cataracts of ignorance have not yet been removed, he employs the skillful means of proclaiming his death to awaken them and inspire the cultivation of goodness, saying that such an encounter is difficult to achieve and exceedingly rare, even if one passes through immeasurable eons.
Even after the passage of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, there remains the distinction between those who can see [the Buddha] and those who cannot.

Therefore, the following section concludes by establishing the original intent of the proclamation of extinction. II. Manifestation through Simile (3 parts): 1. Stating the Dharma; 2. Establishing the Simile; 3. Applying the Simile.
First: Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false.
To "cite the same as all Buddhas" reveals that this skillful means of manifesting extinction was not initiated by myself alone, but was employed to transform those in the five turbidities.
This is the standard rule. △ Second, establishing analogies, in four parts: First, the good physician departs; second, the good physician manifests extinction;
third, the good physician does not undergo extinction; fourth, the good physician is without falsehood. Now, the first part.
For example, it is like a skilled physician, wise and sagacious, who for some reason travels far to another country.
The physician is a metaphor for the Buddha; the sons are a metaphor for those sentient beings who have already been transformed by his teaching.

He is called "skilled" because he possesses inner wisdom and outward mastery of the scriptures and skillful means (*upāya*), knowing both the medicine and the disease—just as the Buddha possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom (*prajñā*) to know [the afflictions and their remedies].

The "capacity" (jī) refers to the Dharma. As for the person below [this level], one clarifies the intimacy or distance of the meaning of "son" by approximating it according to the number of those with the faculties of the Three Vehicles:
ten individuals are assigned to Bodhisattvas, twenty to Pratyekabuddhas, and one hundred to Śrāvakas.
If these are assigned to the three types of causes, then through unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), one regards the great earth as equal to one's own children; this is because...

The direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) may be said to consist of one hundred [factors]. If we consider those who previously heard the Dharma but have not yet given rise to understanding, twenty factors can be assigned to the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
However, for those who, having drunk the milk of the Dharma in past lives, first gave rise to understanding and resolved their minds [on enlightenment], [the situation is different].

Subsequently, he withdrew from the great [assembly]. This refers to those who have fully realized the causal stage; they can be categorized into ten types. Here, however, they are mentioned collectively.

Regarding the passage "Because there are those below": it is like when conditions elsewhere have ripened and he manifests birth there, yet in this land, one sees the fire extinguished as the fuel is exhausted.
**II. The Good Physician Manifests Extinction (in six parts):** 1. The sons drink poison. 2. The father returns home. 3. The sons...
Seeking help: (1) the four excellent physicians and their medicines; (2) differences in whether they are taken or not; (3) the skillful means of manifesting extinction. Now, for the first [point]:
later, the sons drank other poisonous medicines, and when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disordered, writhing upon the ground.
Later, he drank poison; because he himself sought to drink it, he drank it, which caused the medicine to take effect.
This is like those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, falsely receive heterodox teachings and thus increase their cycle of saṃsāra. △ Second, the father returns home.
At that time, his father returned home.

Upon his return, he found that his son had mistakenly ingested poison. This was just as the Buddha perceives sentient beings who have deeply entered into false views—all of which are brought about by seeking through wrong means.
Therefore, moved once again by great compassion, he manifested his physical form. It may be said in private:
Although the teachings they uphold may be either heterodox or orthodox, their minds that weary of suffering and seek deliverance are no different.
Therefore, even heterodox seeking provides the conditions for a response to the orthodox.
Thus, when the Buddha appears in the world, those he first delivers are his great disciples, many of whom have come from among the heterodox and external paths. △ Third, the sons seek rescue.
The sons drank poison and some lost their original minds... (up to) "I pray for rescue and healing, and grant me further life.
Seeking rescue is like knocking upon the Sage with urgency as the situation requires. Drinking poison is like those who accept and adhere to false teachings.

However, there are two types of faculties: sharp and dull. The dull are those who have lost their minds because they are deeply attached to illusory phenomena; even the benefit of being matured and liberated [cannot reach them]. Furthermore—
In the future, their benefit shall be such that they do not lose their minds. Regarding those who obtain benefit in the present:

although these two persons see the same physical forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), neither knows the limits of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) or the Reward-body (*vipāka-kāya*); therefore, it is said they "see from afar. Nevertheless, both are able to give rise to the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*).
"Please turn the Wheel of Dharma. This refers to the causes and conditions for attaining deliverance. △ Fourth, the skilled physician provides medicine.
The father sees that his sons and others are suffering in this manner... (until)... quickly eliminate their suffering so that they no longer have these manifold afflictions.
The sons of the Buddha, before they had yet encountered the Buddha, maintained heterodox views and increased their suffering.

Now that they have encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One follows ancient precedent to preach for them, enabling them to transcend suffering. The sūtras are like the ritual of transformation; the medicinal herbs are like the method of transformation.
Their color, fragrance, and flavor are like the precepts, concentration, and wisdom expounded within the teachings—capable of subduing and severing [afflictions]. Part One.

Pounding [the medicine] is like severing conceptually arisen afflictions; sifting it is like severing innately arisen afflictions; blending it is like realizing the principle through true wisdom, attaining a silent accord that is indivisible.
The phrase "and then prepare" expresses the intent of encouraging practice based on personal realization. △ Fifth, the differences in taking [the medicine].

Among those sons, those who did not lose their minds—up to those who, regarding these fine colors, fragrances, and medicines, deemed them unpalatable—are like those who, having previously exhausted the *niṣyanda-hetu* (flow-on cause), now encounter a Buddha and again give rise to the *utpatti-hetu* (arising cause), thereby swiftly transcending birth and death;

this is what is meant by "the seed of the Buddha arises from conditions. Those who do not take the medicine are like those who have already fully possessed the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) in past lives.

Although he now encounters the Buddha, he instead gives rise to arrogance and self-indulgence; because he still does not follow the teachings, the Tathāgata utters the lament of his passing into extinction.
△ Sixth, the skillful means of manifesting extinction.
The father thought thus: "This son is to be pitied... (up to) "...he sent a messenger back to inform him that his father had already died.

Although sentient beings in the world encounter a Buddha through the cause of conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*), they are struck by the three poisons and are unable to give rise to the cause of origination (*utpatti-hetu*);
they merely establish a connection for future affinity (*karmic connection*). Therefore, the World-Honored One toils, first using the proclamation of extinction to awaken them, and subsequently...

He manifests extinction to uproot [afflictions], causing them to plant seeds of goodness in this life and to ripen for liberation in future lives. His aging and decline are like the conclusion of a transformation;

his arrival at death is like entering final nirvana. He leaves behind medicine like the Bequeathed Teachings and delivers instructions like those to the Bodhisattvas on the Four Reliances, entrusting them with his final testament to propagate the Dharma.
△ Third, the Good Physician Does Not Pass Away, in two parts. First, the Sons.
The illness was cured. The two excellent physicians appeared once more; this is the first instance.
At that time, when the sons heard that their father had passed away, they immediately took [the medicine] and ingested it, and their toxic illnesses were all healed.
Sentient beings, seeing the Buddha enter extinction, feel they have no reliance; therefore, they resolve their minds and practice cultivation, considering themselves capable of evoking a response.
Thus, the Buddha’s act of manifesting extinction is precisely for the sake of future sentient beings, serving as the condition for their deliverance and acting as the cause that evokes a response.
This demonstrates that the Buddha’s work is not in vain. 2. The Good Physician Returns.
Manifestation.
When the father heard that his son had fully recovered, he immediately returned and saw him face to face.

That the recovery was immediate and capable of such an effect means the cause for manifesting the body has already been established. As for this "seeing," it is a realization that is as clear as the sky.
This refers to the wisdom that is eternally present and indestructible. Nevertheless, it is only through taking refuge that one subsequently perceives it;

thus, its purpose is identical to severing afflictions and awakening to the true permanence. This is like the previous section on the recovery from illness, where the capacity to evoke [the healing] was discussed;
here, "perceiving" may also be understood as the severance of delusions. △ Fourth, the Good Physician is Without Deception.
"What do you think, sons of good family? [The question continues] "...is this not a false offense? "No, World-Honored One.

This section is specifically for the sake of the Tathāgata. Since he manifests birth within non-arising and manifests extinction within non-extinction, it might seem subject to the charge of falsehood and thus be open to criticism.
Therefore, he employs the analogy of a skilled physician traveling abroad and returning home to clarify this point, revealing that it is not merely a matter of manifesting illumination.
The benefit of sentient beings in the present world is not in vain; furthermore, this also reveals that the two other periods—past and future—are just like today.
By means of the Buddha-work of illusory flowers, all sentient beings truly obtain abundant benefit.

Thus, the principle that the benefit of sentient beings across the three periods of time is not in vain overflows beyond words. Therefore, the previous heading stated: "For the sake of delivering sentient beings, all is real."
"Empty. Now, within this summary, he again poses the question regarding emptiness and falsity. △ Third, the conclusion.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this" (up to) "if one speaks of my faults as being empty and false according to the Dharma."
△ Part Two: The Verses, in two sections. First, a general explanation of the long duration; second, a specific revelation of the skillful means. Now, the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From the time I attained Buddhahood (until) leading [beings] into the Buddha-way, it has been immeasurable kalpas.

By using the two characters "immeasurable" (*wúliàng*) to qualify the preceding terms such as "hundreds and thousands," the text precisely reveals this number; it is something that none but a Buddha can fathom.
Furthermore, it demonstrates the scope of those being transformed: if even they enter the Buddha-way, how could the capacity of the One who delivers them be measured? △
Second, the specific explanation of the skillful means has two parts: first, eternally abiding without extinction; second, not being extinguished yet manifesting extinction.
The first part has two sections: first, the general heading; second, the detailed exposition. Now, the first [section].
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests nirvana through skillful means, yet in reality he does not pass into extinction; he eternally abides here preaching this Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "eternally abiding here": among the Tathāgata’s eight kinds of sovereign mastery, the fourth clarifies his manifestation of immeasurable classes [of beings] while constantly dwelling in a single land.
This means that although the Tathāgata manifests bodies of various classes for the sake of sentient beings, he...
The place where he dwells is always in one location, sovereign and unimpeded. As a sutra says:

"The mind of the Tathāgata abides peacefully and immovably, yet it can manifest immeasurable forms according to the various types of beings. It further says: "The body of the Tathāgata eternally dwells in a single land."
And yet, all [beings] in other lands see him completely. △ Second, the explanation for establishing this:
"I constantly abide here" (up to) "always remaining on Vulture Peak and in other various dwelling places."
Following the above, there should be a question: "If you have always dwelt here, why do we not see you? Therefore, it is explained:
"Although I have always dwelt here, by means of my supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), I cause those who are subject to inversion (*viparyāsa*) not to see me, even though I am near.

Regarding the phrase "the multitude sees," this specifically refers to how [the Tathāgata] appears to undergo extinction throughout the three periods of time; although he manifests the appearance of existing or passing away according to the needs of beings, in reality, he is eternally dwelling and never perishes.
The first two verses clarify the timing of the response in the past. The subsequent one and a half verses—specifically the first half—respond by demonstrating birth through non-birth.
The next verse speaks of longevity to discuss permanence. The remaining one and a half verses clarify the response in other lands.

Once this is accomplished, one should then relinquish it. I see that the latter half of the following verse clearly demonstrates the causes and conditions for cessation, while further establishing future sensation and response.
Regarding "supernatural powers" below, this concludes the establishment of permanence and non-extinction.

When it says "permanent" in reference to Vulture Peak, and "reaches" in reference to other locations, it is like the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s description of not departing from the Bodhi tree while ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The principle regarding the "beneficial function" (*liyong*) and so forth is the same as for the others. Question: Since the Tathāgata’s great function is said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm by virtue of its essence, why is there a distinction among sentient beings between those who see the Buddha and those who do not?
Answer: The great function is a gate of arousal; it necessarily manifests only in response to an invocation.
Therefore, there is the presence or absence of seeing [the Buddha]. This is not comparable to the "greatness of essence," which is the gate of non-arousal. Part Two.

"Neither extinguished nor manifesting extinction" has two parts: first, revealing permanence by way of location; second, establishing that it is not in vain through a metaphor. The first part has two sub-sections: first, specifically observing the exhaustion of the kalpa;
second, the differing natures of sin and merit. Now, the first [sub-section].
Sentient beings see the end of the kalpa... [down to] ...filled with such sorrow, fear, and various afflictions.

This section below specifically clarifies the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment). Because, within the gate of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), essence and characteristics are unimpeded and the environment and its inhabitants are of one suchness, it is said that when referring to the "inhabitant" (*sattva*), the hidden and the manifest are of one principle;
when referring to the "environment," its arising and ceasing are inconceivable. As previously stated in the section on length...
The text: Although the permanence [of the Tathāgatagarbha] has already been correctly elucidated, the supporting realm (*dhātu*) has not yet been revealed.

Furthermore, the defiled and the pure share the same source and do not exist apart from one another; thus, when one exists, the other ceases. Though their cessations do not occur simultaneously, their arisings must occur in the same place.
Therefore, for those who do not understand that birth, death, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, this section is now separately provided to demonstrate its pervasiveness.
The principle that the Perfect Immovable [Pure Land] eternally abides is first elucidated by a half-verse concerning the inconceivable nature of the kalpa-conflagration:
those with evil karma perceive only the destruction by fire and do not see anything remaining undestroyed; this which is destroyed is merely the coarse aspect of a transformation.
Next, two and a half verses clarify its subtle persistence. This persistence arises from two causes; the first pertains to the Buddha.

There are two types of wholesome karma. First, with respect to the Buddha: he does not depart from the realm of fire; he is not only free from suffering, but moreover possesses the dharma-bliss of self-enjoyment.
Therefore it is said, "In this land of mine, there is peace and security. Second, with respect to those of wholesome karma:

they likewise do not depart from the realm of fire or the place of self-enjoyment, and furthermore possess the realm of other-enjoyment as well as the pure land of transformation. Therefore it is said, "The heavens..."
The realm is filled with people; sentient beings enjoy themselves as flowers rain down in offering to the Buddha.
Furthermore, although these noble ones dwelling in this subtle state know that fire exists at that moment, they do not perceive any appearance of fire.

Nevertheless, there are also those who manifest as if seeing the appearance of fire—namely, remaining within existence without ceasing—in order to reveal the true permanence of the Buddha-land and the unity of the environment and its inhabitants.
It is so. △ Second, the difference between sin and merit.
For those sinful beings (up to) "who see the Buddha only after a long time," it is taught that a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
The first two verses clarify that with good and evil karma as the causes that evoke [the response], there are those who do not even hear the name [of the Buddha].
All those who see [the Buddha] obtain this distinction. The first half-verse of the subsequent stanza explains longevity within the context of wholesome karma by fully elucidating the causal factors;
the second half explains the difficulty of encountering a Buddha within the context of wholesome karma by fully elucidating the causal conditions.

△ Second, the metaphorical illustration that [the teaching] is not in vain, in three parts: first, raising wisdom to encourage faith; second, briefly showing the characteristics of the metaphor; third, the application.
From beginning to end. Now, for the first [part]:
"Such is my power of wisdom" (up to) "I shall sever it so that it is forever exhausted; the Buddha’s word is true and not false.

Regarding the fact that what was previously called "by means of various supernormal powers" is now stated as "my power of wisdom," the mutual citation of these two—earlier and later—is intended precisely to reveal [the truth].
The various secret skillful means are all that flow forth from the two powers of spiritual essence and wisdom.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that when I was a bodhisattva, the lifespan I had achieved was not yet exhausted; now it is further stated that this is obtained through long-cultivated practice.
The preceding and following passages all refer to the lifespan of karmic retribution (*vipākāyuṣ*) in order to manifest that [the Buddha] attained enlightenment long ago.

Furthermore, although those emerging from the various stages (*bhūmi*) occupy high positions and are numerous, they are nonetheless beings to be converted after the attainment of the fruit; as for those converted during the time of practicing the causes, [they are not mentioned here].
It is utterly unfathomable; therefore, I exhort the wise not to harbor doubts. △ Second, a brief indication of the nature of the analogy:
It is like a physician who, through skillful means, speaks of his death in order to cure a mad son; though he is actually alive, he says he is dead, yet no one can claim that he is speaking falsely.
△ Connecting the Beginning and the End:
"I too shall become a Father of the World" (up to) "...may I swiftly attain the Buddha-body through entry into unsurpassed wisdom.
Thinking thus for myself at all times: "By what skillful means may I quickly attain Buddhahood? This is the earnest hope of one leaning upon the threshold for a correct view.
Most urgent indeed. △ Second, the merit of hearing this teaching.
Chapter Seventeen: Distinguishing Merit. Regarding "Distinguishing Merit":
when the Buddha spoke of his lifespan, those who had constantly followed him on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and those who had previously gathered like clouds were all assembled in great numbers.

The Jewel followed him; his emanated attendants, the dragon hosts surging from the sea, and the venerable elders emerging from the earth gathered in successive ocean-like assemblies within a single seat.
Upon hearing the sound of the Dharma but once, their worldly afflictions were instantly stilled and their concentration and wisdom became clear and bright.

All this was due to the merit of hearing the Dharma, which they attained within their hearts; hence it is called "merit" (*guṇa*). Furthermore, there are varying degrees of benefit, ranging from shallow to deep.
There are hierarchies of rank; were it not for the Buddha’s teaching, by what means could they be known?

Therefore, they must be distinguished. At the beginning of this chapter, the subject and object are presented together; thus, it is called "Distinguishing the Merits. Question: Why is the benefit of hearing [the Buddha's] lifespan superior to the benefit of hearing the correct exposition of the Dharma?
Answer: When hearing the correct exposition, one only knows that Śākyamuni Buddha [taught] from the Deer Park up until the present assembly.
Only now has his original aspiration been fully realized; yet what he had previously awakened to was merely the matter of a single transformation.
Therefore, those who benefited were limited to the disciples of the Three Vehicles. Now, upon hearing [the Buddha’s] lifespan, he has attained a sudden and vast awakening.

That Śākyamuni Buddha attained the Way long ago—such as when he preached extensively under the guidance of Dīpaṃkara and received his prediction—is but a provisional teaching from the middle period. Furthermore, he has advanced...

Having realized the three bodies and the three lifespans, the principle of perfect fusion and eternal abiding is established; therefore, compared to previous gains, this is both more abundant and superior.

Furthermore, as for the great assembly, from the beginningless kalpas until now, they have repeatedly witnessed the Tathāgata’s manifestations of birth and manifestations of extinction within the process of perfuming and refinement.
Thus, upon hearing this single revelation of the truth, they suddenly bring forth their past roots of goodness.

They are developed simultaneously; therefore, those who obtain this benefit reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and even their number can be calculated by the dust motes of a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), let alone those who obtain other benefits. Question:

If one judges the benefit of hearing [the Buddha’s] lifespan according to the Tiantai school’s Fourfold Teachings (*sijiao*), it properly belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). If one compares it with our own school, it seems to belong to the Final [Teaching].
[Question: Indeed, one must still transcend the Sudden [teaching] before it can be called Perfect. How are these two systems to be reconciled? [Answer:

If we speak in terms of the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*), once one has ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*), regardless of whether it is the Partial or the Perfect, all are entirely equal. Thus, both schools can be harmoniously integrated.
It is solely because the teachings upheld prior to the stages of the grounds vary in their completeness or deficiency of verbal characteristics that there are provisional and ultimate teachings;
this results in differences in the arousal of the bodhicitta, such that the practices cultivated thereby differ by factors of ten thousandfold or even a hundred thousandfold.
For this reason, those who judge the teachings (panjiao) have taken different perspectives, resulting in differences between the two schools that cannot be reconciled.
Furthermore, if one compares it with the present sutra, the terminology within the Perfect Teaching (yuan) appears somewhat deficient; thus, it might seem unnecessary to reconcile them.

However, if one assigns it to the category of the Perfect Teaching, there is no reason why they could not be reconciled. Nevertheless, this still leaves open the possibility that later arrivals might occupy a superior position.

...this sigh of lamentation. Furthermore, while your school (the Tiantai) regards the threefold contemplation within a single mind as "perfect" (*yuan*), our school maintains that this contemplation still belongs to the stage of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*).
One must transcend the discussion of principle to speak of phenomena alone; only upon reaching the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*) does one attain the ultimate.
Although the Tiantai school also speaks of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena, it is specifically because they have not yet applied the analysis of the six aspects (*liu xiang*).

The profound mysteries of the ten mysterious gates of dependent origination (*daśa-guhya-pratītyasamutpāda*) and other such meanings are thereby revealed. Although these are all equally termed "perfect" (*yuan*), their meanings are in fact distinct.

Question: What are the distinctions among the various teaching paths? Answer: As in the stages of the five teachings of our own school, they are unified by the depth of the path of contemplation (*guan-dao*), which serves as that which subdues and that which severs;
and the nature of mind within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-cittatā*), which serves as the object of focus and the realization. Furthermore, regarding the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa*)—...

The various categories and subdivisions of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both seeds and manifestations are taken as that which is to be severed. However, in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), this is discussed solely in terms of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
As for the latter four teachings, each reveals progress according to the degree of subtlety or coarseness of the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) inherent to its respective school.

Therefore, among those who proceed suddenly according to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*), while at the stage of the Three Worthies (*traya-puṇya-bhūmi*), they merely suppress the two obstacles arising from discrimination.
Those who proceed gradually sever only the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). After exiting the realm [of desire], they merely hear the name of the "ox-cart," yet neither of them boards it.
As for those with sudden faculties at the initial *vihāra*, they immediately attain the permanent suppression of the two obstacles arising from discrimination.
In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, one is reborn there according to one’s vows, attaining a state equal to that of the first bhūmi from the very beginning.

As for the gradual [approach], one may suppress the active manifestation of the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) within the ten stages of faith, or gradually suppress and eliminate it within the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ śaikṣāḥ*).
These two teachings both rely on the successive cultivation and realization of the stages and grounds; therefore, they are called the "gradual teaching. Within the fourth, the sudden [teaching], all—

He does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), but only elucidates true nature (*tathatā*). Furthermore, there is no Buddha who is not Buddha; there is neither arising nor non-arising. This very mind is itself Buddha;
it is entirely devoid of stages or positions. Even recently, there have been those within this Sudden Teaching who have established a hierarchy of levels.

This is somewhat contrary to the sudden teaching’s essential intent. In the fifth [stage], the Perfect Teaching, although that which is severed does not differ from the previous [teachings], it is specifically because the contemplative method (dhyāna) mounted upon it has attained perfect fusion and sovereign mastery.

Consequently, the sequential arrangements (pravibhāga) of the former teachings—whether in terms of stages, practices, time, or the subject and object of what is severed—are all simultaneously melted and fused. Thus, one and many become mutually identical.

The mutual interpenetration of phenomena, the reciprocal inclusion of thought-moments and kalpas, and the fruit of the non-obstruction between all things—these are further established through three types of birth to demonstrate swift realization.
Among these three, those such as the hell-dweller and the celestial being are born through seeing and hearing; upon receiving a single ray of light, they immediately ascend to the ten stages.
The bhikṣu in the forest is born through the realization of entry; thus, the Way is accomplished in the space of a single word. These two types of persons...

All [of these] are initiated within the very first thought-moment of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), at which point one immediately awakens to the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and perfectly accords with the single reality (*eka-tattva*), becoming equal to Samantabhadra. These statements are all made from the perspective of the actual meaning of the gate of faith at the beginning of practice.

Regarding the three stages of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), those who attain Buddhahood while dwelling in the final stage do so either through horizontal inclusion (*tiryak-saṃgraha*) or through vertical progression (*ūrdhva-krama*).

If one takes the meaning of "initiating the supreme seeking" as primary and "unfolding" as secondary, this refers to the *xíngbù* (sequential) teaching, spoken with the intent that one shall attain the *yuánjī* (perfect ultimate).

If one takes the meaning of "unfolding the three virtues (*triguṇa*)" and so forth as primary while including the preceding initiation, this refers to the statement that the Bodhicitta—the root of practice—is ultimately endowed with all virtues. Beyond this, there is nothing else.
The Buddha said: "To know how to uphold the teachings and realize the practice, one must first carefully examine the teachings and their meanings. Question:

"Regarding the initial stage of the first abode (*prathamābhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and the initial stage of the first abode at the end [of the teaching], both manifest the eight aspects (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*). Is there still a difference in their meaning?"

Answer: Regarding the manifestation of the eight phases in a world without a Buddha at the very beginning of the first dwelling (*vihāra*), this is a demonstration based on the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), there are two [possibilities]: if one attains Buddhahood while still in that dwelling, it is a case of "the initial encompassing the subsequent," whereby the later stages are subsumed within the first.
Just as Sudhana traversed all the stages within a single lifetime, this is the characteristic of the non-obstruction between the circular and the sequential.

If one attains ultimate Buddhahood, then the various stages are viewed in relation to one another, with the initial stage encompassing the subsequent ones, as in the case of the Dragon Girl and others.
This practice demonstrates that the sequential (vyavasthāna) does not obstruct the simultaneous (saṃbheda). Therefore, the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) cannot be compared to this. Question:

Below this, one hears of those who attain the state of a successor (*kumārabhūta*) through their lifespan; how do they differ from those who achieve the fruit of a single lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or those who have perfected it over vast eons (*kalpa*)?

Answer: Regarding the locus of realization, fundamentally there are not two. If one relies on the provisional establishment of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), because it has not yet delineated the aspects of virtue to clarify the meanings of the tenfold inexhaustibility and so forth, it should belong to the "common teaching" (*tongjiao*). This refers precisely to the commonality between that which can lead [others] and that which is led.

One must not, therefore, apply the principle of "increasing the Way and diminishing birth" universally and thereby negate this meaning. For this reason, the present sutra can be categorized as "sudden and perfect.
The text has two parts: first, the merits manifested in the present; second, the merits for after the extinction [of the Buddha].

The first part has two sections: first, the arousal of the mind to increase the Way; second, deep faith in an instant. The first section further has two parts: first, what the Tathāgata says; second, [what the Bodhisattvas say].

△ Second, the Buddha speaks of five [attainments]. First, obtaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); second, dhāraṇī and eloquence (*pratibhāna*); third, being able to turn the wheel of Dharma;

From this point downward, the Tathāgata has merely distinguished the benefits obtained by those present before him;
he has not yet had the leisure to investigate their past causes. Now, to briefly trace back to their source, one will further see that the merit of this sutra is unfathomable. For instance:

They attain the fruit of equal enlightenment while having one remaining birth among humans. It is not the case that all those who have transcended and ascended [to this state] originate solely from the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and so forth;

logically, there must also be those whose vehicle-zeal is swift but whose ethical discipline is lax, who come from among those in the eight difficult circumstances or from ordinary beings still bound by fetters.
Why is this? Because of the benefit of hearing the [Buddha’s] lifespan and seeing his secondary marks (anuvyañjana).

Furthermore, because there is neither duality nor distinction, those who attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) from this point downward do not solely derive from the initial and second stages of faith within the provisional and shallow teachings.

There must also be ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have currently awakened the great mind (*mahā-citta*), as well as those who have previously awakened the great mind but still remain among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*). All such individuals equally hear of the supreme merit of the [Buddha’s] lifespan.
There is no need to undergo ten thousand more kalpas; all shall transcend and enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

By inferring from these two positions, the various stages explained in the intermediate sections can be understood by analogy. As for the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it means that at the time of hearing the [Buddha’s] life-span, one suddenly awakens to the fact that arising and ceasing are of one suchness, not forming a dualistic interpretation, and knowing that all dharmas are the mind itself.
Furthermore, one knows that the self-nature of this mind is itself all phenomena; thus, principle manifests within one's own mind.
This very nature of the mind is already endowed with boundless virtues. Moreover, the initial possession of subsequent virtues is solely the domain of wisdom.

By perceiving this nature, one accomplishes the wisdom-body, is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and this constitutes the accomplishment of faith—the initial sign of entering and abiding [in the stage].
△ Second, the eloquence of dhāraṇī.

They do not forget or lose any of it. Furthermore, there are those at the lower stage who have entered the ten stages of practice and dedication (*daśa-pratipatti-pūrvaka-bhūmi*);

furthermore, from a small chiliocosm [up to] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

From the first dwelling (*vihāra*) up to this point, in each successive stage, one destroys one grade of ignorance (*avidyā*) and increases one portion of the Middle Way.
Finally, by further destroying one grade of the subtle characteristic of birth (*sūkṣma-jāti-lakṣaṇa*), one enters [the ultimate state].
Wondrous Awakening. In each and every stage, they increase the perfectly wondrous Way and diminish birth through transformation. △ Fifth, the arousal of the bodhicitta:
furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who [aroused] the mind of *samyaksambodhi*.

These individuals—those who have first awakened the bodhicitta, those who have newly entered the stage of the ten faiths, and those who have attained the purification of the six sense organs at the lower level—should be included herein.

The Buddha spoke these various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [up to] singing immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.

For the sake of transforming this class of gradual-capacity practitioners, the World-Honored One has, from time immemorial, refined them through the skillful means (*upāya*) of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Although they have reached the stage of maturation in this present life, they still require gradual guidance; therefore, regarding the speaker—
Regarding the person: first, by concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior, one may establish the provisional based upon the real.

From kalpas as numerous as motes of dust in the past, regarding both the bodies he has manifested and the teachings he has proclaimed, there have been successive layers of profound grace and kindness in his guidance.

Even if one were to offer one’s own body as a seat and carry him upon one’s head for as many eons as there are grains of sand, how could one ever repay even a small fraction of it? Thus, from this point of pure awakening and understanding...
From within their hearts, they flow forth various offerings of Dharma to express their momentary reverence and to exhaust this momentary mind.

Let us examine the virtues accomplished by one who understands this. A single thought-moment is manifest as distinct from many;
one who possesses faith and understanding, having heard within this assembly that the Buddha’s life-span is eternally abiding, immediately advances to realize their own nature.
Since they have already attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they should also be equal to all Buddhas, and likewise equal to all sentient beings.
Whether mundane or supramundane, whether the basis or the correction, all are non-contradictory with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
One possesses a resolute vision, attaining self-confidence within the mind; being entirely free from doubt, clear understanding manifests before one, such that one cannot be led astray.

This refers to the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) attained by an ordinary person still bound by fetters (*paryavasthāna*). Regarding "what is attained" below, this briefly enumerates what has been accomplished.

Regarding this vast merit: even if one were to practice the various perfections extensively over many eons, when comparing the merit accomplished thereby with the merit accomplished within this single moment of faith, the former is shown to be vastly surpassed by the latter.
The only exception is *prajñā* (wisdom), because this sublime faith is itself right wisdom; thus, it is impossible for it to decline.
This is because, within this single moment of the ultimate stage, all vast merits are already fully present and are sustained by clear and lucid faith;
moreover, being encompassed by the secret empowerment of all Buddhas, one attains non-retrogression.
△ Section Two: The Verses. This section has two parts: first, the verse on the capacity for calculation; second, the clarification of possessing merit. Now, the first:

△ Second, clarifying the possession of virtues:

The following section clarifies the causes for being able to have faith. Because of possessing virtue, there is one verse.

The subsequent verse correctly clarifies that only those who have practiced for a long time can give rise to this sublime faith, thus revealing the limitations of superficial practice.
People cannot help but have doubts. Thus, the following three verses clarify that such a person not only possesses faith, but is further able to generate the aspiration to emulate [the Buddha].
The subsequent two verses further explain the reason why they are able to have such faith:
because they possess a profound mind that delights in the True Dharma, they do not give rise to attachment toward worldly dharmas. There is purity...
Because the mind is pure and possesses a straightforward mind free from flattery and crookedness, one can finally give rise to understanding and finally believe without doubt.
The reason for this repeated and detailed explanation is that within a single thought-moment, one can possess inconceivable virtues;
these are not easily believed. II. Conclusion and Illustration of All Practices (in two parts): 1. First, citing the merit of briefly explaining one chapter.
This serves as the illustration. Second, the merit of one who has heard the entire extensive sūtra is cited as the object of comparison. First, regarding the former:

If merely hearing a discourse on longevity can produce the merit of understanding the underlying intent behind the words—
such that one attains non-retrogression and gives rise to unsurpassed wisdom— how much more inconceivable must be the virtue accomplished by those who hear the entire sutra?
Therefore, this is the lower category. How much more so for one who hears it in its entirety? △ Second, citing the merit of hearing the entire extensive sūtra as the object of comparison:

The preceding passage cited the virtue of having heard little as being exceedingly great; this was precisely intended to serve as a comparison for the even greater virtue of having heard extensively.

Thus, the words are that which is believed, and the meaning underlying the words is that which is understood.

Second, the correct presentation of the characteristics of contemplation. Now, for the first [part]:

This section further clarifies that for those who can have deep faith, their merit becomes even greater; thus, they take what was previously non-existent as if it were already possessed.

That is to say, if there is someone who, upon hearing me speak of lifespan, does not merely give rise to faith for a brief moment, but is further able to maintain deep faith in continuous succession from thought-moment to thought-moment, I know that such a person—even if they have not yet [attained...]—[possesses this merit].

Relying on principle to give rise to contemplation—that is, the virtue accomplished within the mind of profound understanding and clear faith—may already constitute seeing the Buddha, dwelling eternally upon Vulture Peak within the adorned land.
Since this wondrous principle is inherently possessed by the mind, one may take this very faith as the name for contemplation.
Furthermore, it must be understood that when the lifespan is spoken of, although it occurs within the transformed purity (*pariśuddha*), [it is nonetheless eternal].

Even after chanting [the mantra] within the earth and after scattering [the offerings], it remains an impure land; it is not established by means of visualization, and thus this pure appearance can certainly not arise.
△ Second, the actual demonstration of the visualization.
If there is one who can contemplate in this manner, it should be known that this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding.
These two characters, "in this manner" (rúshì), serve to reiterate the preceding text, precisely manifesting the characteristics of contemplation.

This means that if there is a person who is already able to maintain profound faith in every thought-moment and further is able to perform contemplation according to the teachings until the visualization is perfected, as described above.
Its marks appear vividly before the eyes and manifest brilliantly within the mind. One should know that this constitutes the successful accomplishment of profound faith through contemplation;

thus, one enters the stage of the Bodhisattva’s ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). In the preceding "momentary" section, clarity was shown regarding faith and aspiration; now, within "profound faith," clarity is shown regarding contemplation.

The merits after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa consist of two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. The first [prose section] has five parts: first, generating a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); second, illustrating by contrast the merit of recitation and retention;
