thus, the virtue of the Four Reliances is all the more unfathomable. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response has two parts:
first, the prose section; second, the verse section. The first [the prose] has three parts: first, the direct answer; second, the supplementary instruction; third...
The structural outline (*jiékuàng*). The first two [sections]: first, citing the fiftieth person; second, using this to inversely illustrate the first person. The first of these two has two parts:
first, the transmission of the teaching reaching the fiftieth person; second, the comparative evaluation of the least capable among them. Now, the first [part].

At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "In this manner, passing from one to another until the fiftieth person, let us set aside for a moment and not even mention the merit possessed by the very first person who was personally present at the assembly and rejoiced."

If one merely takes up the merit successively through sympathetic joy until it reaches the fiftieth person, and then turns back to weigh and compare that which has been obtained, one will find that even the most minute and meager goodness is already unfathomable;
how much more so when it concerns another? Part Two: Comparing the Merit of the Last Inferior Person.
This has two sections: first, citing the person and admonishing them to listen; second, showing the great donor. Now, the first section.
Ajita, regarding this fiftieth [case] (up to): I shall now explain it; you should listen well.

Fearing that one might view the merit of a single moment of sympathetic joy as something to be neglected, or be astonished that the achievement of transcending the mundane and ascending to the sacred is so great, and further fearing that upon hearing this single comparison, one might find it even more superior than that and thus fail to be struck with wonder or doubt—I have therefore first issued this admonition.
△ Second, showing the great donor, in three parts: first, the extensive giving of wealth and Dharma; second, concluding by questioning the greatness of his merit;
third, the actual response regarding its vastness. Now, the first:
"If [four hundred myriads of koṭis of] asaṃkhyeya worlds... all attained mastery and were endowed with the eight liberations."
Taking four million world-systems as the realm of those to be transformed, and the twelve categories of sentient beings as the fields for seeking merit:
those born from eggs include fish, birds, turtles, and snakes; those born from wombs include humans, livestock, dragons, and immortals; and those born from moisture include...
Those that contain crawling insects; those born by transformation, which shed their skins and fly; those with form, who are brilliant and perceptive regarding omens and calamities;

those without form, who dissipate into emptiness and sink away; those with thought, such as gods, ghosts, and spirits; those without thought, whose spirit and essence transform into earth, wood, metal, and stone;
those who are neither with nor without thought, such as the *pulu* (a type of wasp); and those who are neither without nor with thought, such as the earth-owl (*tuchao*).
[And so forth. There was a person who sought merit; this person was thus a great donor. "Seeking merit" refers to the aspiration of the donor.

According to the [text], first, through the practice of giving material wealth, one fulfills that aspiration. It states that every person obtains the seven treasures filling Jambudvīpa, which clarifies the greatness of the gift.
Furthermore, it states they remain full for eighty years, which clarifies the longevity of the gift. This is already a difficult feat to achieve.
...and act accordingly. Furthermore, one should practice the gift of Dharma. First, one reflects: "I have indeed already provided for their livelihood;

how can I guarantee their welfare beyond this life? If I do not urgently rescue and support them with the Buddha-Dharma, then even if I possess material wealth to give, I shall not be called a 'Great Donor.
Therefore, I shall instruct, benefit, and gladden them, so that at this very moment, they may all..."
They attain the realization of supramundane fruits. △ Second, concluding by questioning the greatness of the merit:
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor not indeed vast?"
△ Third, the three realities correspond to a vast multitude.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy. The ancients have said:
First, one bestows worldly happiness and extracts the suffering of the fruits [of existence]; later, one bestows the bliss of nirvana and extracts the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This—
This is a brief enumeration of Brahma-merit for the sake of comparison. To speak more extensively:
the merit of all people filling Jambudvīpa does not equal that of a single person in Aparagoyānī; the merit of all people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal that of a single person in Pūrvavideha;
the merit of all people filling the three continents does not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru. Filling the four continents... [text continues]
An ordinary person does not equal the merit of a single Cāturmahārājika deva; the four heavenly kings do not equal the merit of a single Śakra;
and so on, up to the sixth heaven, which does not equal the merit of a single Brahmā. From this point onward, one should compare them by doubling the merit at each successive level.
Now, let us further model and illustrate this principle: the merit of all beings within a world-system does not equal the merit of a single sage of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Or, the merit of all sages of the Small Vehicle filling a trichiliocosm does not equal the merit of a single person at the first stage of faith in the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna).
Furthermore, that merit does not equal the merit of one who rejoices in a single verse within the Ultimate Teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) which refutes duality. This is because...
Because the mundane does not equal the supramundane; furthermore, because all provisional and shallow dharma-gates flow forth from the single reality.
△ Second, the inverse analogy regarding the first person.
Ajita, even the merit of the fiftieth person in this sequence cannot be compared to that of an *asaṃkhyeya* [of people].
Among these five types of persons, the merit obtained by the first person who rejoices— even though their initial thought has not yet benefited others—
is so vast that the Tathāgata skillfully employs metaphors to explain it, so that you may know it far surpasses the former.

Great Generosity. At the conclusion of the calculation, in order to inspire deep reverence in others, the text now provides a formal comparison to demonstrate the merit of those who hear [this teaching] from the Dharma assembly and rejoice in it;
its inconceivability is thus revealed. The intent behind the title of this chapter lies precisely here.
△ Second, showing the three aspects concurrently: first, going to listen; second, sharing a seat; third, exhorting others. Now, the first.

Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, [receives] precious jeweled carriages and celestial palaces as vehicles—this refers to the retribution received immediately upon changing bodies.
As for the "wondrous elephant," it is a statement regarding the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of having been able to hear [the teaching].
△ Second, the sharing of seats.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, at a place where the Dharma is being taught—or even at a place where a Wheel-Turning Sage King sits—invites them to sit by sharing their seat, first causing that person’s body to be at ease and subsequently their mind to be at ease, they may then listen with sincerity and will not depart from the Dharma assembly;
thus, they obtain two benefits. Therefore, among the fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*), they enjoy both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The retribution for this flow. △ Third, exhorting others.
"Ajita, if there should be another person... (up to) seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and faithfully accepting his instruction.
First, he goes himself; next, he shares his seat to benefit others. However, those whom he benefits are, in fact, [benefiting] themselves.
Come! Now, although that person originally had no intention [to hear], the desire to seek out what they hear is entirely due to my exhortation.
Thus, the benefit of the dhāraṇī rests entirely upon me; therefore, when they change bodies, they will be born in the same place as the sages who possess dhāraṇīs.
Because of exhorting others through Prajñā, one receives the retribution of sharp faculties and wisdom. Furthermore, this exhortation...
Sound necessarily issues from the mouth; therefore, all implements used by the mouth attain purity. To summarize, the three karmas and six sense faculties are not external to this single body;
thus, it is shown collectively that "the human marks are complete," which is a preliminary sign of attaining the purity of the six sense faculties.
However, these are all spoken of in terms of the retribution of birth (*upapatti-vipāka*); as for the "Dharma Master" chapter, it refers instead to the present life.
The response. △ Third, the conclusion of the illustration.
"Ajita, you should observe this... for the sake of others, analyze it, and practice according to what has been taught.
△ Second, the verses consist of five parts: first, rejoicing; second, exhorting to listen; third, going there; fourth, requesting them to sit; fifth, the conclusion.
Furthermore, at the very beginning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If a person [hears this] during the Dharma assembly... how much more so for those who hear it and rejoice at the very beginning of the Dharma assembly?"
The world is like the rising and ceasing of water bubbles, having no fixed origin; how much more so for those who dwell within it? As the Āgama Sūtras state:
when the world was first formed, heavy rains poured down from above, and after the water bubbles had accumulated for a long time, they coalesced to form the world.
Then the water bubbles are the world itself. △ Second, the exhortation to listen:
"If there is one person who exhorts [others]... (up to) ...the fragrance of the *utpala* flower shall constantly issue from their mouth."
△ 3. Going to visit:
If one goes to visit a monastic dwelling (until) by means of precious jeweled carriages or riding in celestial palaces.
△ 4. Requesting them to sit.

If one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras at a place where the Dharma is being preached, by this causal condition of merit, one will obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King.
△ Fifth, the concluding illustration:
How much more so for one who listens with a single mind, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to the teaching; the merit of such a person is beyond measure.

The preceding four sections all addressed those of the most shallow and inferior capacity regarding the planting of profound merit. It is only in this section that the true intent is finally revealed.
II. The Merits of the Dharma Master. This has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the citation of scriptural evidence. Now, the first part.
Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma Master.

At the end of the "Chapter on Differentiation," it clarifies that five kinds of people will obtain benefit by relying on this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within the context of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
There are two distinct types of merit. First, it directly reveals the greatness of the merit of one who rejoices;
second, it concurrently clarifies the specific karmic maturation (*vipāka*) resulting therefrom, which serves as a preliminary sign for entering into faith.

Although the previous section performed a comparative calculation, it did not yet manifest how the power of one who upholds this sutra is exceedingly swift and rapid, such that it can transform their present retribution so that the six sense faculties do not [suffer].
One must relinquish the body born of one's parents to immediately attain purity and enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, as for this practitioner, if compared to those who merely rejoice in the merit, the latter belong to a state of distracted mind and thus obtain rebirth in the future; this [practitioner], however, being single-mindedly sincere, obtains the present retribution (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya-vipāka*).
It should be known that if even the practitioner obtains the present retribution, how much more so the one who explains it, and how much more so the one who both explains and practices correctly.
This chapter follows because those who practice the six perfections [require this teaching]. Question: Previously, it was explained that five types of people obtain benefit by relying on the sūtras;

why now are only the latter four specifically designated as "Dharma-teachers" (dharma-bhāṇaka)? Answer: This is specifically because the one who rejoices (anumodaka) does not initially take the Dharma as their own teacher, nor do they themselves act as a teacher of the Dharma to others.
Thus, although the former four and nine [types] possess the merit of transmitting the teaching, [they are not so designated].
These were also merely coincidental. As for the four individuals who followed, it was not so; therefore, these four categories may be called "Dharma Masters.
[The text] has two parts: first, citing the faculties to provide a general heading; second, explaining them individually in sequence. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent (up to the point where it says) "adorn the six sense faculties and cause them all to be pure.
The address to Constantly Diligent reveals the person who upholds this sutra: if one wishes to attain anything, one must first possess a single-minded, constant resolve as the foundation.
One must eliminate external conditions and regard this alone as the sole reality. Even if one encounters adverse circumstances, one must thoroughly understand the nature of phenomena.
It is like an illusion; it cannot be disturbed. To advance alone without retreating—this is what one may approximate.

Therefore, he called out "Ever-Exerting" (Chang Jingjin) to inform him, so that those who receive and uphold [the teaching] would have a standard to follow. As for the six sense faculties being revealed through numerical enumeration, as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The flow and transformation undergo three cycles: ten, hundred, and thousand. Now, what is "one"? It is precisely the One Mind.

Regarding "flowing transformation": it means that by virtue of this single thought-moment following conditions, the six sense organs are formed and thus fall within the categories of the three times and the four directions.
Therefore, the number may be increased to twelve hundred or eight hundred based on these categories.

If discussed in terms of vertical succession, one takes the three times as primary and then correlates them with the four directions; for within each of the three times, there are [the four directions].
The four directions; thus, they form twelve. If one discusses them horizontally, one takes the four directions as the primary basis;
since within each of these four directions there are likewise three periods of time, their number also amounts to exactly twelve. Therefore, that sutra says:
"Three times four and four times three, revolving to twelve. This is how a single thought-moment is first layered to become twelve. Second...

Furthermore, these are each multiplied by four. Taking the three periods of time as the primary unit, if one takes the three periods of the eastern direction and multiplies them by ten, there are thirty;
the same applies to the other directions, resulting in one hundred and twenty.
In the third stage, these one hundred and twenty are again each multiplied by ten, thereby attaining the number of one thousand and two. This section is named... [the name follows].
Although the numerical counts are the same as those in that sutra, one must know that the meanings revealed are entirely different.

This is because, in that [sutra], the function inherent within the defiled state is termed "merit" (*guṇa*). However, from the perspective of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prakḷpta*), each is fully complete with one thousand two hundred [functions].
It is only because these functions are triggered in response to objects that some are present and others are lacking; thus, the stated numbers vary in their abundance or scarcity. Now...

Because the merit of upholding this sutra surpasses even that of the most powerful and victorious, one is able to manifest a transformation of the six sense organs born of one's parents, thereby attaining a small portion of their pure functioning.
This is designated as "merit" (guṇa), which belongs to the category of what is produced through cultivation.
This is the first point of difference. Furthermore, although they are equal in number and belong to the defiled state, when it comes to their manifesting function, then all...

The mutual functioning of the faculties is yet another point of distinction. II. The detailed explanation of each according to their order, in six parts: first, the eye faculty; second, the ear faculty; third, the nose faculty; fourth, the tongue faculty; fifth, the body faculty; sixth, the mind faculty. Now, the first: The mutual functioning of the faculties is yet another point of distinction. II. The detailed explanation of each according to their order, in six parts:
first, the eye faculty; second, the ear faculty; third, the nose faculty; fourth, the tongue faculty; fifth, the body faculty; sixth, the mind faculty. Now, the first:
These sons and daughters of good family (up to) wishing to restate this meaning spoke these verses:
"If, in the midst of a great assembly (up to) although they have not yet attained the power of the divine eye, the power of the fleshly eye is thus."
*Avīci* means "without interval" (*anantara*) and is also called "without rescue" (*anupāya*). *Meru* means "light" (*prabhā*), referring to the seven golden mountains.
Regarding the six sense organs born of one's parents, they are comprised within the nine kinds of impurity; yet, they are described as "pure" for two reasons:

first, based on the statements of the present teaching, because worldly phenomena are all eternal; second, because the power of upholding this sutra is so superior that it does not depend upon cultivation or realization.

Only upon attaining the Dharma-nature Body (*dharmatā-kāya*) do the five eyes truly exist. Thus, within the very body currently manifesting, one immediately transforms the retribution of the present life;
therefore, one achieves the simultaneous state of being both defiled and pure. Within a single eye, the functions of all five eyes are fully present.

For instance, seeing the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm would properly be called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*); yet, when compared to what is actually seen, this vision far surpasses that. It is, for example, like the retributive attainment of the Brahma King.
The divine eye perceives only its own realm; beyond the great trichiliocosm, it is obstructed by the wind-circle and thus cannot see.
If one is in another realm, one likewise cannot see, because that realm is not under one's governance and is not of the same category.
However, the divine eyes possessed by those of the Three Vehicles can all perceive whatever they are situated within, regardless of whether it is the wind-circle of their own or another’s realm.
Neither can obstruct [the vision]. It is simply because the power of the Path varies in depth that what is seen also varies in proximity or distance.
Furthermore, seeing the causes and conditions of karma is the Dharma-eye; its faculty is exceedingly pure. Seeing through emptiness with wisdom is the Wisdom-eye.
Reaching the point where, within a single thought-moment, one suddenly realizes the nature and characteristics of form and mind—this is a small portion of the function of the Buddha-eye.
If one discusses how a single faculty possesses the functions of all five faculties, it is a partial manifestation of the qualities of the Eightfold Sovereign Self.
△ Second, the ear-faculty.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son of good family (up to) wishes to restate this meaning, he speaks these verses:
"With the ears born of one's parents... (up to) the merit of merely using those natural ears is already such as this."
The faculty of hearing also possesses the functions of five kinds of ears. Hearing the sounds of the six realms of existence is the ear of flesh and the ear of heaven.

Hearing the [teachings of] the two vehicles is the ear of wisdom. Hearing [the teachings of] the bodhisattvas is the ear of dharma. Hearing [the teachings of] the Buddhas is the Buddha-ear. These are heard simultaneously and interchangeably.
It is like the Buddha’s rounded ears. To be unimpaired is to be non-erroneous.

Regarding the passage "the various Brahmās below" and so forth, I privately maintain that the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses already reside in the second dhyāna; how much more so for the higher Brahmās?

What is now referred to as "hearing" likely refers to the mental sounds associated with entering and emerging from dhyāna, or perhaps it refers to the sound produced by the circular halo (*prabhā-maṇḍala*). This is because within the first dhyāna, there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Therefore, from the second dhyāna upward, because the basis for discrimination does not arise. △ Third, the nose faculty.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family (up to) wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
This person’s nose is purified (up to the point where it is said that) the one who upholds this sutra first attains these characteristics of the nose.

"Fragrance" (*gandha*) and "stench" (*durgandha*) are general terms for olfactory objects. In the world, however, that which is pleasing to the senses is called "fragrant," while that which is unpleasing is called "stench.
In this sutra, both are taken in their comprehensive sense, as when one hears [the scent] of wild oxen or water buffalo.
These are the [five] equalities. To smell the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm with the fleshly nose is the celestial nose.
To be neither defiled nor attached is the wisdom nose. To discern without error is the Dharma nose. To smell simultaneously and reciprocally is the Buddha nose.

To manifest these reciprocal functions so as to know the location of things is the function of the eye. To hear, read scriptures, and preach the Dharma is the function of the ear. To know flowers and fruits...

The tongue is the faculty for knowing whether one is emerging from or entering meditative absorption; this is the function of the body. It is the function of the mind to know a heart of desire, delusion, or anger.

Furthermore, discerning whether a pregnancy will reach fulfillment or not constitutes the clarity of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), while the subsequent [discernment] constitutes the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Knowing the thoughts of men and women further constitutes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). To know that which is in accordance with the Dharma...
Through such practice, one draws near to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

As for those who have not yet attained the state of being "born with the nose of the untainted dharma" (*anāsravadharma*), this reveals that although they have not yet ascended to the stage of an *ārya*, by virtue of the superior power of upholding this sutra, they possess wondrous efficacy; thus one perceives its inconceivable nature.
*Sumana* means "well-restraining the mind. Its color is yellowish-white and it is exceedingly fragrant. The tree reaches a height of three or four *zhang*. Below—
It hangs down like a canopy. The *sumanā* flower grows from within it. *Jāti* is translated as "money-tree flower" (*jinqiánhuā*).
*Mallikā* is translated as "garland flower," because it is suitable for making garlands. *Pāṭala* is translated as "reborn flower. *Tamālapatra* is translated as "naturally stainless.
*Tagara* is translated as "root fragrance"; it is the *mùxiāng* tree. *Pārijātaka* is translated as "round."
The Tree-born [deities] are born within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. They are one hundred *yojana* in height, with roots extending five *yojana* into the earth.
Their fragrance wafts against the wind for fifty *yojana* and with the wind for one hundred *yojana*. *Kovidāra* means "Great Play";
it refers to the fragrance of the trees on the ground. △ Fourth, the tongue faculty.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son of good family (up to) wishes to restate this meaning, he speaks in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of this person is pure... [he] constantly recollects and guards it; at times he manifests his body."
Regarding the statement that "the tongue-faculty also possesses twelve hundred merits when apprehending objects within the midst of contact":
the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that when the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its expressions have specific dimensions while its principles are inexhaustible;

therefore, it does not stop at eight hundred. This is because a single verse of profound, pure, and wondrous dharma constitutes one of the four analytical eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*), and thus refers to this Dharma-preacher.

To be able to employ the names and meanings of all phenomena in accordance with their principles, using diverse regional dialects and foreign languages so that each may attain understanding and give rise to joy—this is the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Thus, the functions of the five tongues are fully contained within a single utterance. △ Five: The Body Faculty (*kāya-indriya*).
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family (up to) wishes to restate this meaning, he speaks in verse:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra... through the pure, eternal essence, all things appear therein."
The old commentary states: "All that exists in the world manifests within the body; this is the function of the physical body.

I venture to suggest, however, that it is only the human body that is termed a 'physical body. When discussing the function of such a body, it is capable only of apprehending objects through sensory contact.

It is not the case that the body of a sage’s virtuous marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot naturally illuminate objects and manifest reflections. Even for those possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), although...
Furthermore, it is capable of manifesting illumination; yet this is a function of karma. How could there be such manifesting function in the physical body of an ordinary person?
As for the other four bodies, they are all nothing more than designating that which is manifested as the "capable manifester.

Now, to equate the body of segmented birth with the untainted [body] precisely demonstrates the peerless efficacy of the Sūtra’s merit. Please reflect upon this. △ Sixth: The Mental Faculty (manas-indriya).
Furthermore, Nityodyukta, if a son of good family (up to) wishes to restate this meaning, he speaks in verse:
"This person’s mind is pure... [he] preaches the Dharma through discernment because he upholds the Lotus Sūtra."
"Listen for a moment. This refers to the fact that within a single dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are immeasurable gates;

though such teachings have been expounded for immeasurable thousands of kalpas, the meaning of these two lines—by the power of upholding the sutra—is able to expand from the concise to the vast. "If one speaks below... [refers to the following].
Question: Because the Buddha, due to Śāriputra, subdued the non-Buddhist practitioners who denied the existence of future lives, he permitted bhikṣus to divide a single day into three periods:
to study Buddhist scriptures during the first and second periods, and to study non-Buddhist texts during the final period.
However, he did not permit them to rely upon those [non-Buddhist] views; thus, there was a library within the Jetavana Monastery. This was possible only because of their learning.

[The questioner asks: "Having fully realized [this], why should those who now uphold this sutra not study it so that they may understand external matters and ensure that what they say does not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*)?
[The answer is: "Because the very characters one upholds are themselves the true nature. The *prajñā* of the true nature is the Great Dharani-gate.
There is no mundane or supramundane phenomenon that does not flow forth from this. Therefore, it enables both horizontal and vertical exposition."

It is said that one who attains such a state as the noble ones of the fifth bhūmi, for whom the two truths are harmoniously integrated, and who dwells securely in this rare stage, accords perfectly with the Buddha’s sūtras.
As previously stated, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this sūtra cannot be heard, let alone seen, upheld, or recited;
this precisely reveals the rarity of this Dharma. Therefore, one is able to uphold it.
As for the sūtra: although one has not yet attained the untainted faculty of mind (anāsrava-manas-indriya), one immediately attains the function of a sage.
This is simply because, by upholding this rare dharma, one abides in a rare stage. △ Second, the citation of proof.
Regarding the arrival of the twentieth chapter, "The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging":

the preceding text repeatedly speaks of the retribution for propagating the sutra. For instance, it says that upon changing one's body, one will be born together with bodhisattvas who possess *dhāraṇī*;
this refers to the retribution of birth (*janma-vipāka*). Furthermore, it says that in every life where one is born, one shall behold...

Hearing the Dharma from the Buddha refers to retribution in a future life; both of these matters pertain to the future, and their realization depends on whether one has faith or not, so there is no need to cite scriptural proof for them.
As for the retribution of the purification of the six sense faculties described in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," this is discussed entirely in terms of the present life.
Yet, how is it that those who obtain such visible retribution in the present are so exceedingly rare? For this reason, it is difficult to believe. This is so.
Therefore, the World-Honored One cited his own experience on the causal ground as a witness to the present retribution he had attained;
seeing this rarity, he inspired a heart of reverence and longing for the circulation [of the teaching]. This is why this chapter follows.

As for the title "Not Disparaging," it refers to how, while the World-Honored One was still on the causal ground and before he had fully heard the *Lotus Sūtra*, he internally realized the Buddha-nature within his own mind.

The principle of equality. One perceives externally that all are objects of equality who must not be disparaged; therefore, one practices the conduct of "not disparaging" (adhimāna) through both body and speech.
For this reason, one bows upon meeting anyone and immediately bestows predictions of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) upon them.
This is because one has not yet heard the admonition not to preach this sutra among those without wisdom, nor has one yet attained the power to protect and sustain it.

This is an expedient means (*upāya*). Thus, he causes those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) to be given a name based on the practices they have cultivated, and is derisively called "Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta*).
The text has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse. The first part [of the prose] has three sections:
first, following the preceding to introduce the topic; second, citing antiquity as proof; third, concluding with the benefits and exhorting one to uphold [the teaching]. Now, the first section:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta... [up to] "...the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are purified.

This refers back to what was previously stated in the "Chapter on Honoring the Dharma Master," where it was said that the transgression of disparaging a person who upholds this sutra with even a single evil word is far more grave than the sin of reviling a Buddha for an entire kalpa.
Having just explained the merits of honoring the Dharma master, according to this principle:
Understood. This chapter is specifically intended to cite evidence regarding the retribution of the present life; it is not a general discussion of the three types of retribution.

As for the "marks of a great man" (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), these refer to the locations where the extraordinary features of a great man’s meritorious retribution are brilliantly manifest;

For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he speaks of the eighty-four thousand exquisite primary and secondary marks—the Buddha’s true marks of excellence.

When I first attained the Way at the site of the tranquil and extinguished *bodhimaṇḍa*, for the sake of the great bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Bhadramukha, I already extensively analyzed this in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.

The white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) does not equal the merit possessed by the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).

"Meeting many Buddhas" is the cause for attaining the two types of adornment (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). "All in a single phrase" reveals the profundity of wisdom (*prajñā*);
