That they took their leave of the Buddha and requested to see Mañjuśrī reflects the profound admiration of those who had previously followed him.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s admonition not to treat them lightly was also conveyed through the medium of Gadgadasvara to further exhort those who had followed him. Why is this? Gadgadasvara is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body;

although he knows that the myriad lands are perfectly interfused and that his manifestations and concealments are exercised with sovereign ease, he nevertheless feared that [others might]—though knowing this—[still harbor doubts].
Having realized that dependent origination is like an illusion and that dharmas lack any fixed nature,

how could one who beholds the most sublime and majestic primary and secondary environments [of a Buddha] suddenly perceive them as an extremely inferior buddha-field fail to give rise to non-deluded non-dual understanding?

For what reason would one tread upon this realm of equality— where purity and defilement are identical, and the small and the great are unimpeded— and listen to the Dharma of the Great Wisdom of Equality?
"Entrusting" means to issue a premonition to those being led. "Miaoyin" (Wondrous Sound) and below indicate the reception of the intent.
My journey to that land is entirely due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s path-power, the employment of his supernatural powers, and the adornment of his merit and wisdom;

how could I dare again give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority? "Thereupon" and below demonstrate the protocol for the departure and arrival, first causing those of this land to see [the signs].
Śrīṣeṇa gave rise to doubt; he greatly opened his heart to yearn for [the Dharma], taking this as the foundation for receiving benefit.
"Jambūnada gold" refers to the Jambū tree, which grows on the banks of a river in the region called Jambudvīpa (lit., "under the Jambū tree").
It is so named because the juice of that tree enters the river and dyes the stones, forming gold that is reddish-yellow with a purple luster, surpassing that found among humans.
Gold is a thousand or ten thousand times superior [to other metals]. *Jintuogua* (甄叔迦) refers to a red-colored gem. In the Western Regions there is the *jintuogua* tree;
its flowers are red and shaped like a palm, and the color of the gem resembles it, hence the name. Cien (Yijing) says its form is like a jade scepter (*yanguī*) and resembles red lapis lazuli.
△ Second, responding to the command and setting out, in four parts: first, resolving doubts regarding manifested signs; second...
1. Mañjuśrī seeks an audience; 2. Prabhūtaratna appears for him; 3. He is formally invited to come; 4. His actual arrival. Now, the first [section]:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī (up to) also desired to make offerings and listen to the Lotus Sutra.
△ 2. Mañjuśrī’s Request for an Audience.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “[... up to ... that bodhisattva comes so that I may behold him.

Even a Great Being who has attained Equal Enlightenment still desires to seek an audience; how much more so would others not feel great longing and veneration? This, too, is [the section on] Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī was exceptionally skilled in propagating the sutra; his purpose in seeking an audience was the same as that of the former [Śāriputra], yet each benefited their own respective assembly.
△ Third, the manifestation by Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—[omitted]—stated that Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, wished to see your body.
By manifesting these signs, the World-Honored One of the Śākyas attributes the credit for this to Prabhūtaratna; thus, one can perceive not only his humility, which is overflowing with grace.
This further deepens one’s aspiration and delight for the Dharma assembly. △ Fourth, the actual departure:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (until) came to this Sahā world, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
A Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body can yet fill the entire Dharma-realm with a single body, leaving no trace whatsoever of coming or going.

That he now departs from that place and arrives here, appearing to exist and then vanish, is precisely because he manifests the coming and going of physical action (*kāyakarman*) and dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) for those who are to be saved by such means;
in the very act of manifesting this deportment, he is said to be propagating the Sūtra. Furthermore, regarding the various lands through which he passes:
Since all these auspicious signs have now appeared, it is certain that when one encounters a Bodhisattva, the moment will not have been spent in vain.

An ancient source cites India as having a blue lotus whose petals are long and broad, with distinct blue and white colors resembling eyes; this corresponds to the previous description of "eyes like [those of] Nārāyaṇa.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, this is translated as "Vajra" (Diamond), while in the Jin language it is called "Gongsuo" (Chain-link), or alternatively, "Firm."
Firmly. Some say he was a *ṛṣabha* (powerful man). △ Third, making offerings and inquiring after his well-being:
Having arrived, [he ascends] the seven-jeweled platform... [inquiring] whether he is at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure and dwell for a long time.

With a colossal body forty thousand *yojanas* in height, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara prostrated himself before the subtle form of the Buddha, who was only sixteen feet tall, yet it is said that he did so with his head and face touching the ground;
furthermore, when he presented his jeweled necklaces, there was no appearance of crowding at all.

This precisely sweeps away the traces of "small" and "large," manifesting the true virtue of the Dharma’s lack of fixed nature. As Dongpo said: "The sixteen-foot golden body is not considered large. Only...
How could even a thousand Buddhas be considered small? They too are able to manifest this impartial vision.
Because the Tathāgata manifests in the human realm and displays the same human laws, there are the nine afflictions and ten conditions;

yet through skillful means, he causes all sentient beings to know that the causes of good and evil karma will inevitably result in the retributions of suffering or joy. Thus, when these and those encounter one another—

All such rites of propriety ought to be conducted in this manner. As for the Tathāgata, he has already transcended all obstacles and perfected immeasurable, supreme merits; how could there be any reality of such karmic retribution?
Yet, one who has not yet integrated the hidden and the manifest into a single unity would likewise be unable to pose such a question. △ Fourth, seeking to see Prabhūtaratna.
“World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; for this reason, I have come here.

Although Śākyamuni Buddha had returned to Vulture Peak, Prabhūtaratna still remained in the void. Without receiving the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), how could one possibly behold such a lofty and distant form?
It was for this purpose that he sought [to see him]. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha acted as the mediator. Then, Prabhūtaratna...
Respectfully complying with the request, he immediately offered a virtuous response from within the stupa, saying, "You may indeed see me.

Regarding this, the ancients said: "The mountain streams are distinct, yet the clouds and moon are the same"; thus, it was naturally understood that one could see him. However, some asked: "Why did he close the door? The answer is:
"If you can calculate it, then you have already seen him. Now, based on the sutras, I shall directly demonstrate the inconceivable power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

[Chen] Zhe said: "However, those who are able to maintain [this practice], regardless of whether they are before or upon the stages (*bhūmi*), will all attain the pure and harmonious integration of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) will likewise transcend accordingly, because they share a single dependent origination (*ekapratyaya-samutpāda*).

Therefore, within a single faculty, the functions of all six faculties are fully present. Is it not the case that the eye alone [possesses these]? Is it not the case that the object of sound (*śabda-dhātu*) alone [possesses these], rather than the object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*)? It is precisely so.
One need not seek understanding by looking at the Śrāvakas within the realm of form; reflect upon this. △ Five: Former Cultivation of Merit, in three parts:
first, citing the past; second, correlating [the present with] it; third, pointing to the extensive version. Now, the first.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (up to) now possesses such supernormal powers in the land of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom.
First, he inquires about his merit; second, he inquires about his supernormal powers. In the past, he offered music and a precious bowl; now, he receives this superior reward of flowers.

Therefore, celestial music resounds spontaneously and ritual vessels follow constantly; although these are results of the outflowing retribution (*niṣyanda-phala*), they are nonetheless brought about by the power of unconditioned wondrous virtue.
△ Second, the conclusion and correlation.
"What do you think, Flower Virtue? ... It is this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara.
△ Third, pointing out his extensive [career]:
"Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara [has served] hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas."
The above summarizes the roots of virtue planted to answer the first question. △ Sixth, dwelling manifestly in samādhi has two parts:
first, citing the function of samādhi; second, explaining the name of samādhi. Now, the first part.
"Śāriputra, you have merely seen the power of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s wisdom; such are its manifestations.
From here below, the function of his samādhi is clarified, which serves as the answer regarding his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). This consists of two sections.

The first clarifies how, within this Sahā world, he manifests the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings to propagate the sutra. He speaks only of "rescuing and relieving" because they are currently immersed in the depths of saṃsāra.

They undergo suffering; they have no leisure even for that, so how could they possibly understand the Buddha’s wisdom? The following clarifies that while his inner virtues are full, his external functions are sufficient;
thus, regarding his divine wisdom, there is no impairment whatsoever. By means of forms that accord with various types and voices that accord with various types, [he acts].
According to their respective inclinations, he receives them with Dharma-gates suited to each type; thus it is said that "each obtains what they know.

Following the section on the ten directions below, this explains the propagation of the sutra by manifesting the bodies of the four holy ones; however, the initial passage clarifies the manifestation of the six classes of ordinary beings within the Sahā world.
Now, throughout the ten directions, the four sages manifest clearly; all are masters of literary artistry, appearing to one another within their respective realms without exception.
To summarize: while the bodies they manifest are indeed manifold, the teaching they propagate to spread it far and wide is solely the Lotus Sūtra.
Furthermore, one must know that they have never failed to first take a single dharma as the seed.
Having explained them in various ways, he then gathers these various [teachings] back into one. △ Second, explaining the name of the samādhi:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "...[omitted]... able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings."
The ancient commentaries state that samādhi and dhāraṇī are identical in essence but differ in function.

If one follows the *Awakening of Faith*, it says that in the eighth stage one attains mastery over the three kinds of worlds regarding the nature of form; according to one's mind, there is no obstruction.
In the ninth stage, one skillfully knows the ten kinds of dense forests of sentient beings and attains forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence; this refers to both form and mind.
One distinguishes between the superiority and inferiority of the eighth and ninth stages.

Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that in the eighth stage one can spontaneously manifest various marks such as the golden body (*suvarṇakāya*) and the buddha-fields, while in the ninth stage one attains the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). Thus, when analyzed for their depth and shallowness, there is indeed a difference.
Moreover, it must be understood that although the samādhi in which Gadgadasvara dwells is also called "Manifesting All Physical Bodies," it differs from [the manifestation of the eighth stage].

Those who receive benefit should necessarily experience it differently. Since Miaoyin was one who had attained perfect enlightenment, having already been able to enter deeply into the boundless depths of all samādhis, how could he be compared to those who first attained [realization] at the beginning of the Dharma assembly?
△ Second, the benefits obtained by the great assembly.

When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, [up to the point where it says] they also attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī, those who obtained benefit in both lands had previously seen auspicious signs in the form of flowers and had already developed resolute faith that could not be diverted.

Subsequently, their minds were sealed by the wondrous Dharma; thus, they attained the simultaneous integration of meditative concentration and wisdom. The scriptural text intends to distinguish this concentration...
Because the essence of wisdom is distinct [from the others], the word "and" (及) is added between *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*. △ Third, returning to one's own country, in two parts:
first, restoring the original state as commanded by the Buddha; second, a further summary on universal benefit. Now, the first part.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara (up to) attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies, as for the multitude within the kingdoms through which he passed on his journeys, was there not some incidental benefit during the two occasions of seeing and hearing these auspicious signs?
Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, when our Buddha’s light previously illuminated that land, there must likewise have been incidental benefits; the text [of that occasion] is also...
It is not explicitly stated, yet the underlying intent is certainly present. △ Second, the double conclusion on universal benefit:
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s Coming and Going" was being preached (up to the point where they) attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

When the various devaputras beheld Wondrous Sound manifesting the appearance of coming and going within the wondrous, perfect, and complete body of realization he had attained, and preaching the Dharma of quiescent extinction, those who saw or heard it were led to a vast awakening to all illusory appearances.
Although there is birth, it is not truly born; although there is cessation, it is not truly ceased.
Thus, the principle of the true mark—which is markless and fundamentally unmoving—became clearly manifest in their minds. Therefore, it is said that they "attained."
He attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, within hundreds of thousands of Samādhis of Wondrous Sound, Flower Virtue saw how he could manifest various bodies from a single body and produce various dharmas from a single dharma, preaching the subduing of sentient beings.
He waited until their roots of goodness were matured, then again gathered those various manifestations back into a single principle; the origins of all these were not at variance.
Apart from the Lotus Samādhi, within a single kind of wondrous function, one thereby gathers the provisional back into the real and does not produce dualistic marks,
thus suddenly awakening to the Lotus Samādhi.
△ III. Universal Gate Retention of the Sūtra.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
This follows from the preceding chapter because, although the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara [manifested] through his modes of coming and going and his physical body, [the teaching continues here].
[It is] obscure. Although the propagation of this Sūtra in this land has involved only the mere seven limbs of conduct, how can it compare to Avalokiteśvara?

With the three karmas—body, speech, and mind—which are as vast as clouds and as resonant as thunder, perfectly integrated and inexhaustible, he governs the great void as a single profound gateway of universal response, thereby encompassing all primary retributions.

Thus, from the sages and worthies above down to the insects below, and extending even to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as well as within the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of earth,
water, fire, and wind— wherever there is form or sound that can be relied upon— all are Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) dwelling beyond the cage of bondage.

Therefore, regarding those who are affected [by this influence], one makes no distinction whatsoever between good and evil, the rebellious and the compliant, or those capable of being moved and those incapable.
As for "inspiration," it means harmonizing the myriad transformations within a single principle; none exist outside the universal gate of transformative teaching.
For instance, among the seven perils, those who obtain fearlessness by invoking the name [of the Buddha] do so through the secret empowerment of the Great Being’s wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).

Among the two types of seekers, those who fulfill their aims through prostration do so through the secret empowerment of the Great Being’s wheel of body (*kāyacakara*). Regarding the three poisons and so forth...

Through mindfulness and reverence, one attains detachment. Furthermore, regarding those who possess many names and are preeminent: this is the secret empowerment of the Great Being’s wheel of intention.
Since this method of transformation is more extensive than what preceded it, it follows next. Moreover, within this very context:
Although he has not yet manifested his body to preach the Dharma, he causes hundreds of thousands who suffer from afflictions to simultaneously attain fearlessness;

this specifically refers to the person of the Universal Gate (Pumen) in order to manifest the Dharma of the Universal Gate. There is no need for form or sound, because the person is itself the Dharma.
The following thirty-two manifestations further use the Dharma of the Universal Gate to manifest the person of the Universal Gate; such is the reason for their employment.
And as for form and sound, because the Dharma is identical to the person, the reach of its transformation is even broader than before. Question:

What constitutes the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) Dharma? Answer: Within the provisional and shallow teachings, it is said that names lack the power to grasp objects, and objects lack the reality to correspond to names;
thus, name and reality do not mutually encompass one another. However, in this present sutra, it concerns the contemplation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Illumination and words, though three, are one; to raise one is to manifest all three. How could the sacred title of the Great Being not be Prajñā?
Precisely because it is Prajñā, it is profoundly inclusive and vast, wherein the one and the many are equal, and this and that are without obstruction;
its myriad virtues are brilliantly radiant. Through this, one perceives the profound sphere of practice of the Great Being, which is not attained in a single lifetime.
Regarding that which is bound, the Bodhisattva cannot fathom its ultimate depths;
yet when it comes to the Buddha, his speech encompasses all meanings, being perfectly equal and without distinction—this is the Dharma of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).

One must know that because the Great Being integrates the Dharma of the Universal Gate into the *dharmadhātu*, those with karmic affinity and those without alike attain the spontaneous cessation of suffering. Nevertheless, there is one inherent nature...
The Essential Nature of Avalokiteśvara dwells on the stage of fearlessness and delivers sentient beings of the nine realms.
As for the title of this chapter, "Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara," it is a designation that names both the person and the dharma. Now, first the person will be explained, followed by the dharma.
Regarding the person named Avalokiteśvara, as stated in the "Chapter on Fearlessness" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "First, because I do not observe myself..."

Regarding "Avalokiteśvara": By means of contemplation, he contemplates those who contemplate him, causing suffering sentient beings to receive his contemplation upon their voices and thereby attain liberation;

thus, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions. According to the present text, however, when suffering and distressed sentient beings single-mindedly invoke his name, the Bodhisattva contemplates their voices and they attain liberation;
thus he is named "Avalokitasvara. I venture to say that these two [explanations]—

Although the chanting of the name is the same in the sutras, their underlying emphases differ. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states, "By me receiving [the invocation], I was able to escape suffering," placing primary weight on the capacity to respond;

thus, it is named Avalokiteśvara (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World). In the present text, although it speaks of escaping suffering, it appears to value the single-minded recitation of the name;
yet its true intent actually embraces both aspects—the resonance of the invocation and the response of the Buddha—meeting in a path of mutual interaction.

The meaning is as follows: "Guanshiyin" (Avalokiteśvara) indicates that "Guan" (Contemplation) refers to the Great Being’s capacity for responsive manifestation, while "Shiyin" (World-Sound) refers to the capacity of sentient beings for evocation.
Because the resonance of the response and the evocation manifest together, it is called "Guanshiyin. Next, to explain the term "Fa" (Dharma), it refers to the "Universal Gate" (Pumen).
This is precisely what the Great Being has realized: the essence and function of the *prajñā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Universal" (*pu*) refers to the essence that vertically exhausts the past and future and horizontally pervades all directions; "gate" (*men*) refers to the meaning of unimpeded entry and exit.

By means of these, they metaphorically illustrate how the Great Being’s manifest and hidden empowerments both flow forth from non-active, wondrous function, and how sentient beings’ manifest and hidden responses likewise [arise]. All...
Only by entering into the wondrous function of non-action can one begin to escape suffering;

thus, while the two terms "Universal Gate" constitute a pair of essence and function, they also form a dyad of dharma and metaphor. For sentient beings of the nine realms, there is no way to escape except through this single gate.
There is no other divergent path; it is the realization of the path to liberation, and is therefore called the "Universal Gate" (Pumen). To explain this more briefly:

this Great Being’s contemplation is the wisdom in which quiescence and illumination flow as one, and wherein the provisional and the ultimate are unimpeded. By means of this, he severs delusions and realizes the Truth, thereby achieving self-benefit.

By means of this, he extracts others from suffering and bestows upon them happiness, thereby achieving the benefit of others. Furthermore, through this contemplation, he cuts off falsehood and leaves behind defilement. It encompasses...

Exhaustively reaching the ultimate limit and dissolving all distinctions between love and fear, the subsequent verses each establish the names of the five contemplations according to their respective virtues, thereby demonstrating the vastness of the Bodhisattva’s extensive propagation and guidance for the benefit of others;

thus they are termed "contemplations" (*vipaśyanā*). "Worlds" (*loka*) refers here to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of the Perfectly Awakened One (*jñāna-samyak-saṃbuddha-loka*); these are all the spheres of transformation for the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, "sound" refers both to that which is responded to and to the responsive capacity of the one who invokes it; there are two such types, namely, vocal sound and the sound of the mind.

If a Great Being, through compassion of identical essence, manifests the thirty-two sublime marks and preaches the nineteen honored teachings to bestow happiness upon others, this constitutes a manifest response to the capacity for silent resonance within the sound of the mind. If the Great Being...

Through compassion of identical essence, he universally bestows fearlessness and uproots their suffering; this constitutes the response in darkness to the manifest invocation of those who call his name.
To investigate the wondrous response of the Great Being is like the moon in the sky: wherever there is water, it is reflected, without any distinction between "this" and "that.
Even if sentient beings lack the capacity for invocation, he has never abandoned them. It is precisely like the bright sun adorning the heavens, which does not— [selectively shine].

Though they lack eyes, they abandon the light of illumination; therefore, through diverse sounds and distinct responses, they are able to gradually uproot those of the three vehicles who rely on provisional means, while this [Bodhisattva] is able to gather them all at once.
Thus, it is collectively titled "The Universal Door Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

△ The text has three parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse; third, the conclusion on benefits. The first part has two sections: first, the initial round of question and answer; second, the second...
The Questions and Answers in Sections. Part One: Two Sections. First, the Question; second, the Answer. Now, the first:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to) "by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?"
The text contains two rounds of question and answer. First, the person is questioned; next, the Dharma is questioned. Regarding the first, the questioner named Akṣayamati:

the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that a Bodhisattva on the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), makes vast vows as expansive as the Dharma-realm and achieves them through ten inexhaustible phrases. If these ten phrases were to come to an end, then I—
The vows are thus inexhaustible. Because these ten items are inexhaustible, my great vow is likewise inexhaustible. These ten inexhaustible things are:
the realm of sentient beings, the realm of worlds, the realm of empty space, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the realm of nirvāṇa.
The realm where Buddhas appear; the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; the object of the mind upon which the Buddha-wisdom enters;

the inexhaustible turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom—this Bodhisattva, at the very first stage of his entry into the grounds (*bhūmi*), establishes his name by taking these ten as his object of focus.
Therefore, he is called Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible Intention). He intends to reveal the Dharma of the Universal Gate and thus issues forth [his discourse] with an inexhaustible intention.
"Arising" (qǐ) correctly reveals that the questioner and the subject of the question, together with the Universal Gate Dharma, all converge in the inexhaustible.

△ Second, the answer has three parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, the incidental instruction on bowing and recitation; third, the comparison of excellence with others. The first [of these three] has two parts:
first, the general indication; second, the specific indication. Now, the first [the general indication]:
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to): "At that moment, by observing their voices, all attained liberation.
This was because the Great Being shared the same compassion and longing as sentient beings, and furthermore, because he was both person and dharma;

thus, first employing the person to manifest the dharma, he was able to uproot suffering without relying on physical form, countenance, or verbal discourse, so that ten billion types of capacities attained liberation."
This collectively manifests the multitude who respond through universal resonance. Now, regarding those who achieve response by holding the name:
when a great calamity suddenly falls upon one's head, in that state of frantic terror and seeking rescue, the mind has no leisure to deliberate upon the principles and practices of mindfulness.
At such a time, by simply employing this present single-mindedness to hold the name within the sound, one has already encompassed them all.

The six sense organs encompass all three types of karma; advancing, they serve as the mechanism for creating karmic retribution, while retreating, they become the foundation for liberation from suffering.

By causing this body, which is on the verge of perishing, to transform into the mindfulness of single-mindedly reciting the Name, through the continuous succession of every thought-moment, [one attains liberation].

One is not afflicted by suffering. At the very moment when the present mind is interrupted, it is precisely the time when the self-nature Avalokiteśvara appears amidst the emergency and transforms into a pure breeze.
You have asked: "By what causes and conditions is one named Avalokiteśvara?

Although the causes and conditions are vast and manifold, the name is derived from the principle of responsive resonance. Nevertheless, there are two meanings. First, if we speak in terms of sentient beings:

Thus, the sound of the name being invoked as a manifestation of response serves as the cause (*hetu*). Within the Universal Door (*samantamukha*), the profound resonance of compassionate contemplation (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*) serves as the condition (*pratyaya*).
Through the mutual interaction of these causes and conditions, sentient beings are enabled to leave suffering behind; therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara.

Second, if we speak in terms of the Bodhisattva himself, the method of Universal Door contemplation serves as the means of salvation, while the world of sentient beings’ sorrowful longing serves as the occasion.
Sound serves as the condition; it is also the harmony of causes and conditions that grants relief from suffering, hence the name Avalokiteśvara.
The reason such a resonance occurs is that the true and the delusive interpenetrate and pervade one another.
This means that outside of the true there is no delusion; therefore, regarding the sentient beings within the mind of Avalokiteśvara, whenever they have a request, his response should be known.

Echo. Furthermore, by penetrating the false to reach the true source, at the very moment of compassionate yearning, the Avalokiteśvara within the hearts of sentient beings spontaneously manifests to extract their suffering.
This briefly demonstrates the causes and conditions for the name "Avalokiteśvara" amidst fearlessness.
In the following verses, the World-Honored One explains "Avalokita" based on the Dharma-gate realized by the Bodhisattva himself, stating: "True..."
Regarding the "Contemplation of Purity" and so forth, they are explained in terms of the "Brahma Voice" and the "Ocean Tide Voice.
△ Second, the specific demonstration has two parts: first, clarifying the seven calamities; second, concluding with the supernatural power. Now, the first part:
"If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... (up to) because they call upon his name, they immediately attain liberation.

From here on, the explanation is based solely on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. It means that by the power of the Bodhisattva’s virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), he bestows his grace upon the Dharma-realm;

it occurs spontaneously and naturally, enabling beings to leave suffering behind and reach the state of fearlessness. This is the intended interpretation, and there is no need for further detailed exposition.
Delusion, karma, and so forth are like water, fire, and wind. If one were to establish a separate text for contemplation, then there would be a contemplation existing apart from the teachings;

how then could it be called "contemplation based on the sūtras"? Therefore, it may also be omitted. Now, first, let us take the Bodhisattva as our point of reference, speaking in terms of the Wheel of Speech reaching sentient beings.

As for why he is able to rescue them from the calamity of fire: it is because the faculty of seeing (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) belongs to the element of fire. This is due to the Bodhisattva’s [identity] with...
First, because the power of the revolving of the body’s perception is added, those who call upon his name will not be burned by fire.

Second, because hearing and sensation belong to the element of water, through the Bodhisattva’s application of the power of the revolving of auditory perception based on the contemplation of universal identity (*samatā*), those who call upon his name will not drown.
Third, because the power of extinguishing delusion and severing killing is added, the *rākṣasa* demons [cannot harm them].
As for the ability to liberate all others when a single person calls upon the name:

it is because the Bodhisattva, through the pervasive influence of his great compassion of identical essence throughout the Dharma-realm, has entered deeply into the ocean of the minds of sentient beings; therefore, those who hear the sound of the name being invoked are liberated.
They too were granted liberation. Under the jurisdiction of King Vaiśravaṇa, there are two classes of spirits:
the first are called yakṣas, which are swift-moving spirits; the second are called rākṣasas, which are man-eating spirits. They are found everywhere, even in the dwellings of human beings.
Due to the power of karma, the two do not obstruct one another. Furthermore, beyond the sea, there are others...
There is a land that is inhabited exclusively [by them]. Fourth, because the six sense faculties have been purified and restored, they are augmented by the power of hearing sounds;
therefore, the weapons of war cannot cause them harm, as their six sense faculties are identical to those who hear sounds.

Fifth, because Bodhisattvas augment them with the power of the clarity and brilliance of hearing-perfuming, the demons of ignorance and darkness do not dare to look directly at them, much less [harm them].
Sixth, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s voice—which is perfectly refined to eliminate all sensory dust and delusion—it is added to them;
because they have lost the dust, their physical forms also vanish. How could shackles and fetters not be cast off?

Seventh, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s cessation of sound—which is perfectly heard and universally generates the force of compassion—it is added to them; thus, he is able to cause the merchants to walk with steady steps through the midst of enemies and bandits.
The perilous path. △ Second, the conclusion on the supernormal powers:
"The majestic power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Immeasurable Meaning, is as lofty and sublime as this.
These four characters, "lofty and sublime as this," point to the Bodhisattva, who from time immemorial has filled [the world] with great supernormal powers.
It fills the dharma-realm and universally uproots all suffering; the intention does not cease with these aforementioned seven matters.
△ Second, the simultaneous demonstration of prostration and recitation has two parts: first, the benefit of mindful reverence; second, the benefit of prostration and offering. Now, the first.
If there are sentient beings who abound in lustful desire... (up to) "for this reason, sentient beings should constantly maintain mindfulness in their minds.

The heading says "Constant Mindfulness," and the conclusion says "should constantly maintain mindfulness in their minds. This expands upon the previous [section on] "Sublime Sound," which employed only the wheel of the body (*kāyacakra*) for the sake of gathering and transforming beings.
Now, in revealing Avalokiteśvara, it is augmented by the wheel of the mind (*manas-cakra*) to reach out to all things. Furthermore, compared to the previous [method] which used only...

The wheel of speech is beset by seven difficulties, and the mind is likewise not uniform. Sentient beings with excessive lust have, since beginningless time, conjoined their habitual desires with sensory objects;

thus they are ravaged by forms. Now, through the power bestowed by the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of hearing to detach from objects, the sense organs and their objects no longer meet, and the craving of desire is dried up.
Hatred arises when sensory objects conflict with one's emotions; now...
Regarding the Bodhisattva: because they are empowered by the force of the perfect fusion of faculties and objects, wherein there is neither subject nor object, they do not give rise to anger.
As for delusion, it arises from being obscured by false sensory objects and shrouded by ignorance; thus, it is prevalent.

Herein, the Bodhisattva, through the power of dissolving these objects and returning to luminous clarity and unimpededness, is able to depart from delusion. This concludes the section on majestic spiritual power.

Regarding "Powerful and Superior": To add one more point, when one observes that the internal delusions of sentient beings and external obstacles are difficult to eliminate, it is absolutely impossible to repel them without possessing vast and great supernormal powers (*mahā-rddhibala*). △ Second, the benefits of prostration and offerings.
If there are women who wish to obtain a son (up to the point mentioned), they should all uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Those seeking a son shall, by virtue of the Bodhisattva’s merit—having manifested a transformed body to engage with the world, having served all Buddhas as a Prince of the Dharma, and having pervaded the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—immediately give birth to a son upon their request. Furthermore, this is because he upholds and accords with the secret [teachings].
One receives the virtue of being free from error, which also extends throughout the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), thereby enabling those who seek it to immediately obtain a daughter;

thus, this is even more sublime than the *Sudhana-śrī* (Wondrous Sound). Regarding the concluding words, the initial homage to the body wheel reflects the seven difficulties, the three poisons, and the two types of seeking mentioned above;
all of these demonstrate how the Bodhisattva, through the three wheels, responds to the responses of the three karmas. Next, furthermore...
The concluding exhortation to those who hold the Name clearly reveals that the contemplation of the Dharmakāya through the Universal Gate is entirely not outside the scope of the *prajñā* of words.
Thus, the single practice of holding the Name is the most direct and expedient dharma-gate for escaping suffering and attaining bliss.
△ Third, citing others to demonstrate its superiority.

Akṣayamati, if there is someone who upholds [this teaching]—up to—the benefit of immeasurable and boundless merit, such that the merit of upholding many names is equal to the merit of upholding a single name, it is because the Bodhisattva has attained true and perfect penetration within the Sahā world as his practice;
therefore, he attains the equality of the one and the many. △ Second. [Section Two]
Section Two: Questions and Answers. First, the question; second, the answer. Now, the first:
Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “[... up to ... What are the matters concerning the power of skillful means?”

The previous answer concerned the names of persons. Because the Bodhisattva responds to the stimuli of the three karmas through the integration of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), he explains the reason for his names by means of the Universal Gate Dharma (*samantamukha-dharma*).
Hereafter, the person is manifested by way of the Dharma; even if the capacity for response (*indriya*) were not stimulated, [the Dharma would still be revealed].
It is specifically because the Great Being’s function pervades everywhere in accordance with its essence; like the moon in the sky, its light also pervades everywhere accordingly.

Thus, when encountering latent goodness, at the moment when superior understanding (*adhimukti*) manifests in full, this is precisely the time of the secret resonance between mind and sound, like the appearance of the moon when the water is clear.
For this reason, he manifests his body, displaying the responses of the three wheels, skillfully accommodating the capacities and needs of beings as he appears.

He preaches the Dharma, yet all is accomplished without any private self-interest; with this he answers the question. △ Second, the answer has three parts: first, responding to the capacity of beings through wandering and transformation; second, extolling virtues to encourage offerings; third, concluding by manifesting sovereign mastery. Now, the first part: The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "What do you think? If there were a man who, for the sake of his parents, were to build a great stūpa made of the seven precious substances, as high as Sumeru, and if he were to offer incense, flowers, banners, canopies, music, and various delicacies to that stūpa for a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas—would that man, because of this, generate much merit? Śāriputra replied to the Buddha: "Indeed, World-Honored One, that person would generate immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "If a good man or a good woman hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and, having heard it, accepts it with faith, understands it, and practices according to its teachings, the merit they generate will be even greater than that. Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have all emerged from this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as all the rivers, streams, and springs in Jambudvīpa ultimately flow into the great ocean, so too, Śāriputra, all the various dharmas practiced by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ultimately lead to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as all the grasses, trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs in Jambudvīpa rely upon the earth to grow, so too, Śāriputra, all the various dharmas practiced by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas rely upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to attain their realization. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the great ocean is the king of all waters, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the king of all sutras. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as Mount Sumeru is the king of all mountains, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the king of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the sun is the king of all luminaries, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the king of all teachings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the moon is the king of all stars, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the king of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the great Brahmā King is the lord of all the gods of the desire realm, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the great Indra King is the lord of the thirty-three heavens, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Vaiśravaṇa King is the lord of the yakṣas, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Four Heavenly Kings are the lords of all the gods of the four quarters, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas.

Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is the lord of all bodhisattvas, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the lord of all dharmas, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the lord of all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the father of all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the father of all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the teacher of all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the teacher of all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the refuge of all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the refuge of all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the ultimate reliance of all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the ultimate reliance of all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most honored among all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most honored among all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most venerable among all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most venerable among all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most worthy of offerings among all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most worthy of offerings among all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most difficult to encounter among all sentient beings, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to encounter among all dharmas. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most rare in the world, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most rare in the world. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most difficult to please in the world, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to please in the world. Śāriputra, it is like this: just as the Tathāgata is the most difficult to serve in the world, so too, Śāriputra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍ
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to the point where he) travels through various lands to deliver sentient beings.
From this point downward, in each section, the six characters "should manifest in accordance with [the needs] to preach the Dharma" are used to answer the questions regarding the three karmas.

Thus, the two characters "should manifest in accordance with" (yīng yǐ) specifically refer to the mental karma (*manas-karman*) of the Great Being, serving as the skillful means for discerning and responding to hidden resonances.
This is why he is able to manifest his body: because the Great Being shares the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata, his body becomes a wondrous response, entering all lands.
However, regarding the number and types of bodies explained in this sutra compared to those in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra—
Regarding the mutual variations in expansion and contraction, the formal exposition of the four and eight [bodies] is not the ultimate teaching.
One must follow the conclusion of the subsequent text, which describes how [the Buddha] "travels through various lands in manifold forms," to fully encompass all categories.
Now, examining the manifested bodies and the teachings spoken, there should be four permutations for each: namely, first, with one body...
First, responding to a single capacity with a single body; second, responding to multiple capacities with a single body; third, responding to a single capacity with multiple bodies;
and fourth, responding to multiple capacities with multiple bodies. Thus, the first three phrases refer to sequential manifestation, while the fourth phrase refers to simultaneous manifestation.
The teachings he expounds should likewise consist of four such phrases, which may be understood by analogy with the above. Now, regarding this sutra...
Regarding what is clarified here: there is only the first phrase; the remaining three phrases are all contained within the concluding text.

One must understand that the "body" elucidated in this passage is truly but a single grain within the vast granary of the Dharma-realm. Now, first, I shall briefly indicate the general outline of the Buddha-body.
Within the ten dharma realms, none is more supreme or extraordinary than the Buddha-body; therefore, regarding the six...
On the path, there are places other than those of humans and devas where it is unfit to set foot.

Furthermore, since humans and devas differ in category and their karma is as diverse as the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha-bodies they perceive likewise vary in excellence and inferiority in many ways. Thus, the sutras contain the analogy of the elephant and the blind men;
for instance, in the Hinayana teachings, the Buddha-body perceived by a person who has first resolved to attain enlightenment must be inferior [to that perceived by others].
Regarding the initial orientation: as one gradually ascends from this initial orientation, even the vision attained at the stage of the four fruits is inferior to that of the beginning;
how much more so for the subsequent teachings, each of which possesses its own gradations of the three worthies and ten sages?

Since this single Buddha-body already contains such various levels of progressive advancement, the rest may be inferred by analogy. Question: Let us set aside the fundamental nature of the Great Being for a moment; consider only...
Regarding the manifestation of the present traces: within the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), is the body manifested therein also benefited by that Equal Enlightenment?
Answer: It is both benefited and not benefited. As for that which is not benefited: in proclaiming the transformation of the Dharma, they act together to benefit sentient beings.
As for that which is benefited: the great ocean does not refuse even a tiny stream; thus, the World-Honored One does not abandon even the minute merit of threading a needle, let alone [greater acts].

Regarding those who are superior: among the four types of noble ones (*ārya*), the bodies of bodhisattvas are omitted briefly; the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary beings) are combined with the *pratyekabuddha* as one category.
As for the manifestation of the śrāvaka, in all cases it is through "inner secrecy and outer manifestation," using skillful means (*upāya*) to lead toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).

The following cases are all analogous to this. Among the six classes of ordinary beings, the Brahmā king is first mentioned because he possesses the dharma of speech and is able to govern those above him.
Below the crown [of the head], he is the lord of the trichiliocosm; thus Śakra is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

Furthermore, as he is equal to the Brahmā King and constantly follows the Buddha, he is mentioned first among them. Īśvara is the lord of the desire realm, while Maheśvara is the lord of the form realm.
This clarifies that even the bodies of the deities at the summit of the two realms are merely manifested forms;

how much more so for the celestial generals who govern them, such as Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of the Four Heavenly Kings, who leads spirits and ghosts. These all manifest superior forms while their subordinates manifest inferior ones.
This is the principle of "the wind blowing and the grass bending," where the superior leads the subordinate. The same applies to those below. Among kings and ministers— [End of excerpt]
Regarding the statement that "the universal monarchs and others are not mentioned": this implies that even the bodies of minor kings are seen to manifest, let alone those of greater rank;
this is the intended meaning of the inverted inclusion. "The Elder" is as explained previously.

One who possesses the ten virtues refers to a layperson who abides in the Way, a high official who can assist his superior and adjudicate cases for his subordinates, and a Brahmin who gathers followers through ritual arts and calculations.
They are practitioners of purity who have entered the fourfold assembly of the Path; all are those who uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Manifesting in female forms, they transform and guide those within the domestic sphere. Boys and girls are those who preserve the Great Harmony and do not lose their innate truthfulness;

dwelling in pure integrity, they do not seek out aggression or violence. Among the eight classes of beings, these are the "non-humans" (amanuṣya); they correspond to those above, reaching up to the Formless Realm.
Reaching down to the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), these are contained within the text but not explicitly revealed.
As for the Vajrapāṇi: in Sanskrit, *vajra* means "diamond" (or "thunderbolt") and *pāṇi* means "hand. Thus, he is one who holds a vajra in his hand;
he has vowed to act as the Dharma-protecting deity of the thousand Buddhas. Regarding the statement that he can manifest various bodies: by means of diverse forms, those who are transformed...

Regarding the "objects" (境), it refers to all lands (*kṣetra*). This collectively manifests their vastness, multiplicity, and inconceivability. The bodies that perform the transformation have already been briefly explained above.
As for the lands that are transformed, as cited in the *Huìxuán* from the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the lands within the void are more numerous than the atoms of a great trichiliocosm;
yet, because their karmic actions differ, they do not [interfere with one another].

Furthermore, as for the substance of the land, where the marks of defilement and purity are exhausted and it is inherently sovereign, it enables those who behold it—whether they be the four types of noble ones—to see four lands within a single land;
and whether they be the six classes of ordinary beings, each perceives and knows this according to their own individual capacity.
None of these fall outside the scope of the Universal Gate’s gathering and transformation. II. Exhorting Offerings by Citing Virtues (in four parts). First, Receiving... [text continues]

First, exhorting others to make offerings; second, making offerings by following a command; third, accepting an invitation to receive offerings; fourth, dedicating the merit to a superior field of merit.
Now, for the first: "Therefore, you all should with one mind... up to "...all shall be called those who bestow fearlessness."
The first phrase is a direct exhortation to make offerings. The section beginning with "This contemplation" explains the intent behind the exhortation to offer.

The section beginning with "Therefore" indicates that, based on the preceding discussion of the Universal Gate Dharma, Avalokiteśvara rescues beings from suffering upon hearing their cries; according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, this name was bestowed by an ancient Buddha.
Therefore, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Hereafter, the text again focuses on the Universal Gate (Pumen) Dharma;
within this world-system, he specializes in rescuing those in urgent distress. Thus, all sentient beings bestow upon him the title "One Who Bestows Fearlessness" (*abhaya-dātṛ*) to praise his virtue.
Consequently, the appellation "Bestower of Fearlessness" is uniquely and exclusively attributed to him in the Sahā world. △ Second, the Offering.
[The Buddha] commanded that an offering be made.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “[He] shall accept this precious necklace as a gift of Dharma.
To provide for this with the wealth of the necklace is what is called a ‘gift of Dharma. It originates from the wondrous wisdom of the inexhaustible Middle Way.”
Because it is that which is produced; furthermore, because its very substance is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). △ Third, not accepting the exhortation to accept:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... [down to] ...humans and non-humans, etc., accepted this necklace.
Regarding "not accepting": the intention is that since you have been commanded to perform the offering while I have not yet received such an order, how could I dare to accept it rashly?
Moreover, the Most Honored One is present before us; therefore, he declined it. As for the repeated statement, "Have compassion on us," this means:

because I am compassionate toward the assembly regarding their giving, you, O Benevolent One, must likewise be compassionate toward the assembly regarding your receiving. Thus, the Buddha also encourages [the act] by taking compassion for the assembly as his motive. This is the ultimate universal [principle].
Within the Dharma-gate, there is absolutely no characteristic of equanimity; yet, this does not obstruct the fact that characteristics are themselves non-characteristics.
Therefore, it does not preclude the existence of sensation for sentient beings. △ Fourth, dedication to the supreme field of merit.
At that moment, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva... [up to] ...offered one part to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
By turning back all subtle causes, they together proceeded toward the supreme fruit. △ Third, the conclusion revealing sovereign mastery.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Infinite Intent... travels throughout the Sahā world. △ Part Two:
The Verses, which has two sections. First, the praise and inquiry; second, the verse response. Now, the first section.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:
"World-Honored One, you are endowed with wondrous marks; I now ask again: for what causes and conditions is that Son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?"

The two characters "repeatedly asked" (*chóngwèn*) simultaneously encompass the aforementioned inquiries regarding names and the intent behind the travels, etc. Because he wishes to introduce the following text, he first asks about the conditions (*yuán*).

First, a general presentation of the practices and vows; second, a specific manifestation according to the capacities of sentient beings. Now, for the first:
"Listen well to the practices of Avalokiteśvara... [down to] ...the mental recitation is never in vain, for it can extinguish all suffering within the realms of existence."

The practices and vows each consist of two aspects. That is to say, "skillful response" refers to the practice of benefiting others, while "serving the Buddhas" refers to the practice of self-benefit.
"Vows" refers both to the Four Great Vows initially undertaken and to the subsequent vows made continuously as one serves successive Buddhas.
As for "skillful response," it is like a great bell suspended upon its stand: whether the sound is small or large, it issues forth entirely according to how it is struck.

Spontaneously free from mind, the two responses—hidden and manifest—of the Universal Gate are like this. △ Second, specifically revealing [the response] according to the capacities of sentient beings, in two parts:
first, a verse on the initial answer; second, a verse on the subsequent answer. Now, the first.
"Even if one should give rise to harmful intent... (up to)... by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, it shall be dispersed at that very moment.
This consists of twelve verses, distinguished as both *saṃgīti* (repetitive) and *udāna* (isolated) verses, which are self-evident from the text itself.

Regarding the "that" in "recollecting that," it does not seem to refer to the "this" versus "that" dichotomy; rather, when a great calamity confronts one and one seeks refuge, there is simply nothing more urgent.
With single-minded recollection of the Holy Name, the Great Being’s compassion immediately rescues one’s own heart and mouth;

how, then, could there be any distinction between self and other? When the Buddha says that by recollecting him one is liberated from suffering, he is describing the swiftness of his spiritual response.
Mount Sumeru’s peaks and the Diamond Mountains are all metaphorical expressions intended to manifest their height and solidity; they are the places where people are most easily harmed.
That these [metaphors] instead apply to the person themselves is likely to wither their evil thoughts before they have even taken root.

The ancients said that the reason a Great Being (Mahāsattva) is able to save universally is because both the primary and secondary worlds (the sentient and the insentient) are all the wondrous form of the Great Being.
Wondrous Mind! All sentient beings create obstacles for themselves regarding the sacred form and mind; their cry for salvation is itself the three karmas of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
Therefore, there is a response whenever there is a resonance. Furthermore, as previously stated, "transforming even insects" refers to species such as vipers, snakes, adders, and scorpions.
△ Second, the verse that answers the second [question] in sequence. First, following the previous [section], the formal [response].
Verse: A double praise of compassion and wisdom. Now, the first [part]:
"Sentient beings are beset by calamities... [until] gradually causing them all to extinguish the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
The first verse concludes the preceding section. It reveals that the minds of sentient beings are stirred by the three poisons and their bodies are constrained by the bonds of karma;
thus, they are brought to suffering and affliction. The Great Being, through the wondrous wisdom that afflictions are themselves bodhi, [responds].

The outflow of great compassion of identical essence saves sentient beings who are its own self-nature. This is fully contained within the following two verses, which provide a brief answer to the subsequent question.
Since the scope of its universal pervasion and sovereign mastery have already been detailed in the preceding text, they are not repeated here. II. A Double Praise of Compassion and Wisdom. A.
Praising the Essence of Compassion and Wisdom. B. Praising the Function of Compassion and Wisdom. Now, the first part: Praising the Essence of Compassion and Wisdom.
"True contemplation, pure contemplation, vast wisdom contemplation, compassionate contemplation, and loving-kindness contemplation—may I always aspire to and constantly gaze upon them.
The first half praises wisdom; the second half praises compassion. These two are the foremost virtues arising from within the mind of contemplation.
Regarding the first, it refers to the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, which necessarily flows forth from the non-delusive ultimate truth; therefore, it is called "true."
Furthermore, because this wisdom-nature is not a defiled dharma, it is called "pure. Because it fundamentally pervades the Dharma-realm, it is called "vast.
It is thus both three and one; it is the contemplative essence that universally illumines the Three Truths.

The second half [of the verse] reveals that within this contemplation there further exists the sublime merit of benefiting sentient beings in two ways. Therefore, all sentient beings should constantly...
Constantly recite his name and cultivate the practice of gazing up with reverence. △ Second, praising the function of compassion and wisdom:
"Stainless and pure light... by mindfulness of that Avalokiteśvara’s power, all enemies shall retreat and scatter."
The preceding verse reveals the virtues of the essence itself; from here on, it reveals its functions in relation to external objects.

Thus it says, "shattering darkness, removing calamities, extinguishing flames," and so forth, thereby manifesting the functions of compassion and wisdom. Question: According to the praise of the essence, wisdom possesses three meanings.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) has two meanings. Here, we employ the meaning of "middle wisdom" (*madhyama-prajñā*). Furthermore, there is "stainless compassion" (*vimala-karuṇā*), which carries the sense of thunder and rain.
Why, then, does this section speak only of praising compassion and wisdom? Answer: Among the myriad virtues of the Sage, compassion and wisdom are universally primary.
If one discusses virtues by taking wisdom as the gateway, then all [virtues] are wisdom. Other meanings are like space; [compassion] is taken as... [the basis].
The same applies to the "Gate. The single verse on "Contention" further explains the "Blaze of Afflictions.
This refers to when worldly people are entangled in public courts, standing on the edge of battlefields, their minds anxious over legal punishments and their lives threatened by military slaughter;

when past and present grievances converge all at once, this is precisely the state where afflictions burn fiercely like a raging conflagration. If such conditions can still evoke a sense of spiritual resonance, how much more so [should one feel it] in other circumstances?
He. △ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to pay homage and recite the name, in two parts: first, praising the name to exhort recitation; second, praising the virtues to exhort homage.
Now, the first:
"The One of Wondrous Voice, the Observer of the World’s Sounds" (throughout), "therefore one must constantly recite his name at every thought and not give rise to doubt."
The Great Being invokes names of virtue; there must indeed be immeasurable Buddhas. To praise them by way of five meanings is merely to allow one to see a single aspect.
However, sound is the object of contemplation; because object and wisdom are fused, both subject and object vanish.
Thus, by using the object of contemplation to praise the contemplating subject, he demonstrates that it is "mind-only," so that one may know that mind and its objects are but one.

It does not miss its appointed time; thus it may be called the "Sound of the Ocean Tide. Fifth, because it transcends the nine realms, it is called "Superior to the Sounds of the World.
Furthermore, among these five qualities, the mention of any single one encompasses the remaining four and all virtues, as they all converge therein.
If sentient beings take mindfulness as the Dharma-realm, then the merits of all sages and worthies—none [will fail to be attained].

There is no other dharma whatsoever apart from these different realms of existence; how much less so for this Great Being? If one can develop deep faith and patient acceptance, one may sever all doubts and hesitations.
If one maintains this continuity from moment to moment without interruption, what suffering will not be transcended, and what joy will not be attained?
It is simply essential not to give rise to doubt or confusion; therefore, at the very end, the single word "Do Not" is used to prune away and warn against it. II. Praise.
Virtue encourages reverence.
Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One (up to) "an immeasurable ocean of masses of merit"—therefore, one should prostrate to him.

To completely extinguish all defilements is called "Pure" (*viśuddha*); to reach the ultimate stage is called "Holy" (*ārya*). This is the designation received based on the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Regarding the section on suffering: it concerns the bestowal of grace upon sentient beings.

Like compassionate parents who act as a refuge, like a wish-fulfilling jewel endowed with all virtues, they regard the great earth with compassion as if looking upon an only child fallen into a place of suffering.
To summarize: the Great Being is a mass of merit, whose height is difficult to gaze upon; he is an ocean of wisdom, difficult to fathom.
Because it is so profound, I, with an expansive and unerring sincerity, exhort all sentient beings: you should single-mindedly prostrate yourselves before it.
Whatever you seek, you shall surely obtain as you wish. △ Third, the benefits gained from hearing this chapter, in two parts: first, praising those who hear this chapter;
second, concluding with the benefits of generating the resolve. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara... [omitted] ...one should know that this person’s merit is not small.

When he had finished speaking, Dharaṇīdhara emerged to offer praise. This was because the practice of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) upholding the sutra and the conduct of Dharaṇīdhara were equal.
That is to say, after Dharaṇīdhara had attained the "Level Mind Ground" (*sama-citta-bhūmi*) from the presence of Vipaśyin Tathāgata, he contemplated all...

Whether sentient beings arise [in delusion] or fall into inversion, they are all sustained by the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*). Those who are able to advance toward the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) are certainly included within its embrace;

even those who turn their backs on it and stray onto divergent paths remain within the reach of its unconditional great compassion (*nirālambana-mahākaruṇā*), for turning away or turning toward, as well as arising or falling into inversion, are fundamentally of one and the same nature.
Thus, the Earth-Holding One (*Dharaṇīdhara*) did not praise the person or the Dharma of the Universal Gate.

Yet, it specifically extols those who are able to hear; this is precisely because the extolling is profound. Since the Dharma of Universal Excellence has entered their ears through its extraordinary merit, the resulting virtue is not small.
△ Second, the conclusion on the benefits of generating the aspiration for enlightenment.

Since the holy teachings were transmitted to the East and the Semblance Dharma first appeared, their influence has spread far and wide; those who have benefited from them fill the land within the seas.
Since the Six Dynasties, the famous monasteries of Jinling have stood as closely packed as the teeth of a comb, and the study of Buddhist doctrine has flourished.
Among them was my late High Ancestor, Great Master Xuelang, who succeeded to the lineage of the Elder Wujie of Tientai and inherited the twenty-third generation of the Xianshou school.

He propagated the Way of the Dharma and continued the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom. Subsequently, there appeared the successive generations of ancestors, including Yuyu, Yunpo, Bi, Kongyue, and Tantong.
Following them, he finally met the patriarch Pude, who governed the wheel of great vows and strove mightily to propagate the vehicle of the teachings.
Consequently, the school of Xianshou was for a time revered throughout the land as a light of restoration, and those who received its instruction—

The number of those who sought instruction was so great that one’s fingers could not count them all. Among the disciples of this Great Master of the Supreme Vehicle, [the author] was the very last to receive his personal guidance.

Yet, before long, he was able to conceal his brilliance and withdraw from the limelight to investigate the most profound mysteries. He transcribed palm-leaf manuscripts upon his own conch-shell-like hair-tufts and collated the catalogues of the Tripiṭaka within the mountain valleys.

Disregarding the passage of seasons—whether cold or warm—he nearly forgot both sleep and food. When the Patriarch passed away, his fellow practitioners successively took up the seat, continuing down to the present day.

Regarding his master, he repaired what was old and augmented what was new; there were no matters concerning the permanent endowments (*sangha-sthiti*) that remained unfinished which he did not carry out with all his might.

He poured forth his very heart's blood; were it not for one who practiced exactly as he preached, how could he have reached such a state? (De) Formerly, he admired the single school of Ci'en in Jiangnan.

Preface. (De) I consider that among all the teachings of a single lifetime, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* alone is able to encompass the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata’s employment of expedient means (*upāya*) for the purpose of harmonizing and guiding sentient beings;
it is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand. In the past, when my late grandfather Pude lectured on this sūtra, he would sigh three times upon reaching the scroll.

He established a new structural outline (*ko-wen*), systematically classifying the seven fascicles, and by tracing the profound mysteries and unraveling the obscure, he completely washed away the stale conventions of former interpretations. And...
The Master then continued and expounded upon their essential teachings, refuting the confusions and errors of recent generations and resolving the doubtful cases of a thousand ages.
He caused the single source of the worthy ones to flow as drop by drop of true milk, like pouring nectar from the center of the heavens, and erected a guiding compass at the crossroads.
Not a single word or character has emerged from my own breast; it is titled *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), for there is a specific reason for this.

There is one fascicle each for the topical outline (*kepan*) and the introductory discourse (*xuantan*), and eight fascicles for the commentary (*shu*). Those who read this commentary should first investigate the fundamental intention of the Original Buddha, which he long maintained in silence.
